en: [Auspiciousness] [1.i]:

He who, having abandoned his primordial form, manifests in manifold ways for the sake of favoring the world—he whose mass of afflictions is utterly destroyed, who is like a serpent with virulent venom, who possesses many faces, and who is endowed with sublime enjoyments; [to him I bow].

May that Lord of Serpents, from whom all knowledge is born, who is eternally delighted by his serpent-retinue, whose body is white and stainless, who bestows yoga and is himself united with yoga, protect you.
The First Chapter: On Concentration [1,ii] "Now, the instruction on yoga" (1.1).

[1, iii] Now, the word "atha" (now) has the sense of introducing a topic (*adhikāra*). It should be understood that the treatise (*śāstra*) concerning the instruction on yoga (*yogānuśāsana*) is hereby commenced. Yoga is *samādhi* (concentration). And that is a quality (*dharma*) of the mind (*citta*) that pertains to all stages (*sārvabhauma*). <2> The stages of the mind (*cittabhūmi*) are: the distracted (*kṣipta*), the stupefied (*mūḍha*), the scattered (*vikṣipta*), the one-pointed (*ekāgra*), and the restrained (*niruddha*). Among these, concentration existing in a distracted mind, being subordinate to distraction, does not belong to the category of yoga. [3, i]

But that which, when the mind is one-pointed, illuminates the true object, attenuates the afflictions, loosens the bonds of karma, and brings cessation (*nirodha*) face-to-face, is called "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) yoga. We shall explain later that this is accompanied by initial thought (*vitarka*), sustained thought (*vicāra*), joy (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*). However, when all fluctuations have ceased, it is "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi. With the desire to state its definition, this aphorism was composed: [YS 1.2] *vyutthānanirodhasaṃskārayor abhibhavaprādurbhāvau nirodhakṣaṇacittānvayo nirodhapariṇāmaḥ* // 3 // [The transformation of cessation is the sequence of moments of the mind, characterized by the suppression of the subliminal impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the subliminal impressions of cessation.]
[4,ii] “Yoga is the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind” (1.2).
[4,iii]

Because all sounds are no longer perceived, even this state is designated as *saṃprajñāta-yoga*. For the mind (*citta*) consists of the three *guṇas*, owing to its nature of luminosity (*prakhyā*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and stability (*sthiti*).

Indeed, the *sattva* of the mind, whose form is luminosity, when conjoined with *rajas* and *tamas*, becomes fond of sovereignty and objects of sense. That same [mind], when permeated by *tamas*, becomes possessed of unrighteousness (*adharma*), ignorance (*ajñāna*), lack of dispassion (*avairāgya*), and lack of sovereignty (*anaiśvarya*). That very same [mind], when the veil of delusion (*moha*) has been destroyed and it is shining forth on all sides, being permeated only by a trace of *rajas*, becomes possessed of righteousness (*dharma*), knowledge (*jñāna*), dispassion (*vairāgya*), and sovereignty (*aiśvarya*).

[5,i] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle. It is also called ‘The Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas,’ and it is also called ‘The Perfection of Wisdom. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With that, the Venerable Ānanda and the Venerable Śāriputra, as well as the entire assembly and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Blessed One had spoken. That very [mind], when freed from even the slightest speck of impurity, becomes established in its own nature, consisting solely of the discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) between the intellect (*sattva*) and the Self (*puruṣa*), and attains the meditation known as the "Cloud of Virtue" (*dharmamegha*). Meditators call that the supreme *prasaṃkhyāna*. The power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) is unchanging, non-transmigrating, has objects presented to it, is pure, infinite, and consists of the quality of *sattva*. Discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), however, is the opposite of this. Therefore, the mind, becoming detached even from that discernment, suppresses it as well. In that state, it becomes a mere residue of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*). That is seedless concentration (*nirbīja-samādhi*). Because nothing is cognized therein, it is called "non-cognitive" (*asaṃprajñāta*). Thus, Yoga is twofold: the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind.
[7,i] When the mind is in that state, since there is an absence of objects, what is the essential nature of the Puruṣa, whose essence is the awareness of cognition? —
"Then there is the establishment of the seer in his own nature" (1.3).

At that time, the power of consciousness is established in its own nature, just as in the state of isolation (*kaivalya*). However, while the mind is in a state of emergence (*vyutthāna*), even though it exists in that same way, it does not exist in that same way.
[7,iv] How then? Because its object has been demonstrated—

"Similarity of modification in other cases" (1.4). During emergence (*vyutthāna*), the Puruṣa possesses a modification that is not distinct from those modifications of the mind. And thus the Sūtra says: "The seeing is one alone; the seeing is indeed manifestation (*khyāti*). The mind, which is like a magnet, assists by its mere proximity and becomes the object of perception for the Lord, the Puruṣa. Therefore, the cause of the Puruṣa’s awareness of the mental modifications is an beginningless connection.
Furthermore, those [mental factors] are to be ceased when there is multiplicity of mind—
The fluctuations are of five kinds, both afflicted and unafflicted.

Those [modifications] caused by the afflictions (*kleśa*), which serve as the field for the accumulation of the latent deposits of karma (*karmāśaya*), are afflicted (*kliṣṭa*). Those whose objects are discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) and which oppose the mandate of the *guṇas* are unafflicted (*akliṣṭa*). Even those falling within the stream of the afflicted are unafflicted; unafflicted modifications occur even during the intervals of the afflicted, and afflicted ones occur during the intervals of the unafflicted. It is by means of these modifications alone that such formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) are produced, and by means of those formative impressions, the modifications [are produced]. In this way, the wheel of modification and formative impression revolves incessantly. When the mind has thus reached the end of its mandate, it either remains in a state resembling the Self or undergoes dissolution. These are the fivefold modifications, both afflicted and unafflicted.
[10,i] “Valid cognition, error, conceptual construction, sleep, and memory” (1.6) [10,ii]
"Perception, inference, and verbal testimony are the means of valid cognition" (1.7).

[11,i] Perception is the cognitive modification (*vṛtti*) of the mind, primarily characterized by the ascertainment of the specific features of an object—which consists of both the universal and the particular—arising from the coloring of the mind by external things through the channel of the senses. The result [of this process] is the unqualified awareness of the mental modification by the Puruṣa. We shall demonstrate later that the Puruṣa is the experiencer.

[11,ii] The second section concerns the nature of the object of knowledge. It is as follows: "The nature of the object of knowledge consists of the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected. This means that the nature of the object of knowledge is established by way of three natures: the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Among these, the imagined nature is the appearance of the duality of grasper and grasped within the dependent nature; it is so called because it is merely imagined and does not exist as a real entity. The dependent nature is the very basis upon which that duality is imagined; it is so called because it arises in dependence upon other conditions. The perfected nature is the state of the dependent nature being eternally free from the imagined nature; it is so called because it is the ultimate reality, unchanging and perfectly accomplished. Thus, the nature of the object of knowledge is established through these three natures. Furthermore, this is taught in the *Mahāyānasūtrālaṃkāra*, where it is said: "The object of knowledge is the three natures: the imagined, the dependent, and the perfected. This is the meaning. This concludes the second section.

Inference (*anumāna*) is a cognitive process whose primary function is the ascertainment of a generality, having as its object a relationship that follows after things of a similar class and is excluded from things of a different class regarding the subject of inference. For example: "The moon and stars possess motion because they reach other locations, like Caitra; whereas the Vindhya mountain does not reach [other locations] and thus lacks motion. Scriptural testimony (*āgama*) is the cognitive process of a listener arising from a word, directed toward an object, which is taught by means of a word by a trustworthy person (*āpta*)—who has either perceived or inferred the object—for the sake of transferring his own understanding to another. That scriptural testimony is unreliable (*plavate*) whose speaker is untrustworthy and has neither perceived nor inferred the object. However, when the original speaker has perceived or inferred the object, the testimony is free from error.
"Error is false cognition not established in that form.

Why is that not a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*)? Because it is sublated by a valid means of knowledge, since a valid means of knowledge has as its object a thing as it truly is (*bhūtārtha*). In this regard, the sublation of an invalid means of knowledge by a valid one is observed; for example, the perception of two moons is sublated by the perception of one moon, which corresponds to the actual state of affairs. This ignorance (*avidyā*) consists of five sections: ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and the will to live. These very same factors are designated by their own specific names as darkness (*tamas*), delusion (*moha*), great delusion (*mahāmoha*), gloom (*tāmisra*), and utter gloom (*andhatāmisra*). These will be discussed in connection with the impurities of the mind (*cittamala*).
"Conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is that which follows upon the cognition of words and is devoid of a real object" (YS 1.9).

It does not subsume under the category of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), nor does it subsume under the category of error (*viparyaya*). Even though it is devoid of a real object, a linguistic convention (*vyavahāra*) is observed based on the power of verbal cognition. For example: "Consciousness (*caitanya*) is the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the person (*puruṣa*). Since the person is nothing other than consciousness itself, what is being designated here by what?

[14,i] Furthermore, there is usage in verbal designation, as in "Caitra’s cow. Likewise, when it is said, "The person is inactive, having the nature of a negated entity," or "The arrow stands, will stand, has stood,"—in the cessation of motion, only the meaning of the verbal root is understood. Similarly, in the statement "the person has the nature of non-arising," only the absence of the property of arising is apprehended, not a property inherent to the person. Therefore, that property is conceptually constructed, and through it, linguistic convention exists.
"Sleep is a mental modification whose object is the notion of non-existence.
(Yoga Sūtra 1.10) [15,ii]

And that [sleep] is a specific mental modification (*pratyayaviśeṣa*), because upon awakening there is a reflective awareness (*pratyavamarśa*). How so? "I slept happily; my mind was serene; it makes my wisdom confident. "I slept painfully; my mind was sluggish, wandering, and unsettled; I slept in a deep stupor; my limbs were heavy; my mind was exhausted; it remains listless, as if stolen away. Indeed, this reflective awareness of one who has awakened would not exist if there were no experience of a mental modification [during sleep], and consequently, the memories dependent upon it and having those [experiences] as their objects would not exist. Therefore, sleep is a specific mental modification. And it, like other modifications, must be restrained during meditative absorption (*samādhi*).
[16,i] "Memory is the non-forgetting of an experienced object" (1.11).

Does the cognition remember the cognition itself, or rather the object? The cognition, colored by the object and manifesting in the dual form of both the grasped and the grasping, initiates a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) of that same nature. That impression, when activated by its own manifestor, produces a memory of that very same form, consisting of both the grasped and the grasping.

In this context, cognition (*buddhi*) is preceded by the form of the apprehending subject (*grāhakākāra*), whereas memory (*smṛti*) is preceded by the form of the apprehended object (*grāhyākāra*). Furthermore, that [memory] is twofold: that in which the object to be remembered has been experienced (*bhāvitasmartavyā*) and that in which the object to be remembered has not been experienced (*abhāvitasmartavyā*). In a dream, it is that in which the object to be remembered has been experienced; at the time of waking, however, it is that in which the object to be remembered has not been experienced. All memories arise from the experience of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), error (*viparyaya*), conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), sleep (*nidrā*), and memory itself. And all these fluctuations (*vṛtti*) consist of pleasure, pain, and delusion (*moha*). Pleasure, pain, and delusion, moreover, are to be explained among the afflictions (*kleśa*): attachment (*rāga*) is that which underlies pleasure; aversion (*dveṣa*) is that which underlies pain; and delusion, furthermore, is ignorance (*avidyā*).
[17,i] All these fluctuations must be restrained. Upon their restraint, there arises either cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) or non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi.
Now, as to what the means for their cessation is:
"Their cessation is by means of practice and dispassion" (1.12).

[17.iv] The river of the mind flows in two directions: it flows toward the auspicious and it flows toward the evil. That which inclines toward isolation (*kaivalya*) and slopes toward the object of discernment (*viveka*) carries what is auspicious; that which inclines toward the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) and slopes away from the object of discernment carries what is evil. Therein, by means of dispassion (*vairāgya*), the stream of sense objects is blocked; by the practice of the vision of discernment (*viveka-darśana*), the stream of discernment is opened. Thus, the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind depends upon both. [17.v]
"In that regard, practice (*abhyāsa*) is the effort toward steadiness" (YS 1.13).

Steadiness (*sthiti*) is the state of the mind being free from fluctuations and flowing in a tranquil stream. Effort (*prayatna*) for that purpose is vigor (*vīrya*) or enthusiasm (*utsāha*). Practice (*abhyāsa*) is the performance of the means for attaining that, with the desire to bring it about.
"But that, when practiced for a long time, without interruption, and with reverence, becomes firmly established. (1.14)

Practiced for a long time, practiced without interruption, and practiced with reverence—accomplished through austerity, celibacy, knowledge, and faith—it becomes honored and firm in its foundation. This means that it is not immediately overcome by the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence from meditation; that is, its object is not swiftly suppressed. [18, iii] "Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the consciousness of mastery in one who is free from thirst for objects seen or heard of in tradition" (Yoga Sūtra 1.15).

[18.iv] Dispassion (*vairāgya*) is the state of mastery (*vaśīkārasaṃjñā*), which consists of effortless spontaneity (*anābhogātmikā*) and is devoid of anything to be rejected or accepted, arising through the power of discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyānabala*). This occurs when one is free from thirst for the objects of the seen world—namely women, food and drink, and power—and is likewise free from thirst for the objects of the revealed tradition (*ānuśravika*), such as attaining heaven, liberation from the body, or absorption into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*); even upon contact with divine or non-divine objects, the mind perceives the defects of sense-objects.
"That [is] dispassion toward the qualities, following upon the discernment of the Puruṣa" (1.16).

One who perceives the defects in objects seen or heard becomes dispassionate; through the practice of perceiving the *puruṣa*, his intellect is nourished by the discernment that results from its purification. Thus, he becomes dispassionate toward the *guṇas*, which possess the characteristics of both the manifest (*vyakta*) and the unmanifest (*avyakta*). These two constitute dispassion (*vairāgya*). Of these, the latter is merely the clarity of knowledge (*jñānaprasāda*). Upon the arising of this [dispassion], the yogi, having attained discriminative discernment (*pratyuditakhyāti*), thinks thus: "That which was to be attained has been attained; the afflictions (*kleśas*) that were to be exhausted have been exhausted; the transition of existence (*bhavasaṃkrama*), whose joints are firmly linked—by the non-interruption of which one is born after dying and dies after being born—that has been severed. Dispassion is the supreme limit of knowledge itself. For indeed, liberation (*kaivalya*) is inseparable from this very state.
[20,i] Now, since the mental fluctuations have been stilled by means of the two methods, how can it be called "cognitive" (*saṃprajñāta*) samādhi?
"Conscious concentration (*saṃprajñāta*) arises from following the forms of reasoning (*vitarka*), reflection (*vicāra*), bliss (*ānanda*), and the sense of self (*asmitā*) (YS 1.17).

Reasoning is the gross engagement of the mind with its object; reflection is the subtle [engagement]. Bliss is joy; the sense of self is the cognition of oneness. Among these, the first type of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) accompanied by all four is *savitarka* (with reasoning). The second, devoid of reasoning, is *savicāra* (with reflection). The third, devoid of reflection, is *sānanda* (with bliss). The fourth, devoid of those, is *asmitāmātra* (pure self-sense). All of these are concentrations that possess an object."
[21,ii] Now, as for the samādhi of non-discernment (asaṃprajñāta-samādhi), what is its means and what is its intrinsic nature?
"Preceded by the practice of the cognition of cessation, it is another [samādhi], wherein only residual impressions remain" (I.18).

When all mental fluctuations have subsided, that cessation of the mind, wherein only residual impressions remain, is *asaṃprajñāta* samādhi. The means to attain it is supreme detachment (*para-vairāgya*). Since practice directed toward an object is not suitable as a means to achieve that [state], a cognition of cessation—which has no objective referent—is made the object of focus. That [cognition] is devoid of any external object. Through the repeated practice of that, the mind becomes objectless, as if it had reached non-existence; this is seedless (*nirbīja*) *asaṃprajñāta* samādhi.

[22,i] This indeed is twofold: that which has skillful means as its condition and that which has existence as its condition. Among these, for yogins, there is that which has skillful means as its condition—[22,ii]
"For those who are merged in nature while in the disembodied state, the cause is existence" (YS 1.19).

For the disembodied gods (*videha*), existence is the cause. For they, by means of a mind that employs only its own residual impressions (*saṃskāra*), experience as if it were the state of isolation (*kaivalya*) and pass through the ripening of their own residual impressions of such a kind. Likewise, those merged in nature (*prakṛtilaya*)—when the mind has dissolved into nature while still possessing a mandate—experience as if it were the state of isolation, until the mind returns again under the influence of that mandate.
[23,i] "For others, it is preceded by faith, energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom" (1.20).

The means for yogins is faith (*śraddhā*). Faith is the clarity of the mind. For it protects the yogin like a virtuous mother. Indeed, in one who possesses faith and seeks discernment (*viveka*), vigor (*vīrya*) arises. In one whose vigor has arisen, mindfulness (*smṛti*) is established. When mindfulness is established, the mind, free from agitation, becomes concentrated (*samādhīyate*). For one whose mind is concentrated, the discernment of wisdom (*prajñā-viveka*) returns, by which one knows an object as it truly is. Through the practice of that and through detachment (*vairāgya*) from each respective object, non-cognitive (*asaṃprajñāta*) samādhi comes to be.

Indeed, those nine practitioners possess weak, middling, or superior means (*upāya*). Namely: weak means, middling means, and superior means. Among these, weak means is threefold: weak intensity (*saṃvega*), middling intensity, and intense intensity. Likewise for middling means, and likewise for superior means. Regarding those with superior means—[24,ii] "for those with intense intensity, [the result] is near" (1.21).
[24,iii] There is the attainment of meditative concentration and the fruit of meditative concentration.
"Because of being weak, moderate, or intense, there is a distinction even beyond that" (1.22).

That is to say: weak-intense, moderate-intense, and intense-intense. There is a distinction even beyond that. Due to those distinctions, for one with weak-intense urgency, the attainment of concentration and the fruit of concentration are near; for one with moderate-intense urgency, they are nearer; and for one with intense-intense urgency and intense means, the attainment of concentration and the fruit of concentration are nearest of all.
Is concentration most proximate through this alone? Or is there some other means for its attainment, or not?—
"Or, from devotion to the Lord (I.23).

Through such devotion—a specific form of worship—the Lord is won over and favors the practitioner by His mere will. From that mere will of the Lord, the yogi attains the closest proximity to *samādhi* and its fruit as well.
vi] Now, what is this so-called "Lord" (īśvara) who is distinct from primordial matter (pradhāna) and the individual soul (puruṣa)?—
"Īśvara is a distinct Puruṣa untouched by afflictions, actions, their fruitions, and their latent impressions" (YS 1.24).

[26,i] Ignorance and the like are the afflictions (*kleśa*). Wholesome and unwholesome deeds are actions (*karman*). Their result is fruition (*vipāka*). The latent dispositions (*āśaya*) are the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that correspond to those results. Although these reside in the mind (*manas*), they are attributed to the Puruṣa, for he is the experiencer of their results. Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master; so too, the Puruṣa who is untouched by such experience is the distinct Puruṣa known as Īśvara.

[26, ii] In that case, there must be many who have attained isolation (*kaivalya*) and are now *kevalins*. For they, having severed the three bonds, have attained isolation; yet the relationship of the Lord (*īśvara*) with those bonds has neither occurred in the past nor will it occur in the future. Just as for one who was previously liberated, a prior limit of bondage (*pūrvā bandhakoṭi*) is known, such is not the case for the Lord. Or, just as for one merged in primordial nature (*prakṛti*), a subsequent limit of bondage (*uttarā bandhakoṭi*) is conceivable, such is not the case for the Lord. He is eternally liberated and eternally the Lord. [27, i]

Is that eternal excellence of Īśvara, which arises from his appropriation of a preeminent essence (*prakṛṣṭasattva*), caused by something or is it without cause? The scripture (*śāstra*) is its cause.
But what is the cause of the scripture? It has the preeminent essence as its cause.

[28,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has taught as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has taught. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as an unarisen dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as an unarisen dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a non-arising dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a non-arising dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a non-cessation dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a non-cessation dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there anything that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that is neither defiled nor purified? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that is neither defiled nor purified. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to, that the Tathāgata is called a ‘Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Can the Tathāgata be seen by means of the possession of the marks of a great man? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. The Tathāgata cannot be seen by means of the possession of the marks of a great man. Why is that? Because what the Tathāgata has preached as the possession of the marks of a great man, that is itself no possession of marks. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the Jambudvīpa with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would that person on the basis of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, that person would produce a great deal of merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that which is called ‘merit’ is itself no merit. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill the four continents with the seven precious jewels and give them as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would that person on the basis of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, that person would produce a great deal of merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that which is called ‘merit’ is itself no merit. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a small chiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would that person on the basis of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, that person would produce a great deal of merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that which is called ‘merit’ is itself no merit. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a medium chiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would that person on the basis of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, that person would produce a great deal of merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that which is called ‘merit’ is itself no merit. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? If someone were to fill a great trichiliocosm with the seven precious jewels and give it as a gift to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, would that person on the basis of that produce much merit? Subhūti said: “Blessed One, that person would produce a great deal of merit. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, that which is called ‘merit’ is itself no merit. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because that which is called ‘merit’ is itself no merit that the Tathāgata has preached it as a great mass of merit. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Stream-enterer conceive the thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of Stream-entry’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of a Stream-enterer. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Once-returner conceive the thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of Once-returning’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of a Once-returner. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Non-returner conceive the thought: ‘I have attained the fruit of Non-returning’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of a Non-returner. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does an Arhat conceive the thought: ‘I have attained Arhatship’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of an Arhat. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Pratyekabuddha conceive the thought: ‘I have fully awakened to Pratyekabuddhahood’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of a Pratyekabuddha. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva conceive the thought: ‘I shall fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of a Bodhisattva. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Does a Tathāgata conceive the thought: ‘I have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, complete enlightenment’? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. Why is that? Because, Blessed One, there is no dharma whatsoever that attains the state of a Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that the Tathāgata is called a ‘Tathāgata. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, what do you think? Is there any dharma whatsoever that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that is not a dharma? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. There is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that is not a dharma. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because there is not even the slightest dharma that the Tathāgata has fully awakened to as a dharma that is not a dharma that the Tathāgata is called a ‘Tathāgata.’”

The relationship between these two—the excellence of scripture and the existence of Īśvara—is beginningless. From this [relationship] it follows that He is eternally the Lord and eternally liberated. Furthermore, His lordship is devoid of both equality and superiority. To begin with, His lordship cannot be surpassed by any other lordship; for whatever might surpass it would itself be that very lordship. Therefore, He in whom lordship reaches its ultimate limit is Īśvara. Nor is there any lordship equal to His. Why? Because when two equals simultaneously desire the same object—thinking, "Let this be new" and "Let this be old"—if one succeeds, the other's power of will (*prākāmya*) is frustrated, which entails a state of inferiority. And it is impossible for two equals to simultaneously obtain the same desired object, because the objects are mutually exclusive. Therefore, He alone whose lordship is free from both equality and superiority is Īśvara, and He is a specific kind of *puruṣa*.
Furthermore—
"In that regard, the seed of omniscience is unsurpassed" (1.25).

This—namely, the apprehension of the past, future, and present, whether individually or collectively, and of objects beyond the senses, whether small or great—is the seed of omniscience. Where this, as it increases, becomes unsurpassed, he is the omniscient one. There is a reaching of the limit of the seed of omniscience because it is subject to degrees of excellence, like a measure. He in whom there is the reaching of the limit of knowledge is the omniscient one; and he is a particular kind of person.

[30,i] Furthermore, since inference is exhausted by establishing only the universal (sāmānya), it is not capable of bringing about the cognition of particulars; therefore, the cognition of its specific names and so forth must be sought from scripture (*āgama*). Although there is no benefit for himself, its purpose is the benefit of living beings: "By means of the instruction on knowledge and virtue, I shall rescue transmigrating persons during the dissolution of the eon (*kalpa*) and the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*). And thus it has been said: "The primordial knower, the Blessed One, the supreme seer, having presided over a mind of emanation (*nirmāṇacitta*), out of compassion taught the system (*tantra*) to Āsuri, who desired to know it."
[31,i] This very one—
"He is the teacher even of the ancients, because he is not limited by time" (1.26).

For previous teachers are indeed limited by time; he, however, to whom time does not apply in its limiting sense, is the teacher even of the ancients. Just as he was established through the attainment of excellence at the beginning of this current creation, so too should he be understood to have been so established at the beginnings of all past creations.
[32,i] "The syllable *praṇava* is its designator" (1.27).

The Lord is the denoted object of the *praṇava*. Is its relationship as signifier and signified (*vācyavācakatva*) merely conventional (*saṃketakṛta*), or is it established by its very nature, like the light of a lamp?

The relationship between this denoted object and its designator is established. Convention (*saṃketa*), however, merely manifests the meaning that is already established for the Lord. Just as the relationship between father and son, which exists as it is, is made manifest by convention—such that "this is his father" and "this is his son"—so too, even in other creations (*sarga*), convention is established in that very same way, depending upon the power of the denoted and the designator. Because of the permanence of common understanding (*saṃpratipatti*), the traditionists (*āgaminaḥ*) maintain that the relationship between word and meaning is eternal.
For the yogi who has understood the nature of the denoted and the designator—
"Reciting that [mantra] and meditating upon its meaning" (1.28).

The repetition of the *praṇava* and the contemplation of the Lord who is denoted by the *praṇava*: for this yogin who repeats the *praṇava* and contemplates its meaning, the mind becomes one-pointed. Thus it has been said:
“From self-study one should practice yoga; from yoga one should attend to self-study.”
“Through the perfection of self-study and yoga, the Supreme Self is revealed.
And what happens for him?
"From that, there is the attainment of inward consciousness and the absence of obstacles" (1.29).

[33.vii] First, those obstacles such as disease and so forth do not occur due to devotion to Īśvara. He also gains insight into his own true nature. Just as Īśvara is a *puruṣa* who is pure, serene, absolute, and free from afflictions, so too does he realize that *puruṣa* who is the experiencer of the intellect (*buddhi*).
Now, what are the obstacles which are the distractions of the mind? And what are they, and how many are they?—
[34,ii] "Illness, languor, doubt, heedlessness, laziness, lack of renunciation, false vision, failure to attain a stage, and instability— these distractions of the mind are the obstacles" (1.30).

[34,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive form as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive forms as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive eye-contact as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the sensation born of eye-contact as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the sensation born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the earth element as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive ignorance as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, sensation, craving, grasping, existence, birth, or aging-and-death as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive them as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the conditioned as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the unconditioned as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive the limit of reality as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. He does not perceive nirvāṇa as either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive it as neither existent nor non-existent. For what reason? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are not apprehended, and they do not exist. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, not apprehended, and do not exist, then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he train in the knowledge of all aspects? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent. It is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom trains in the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. It is in this way that he trains in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the noble eightfold path. It is in this way that he trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion. It is in this way that he trains in the knowledge of all aspects. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent, then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas give a gift? How does he perfect the perfection of giving? How does he guard morality? How does he cultivate patience? How does he exert vigor? How does he enter meditative concentration? How does he cultivate wisdom? How does he enter the concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, and the doors of liberation? How does he enter the stages of a bodhisattva? How does he enter the path of seeing? How does he enter the path of cultivation? How does he enter the stage of the non-learner? How does he enter the stage of the Tathāgata? How does he enter the fruit of a stream-enterer? How does he enter the fruit of a once-returner? How does he enter the fruit of a non-returner? How does he enter the fruit of arhatship? How does he enter pratyekabuddhahood? How does he enter the knowledge of all aspects? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent. It is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva who has not yet attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of dharmas gives a gift. It is in this way that he perfects the perfection of giving. It is in this way that he guards morality. It is in this way that he cultivates patience. It is in this way that he exerts vigor. It is in this way that he enters meditative concentration. It is in this way that he cultivates wisdom. It is in this way that he enters the concentrations, the immeasurables, the formless attainments, and the doors of liberation. It is in this way that he enters the stages of a bodhisattva. It is in this way that he enters the path of seeing. It is in this way that he enters the path of cultivation. It is in this way that he enters the stage of the non-learner. It is in this way that he enters the stage of the Tathāgata. It is in this way that he enters the fruit of a stream-enterer. It is in this way that he enters the fruit of a once-returner. It is in this way that he enters the fruit of a non-returner. It is in this way that he enters the fruit of arhatship. It is in this way that he enters pratyekabuddhahood. It is in this way that he enters the knowledge of all aspects. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive a dharma that is neither existent nor non-existent, then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom

There are nine internal obstacles that cause distraction of the mind. These exist together with the fluctuations of the mind (*cittavṛtti*). In their absence, the aforementioned fluctuations of the mind do not occur. Disease (*vyādhi*) is an imbalance of the bodily humors, fluids, and the sense organs. Lethargy (*styāna*) is the mind’s lack of serviceability. Doubt (*saṃśaya*) is a cognition that touches upon two alternatives, thinking, "It might be thus," or "It might not be thus. Negligence (*pramāda*) is the failure to cultivate the means for achieving *samādhi*. Laziness (*ālasya*) is the failure to engage [in practice] due to heaviness of body and mind. Non-abstinence (*avirati*) is the mind’s greed, characterized by a longing for contact with sense objects. Erroneous perception (*bhrāntidarśana*) is distorted knowledge. Failure to attain the stage (*alabdhabhūmikatva*) is the non-attainment of the stage of *samādhi*. Instability (*anavasthitatva*) is the mind’s failure to remain fixed once the stage has been attained; for if *samādhi* were attained, the mind would remain fixed therein. These nine distractions of the mind are called the impurities of yoga, the adversaries of yoga, and the obstacles to yoga.
"Suffering, mental distress, bodily agitation, and inhalation and exhalation are concomitants of distraction. (1.31)

Suffering is that which is internal, external, and celestial; it is that by which living beings are struck and strive for its removal. Mental distress (*daurmanasya*) is the agitation of the mind resulting from the frustration of one's desires. Bodily tremor (*aṅgamejayatva*) is that which makes the limbs quiver or shake. Inhalation (*śvāsa*) is when the breath draws in external air; exhalation (*praśvāsa*) is when it expels the air within the body. These occur as concomitants of distraction and arise for one whose mind is distracted; they do not occur for one whose mind is concentrated.

Now, these distractions are the adversaries of meditative concentration (*samādhi*); they are to be suppressed by those very two means—practice (*abhyāsa*) and dispassion (*vairāgya*). In this context, while concluding the subject matter of practice, he says:
"To suppress them, there is the practice of a single principle" (YS 1.32).

[36,i] For the purpose of preventing distraction, one should practice a mind that takes a single reality as its object. However, for one who holds that the mind consists only of momentary cognitions fixed upon their respective objects, every mind would necessarily be one-pointed, and there would be no such thing as a distracted mind. If, on the other hand, this mind is withdrawn from all [objects] and concentrated on a single object, then it becomes one-pointed; therefore, it is not fixed upon its respective object [by nature].

Even for one who considers the mind to be one-pointed by means of a stream of similar cognitions, if that one-pointedness is a property (*dharma*) of the stream-mind, then there is no such single stream-mind because of its momentariness. If, on the other hand, it is a property of each individual cognition within the stream, then every such cognition—whether part of a stream of similar cognitions or a stream of dissimilar cognitions—is necessarily one-pointed because it is restricted to its own respective object; thus, a distracted mind would be impossible. Therefore, the mind is a single entity, stable, and possesses multiple objects.

And if cognitions were to arise as distinct by nature and unconnected with a single mind, then how could one cognition be the rememberer of what was seen by another cognition? Furthermore, how could one cognition be the experiencer of the latent deposit of karma accumulated by another cognition? Even if this were somehow reconciled, it would be like the logic of the "cow-dung and milk-porridge"—it would be utterly absurd.

Furthermore, if the mind were something else [from the self], it would result in the denial of one's own self-experience. How so? The cognition "I," expressed as "I touch what I saw" and "I see what I touched," presents itself as non-different from the subject of all cognitions despite the difference between those cognitions. How could this cognition "I," which has a single cognition as its object and is non-dual in nature, reside in minds that are absolutely distinct, unless it rested upon a single common subject? Moreover, this non-dual cognition "I" is grasped through one's own direct experience (*svānubhava*). And the authority of direct perception is not overridden by any other means of knowledge; indeed, other means of knowledge derive their practical application solely through the power of direct perception. Therefore, the mind is one, manifold in its objects, and enduring.
[38,i] How is it that this preparatory cultivation (*parikarma*) by means of the treatise is taught for that state of mind which remains established?

"By cultivating loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), sympathetic joy (*muditā*), and equanimity (*upekṣā*) toward objects that are pleasant, painful, virtuous, or non-virtuous, there is clarification of the mind (1.33).

In this regard, one should cultivate loving-kindness toward all living beings who are experiencing happiness; compassion toward those who are suffering; sympathetic joy toward those whose nature is virtuous; and equanimity toward those whose conduct is non-virtuous. As he cultivates in this way, pure qualities (*śukla-dharma*) arise within him, and consequently, the mind becomes clarified. Being clarified, it becomes one-pointed and attains a state of stability.
"Or, by means of the expulsion and retention of breath. (1.34)

The forceful expulsion of abdominal air through the nostrils by means of a specific effort is *vamana* (vomiting), and its restraint is *prāṇāyāma* (breath control); through these two, one may achieve stability of the mind.
[Yoga Sūtra 1.34] "Or, when an activity [of the mind] directed toward an object has arisen, it becomes a cause for the stability of the mind" (1.35).

[39,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is permanent, nor does he perceive that it is impermanent; he does not perceive that it is ease, nor does he perceive that it is suffering; he does not perceive that it is self, nor does he perceive that it is non-self; he does not perceive that it is beautiful, nor does he perceiving that it is ugly. He does not perceive that feeling is permanent, nor does he perceive that it is impermanent... [and so on for perception, volitional formations, and consciousness] ...he does not perceive that consciousness is beautiful, nor does he perceive that it is ugly. Why is that? Subhūti, because form is empty of the essential nature of form. Feeling is empty of the essential nature of feeling. Perception is empty of the essential nature of perception. Volitional formations are empty of the essential nature of volitional formations. Consciousness is empty of the essential nature of consciousness. Subhūti, because form is empty of the essential nature of form, one cannot perceive that form is permanent or impermanent, ease or suffering, self or non-self, beautiful or ugly. Because feeling is empty of the essential nature of feeling... because perception is empty of the essential nature of perception... because volitional formations are empty of the essential nature of volitional formations... because consciousness is empty of the essential nature of consciousness, one cannot perceive that consciousness is permanent or impermanent, ease or suffering, self or non-self, beautiful or ugly. Subhūti, this is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom. [39,v] Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of giving? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, having generated the mind of awakening, gives a gift to all sentient beings, and yet he does not perceive those sentient beings. This is called a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fulfilling the perfection of giving while practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, fulfill the perfection of morality? For one who holds [the mind] at the tip of the nose, that consciousness of divine fragrance is the activity regarding smell. At the tip of the tongue, there is consciousness of taste; on the palate, consciousness of form; in the middle of the tongue, consciousness of touch; and at the root of the tongue, consciousness of sound. These activities, once arisen, bind the mind to stability, dispel doubt, and become gateways to the wisdom of *samādhi*. By this, it should be understood that the activity arising toward the moon, sun, planets, jewels, lamps, rays of light, and so forth, is likewise "possessing an object" (*viṣayavat*), even though the true nature of an object is indeed real as it is understood through those respective scriptures, inference, and the instructions of teachers—since these possess the capacity to convey the object as it truly is. Nevertheless, as long as even a single portion is not personally experienced by one's own senses, everything remains as if beyond perception; thus, regarding subtle matters such as liberation, it does not produce a firm conviction. Therefore, for the sake of strengthening the authority of scripture, inference, and the teacher’s instruction, some specific aspect of the object must necessarily be made directly perceptible. When one portion of the object taught therein has been perceived, then everything—even subtle objects up to liberation—is accepted with faith. It is for this very purpose that this purification of the mind is prescribed: so that when the notion of mastery (*vaśīkāra-saṃjñā*) regarding those objects arises amidst the various mental fluctuations, one will be capable of making each respective object directly perceptible. And that being the case, his faith, vigor, mindfulness, and concentration will proceed without obstruction.
"Or it is free from sorrow and luminous.

The phrase "an activity has arisen that serves as a basis for the stability of the mind" carries over [from the previous sūtra]. For one who holds [the mind] within the heart-lotus, there is a cognitive awareness (*buddhi-saṃvit*); for the *sattva* of the intellect is luminous and like space. Through proficiency in remaining fixed upon that, the activity [of the mind] is conceptualized in the form of the light of the sun, moon, planets, and jewels. Likewise, the mind that has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*) in the sense of "I-am-ness" (*asmitā*) becomes like a great ocean without waves—tranquil, infinite, and consisting of nothing but "I-am-ness. Regarding this, it is said: "Having realized that Self which is subtle as an atom, he discerns it thus: 'I am. This twofold, sorrowless activity—both that which possesses objects and that which consists of mere "I-am-ness"—is called "luminous" (*jyotiṣmatī*). It is by means of this that the yogi’s mind attains a state of stability.
[41,i] "Or the mind has as its object one free from passion" (1.37) [41,ii]
Alternatively, the yogin’s mind, colored by an object that is the mind of one free from passion, attains a state of stability.
Or, as it is said: “or having the cognition of dreaming or sleeping as its object” (1.38).
[41,iv] Or, the mind of the yogi, having as its object either dream-consciousness or sleep-consciousness, attains a state of stability in that form.
"Or from meditation on whatever is desired" (1.39):
one should meditate on exactly that which is desired. Having attained stability therein, one attains a state of stability elsewhere as well.
[42,iii] "Its mastery extends from the smallest atom to the greatest magnitude" (1.40).

For one entering into the subtle, the state of stability is reached at the limit of the atom; for one entering into the gross, the state of stability of the mind is reached at the limit of the infinitely great. Thus, that non-obstruction of the mind as it pursues both these extremes is the supreme mastery. Through that mastery, the mind of the yogi becomes perfected and no longer requires the preparatory refinement produced by practice.
Now, what is the nature and what is the object of the meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) of the mind that has attained stability? To this it is said:

"For one whose fluctuations have ceased, there is, as it were, a gem of noble birth, a meditative attainment consisting in abiding in that and being colored by that, with respect to the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped" (Yogasūtra 1.41).

"Of one whose fluctuations have ceased" means one for whom all cognitive impressions (*pratyaya*) have subsided. "Like a well-bred gem" is the introduction of an illustration. Just as a crystal, colored by various objects due to its proximity to them, appears in the form and shape of those proximate objects, so too the mind, colored by the object of perception (*grāhya*), having attained identity with that object, appears in the form and shape of the perceived object. When colored by subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), having attained identity with the subtle elements, it becomes a manifestation of the essential nature of the subtle elements. Likewise, when colored by gross objects, having attained identity with gross forms, it becomes a manifestation of gross forms. Similarly, when colored by the diversity of the universe, having attained identity with the diversity of the universe, it becomes a manifestation of the universal form.

[43,iii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is not a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them; and because he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell with them. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom become one who does not apprehend any dharma? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive the arising of form, nor does he perceive the cessation of form. He does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive the arising of feeling, nor does he perceive the cessation of feeling. He does not perceive perception, nor does he perceive the arising of perception, nor does he perceive the cessation of perception. He does not perceive formations, nor does he perceive the arising of formations, nor does he perceive the cessation of formations. He does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive the arising of consciousness, nor does he perceive the cessation of consciousness. Subhūti, this is called a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom and does not apprehend any dharma. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: "Blessed One, what is the reason why a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form, nor the arising of form, nor the cessation of form; nor does he perceive feeling, nor the arising of feeling, nor the cessation of feeling; nor does he perceive perception, nor the arising of perception, nor the cessation of perception; nor does he perceive formations, nor the arising of formations, nor the cessation of formations; nor does he perceive consciousness, nor the arising of consciousness, nor the cessation of consciousness? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because form is empty of form, and the emptiness of form is not form, and apart from emptiness there is no form, and form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form. Feeling is empty of feeling... perception is empty of perception... formations are empty of formations... consciousness is empty of consciousness, and the emptiness of consciousness is not consciousness, and apart from emptiness there is no consciousness, and consciousness is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than consciousness. The same should be understood regarding the objects of perception (*grahaṇa*) and the sense organs (*indriya*). [The mind] colored by the object of perception and having attained the state of the object of perception appears in the form of the nature of that object of perception. Likewise, colored by the person who perceives (*grahītṛ-puruṣa*) as its object and having attained the state of the person who perceives, it appears in the form of the nature of the person who perceives. Similarly, colored by the liberated person (*mukta-puruṣa*) as its object and having attained the state of the liberated person, it appears in the form of the nature of the liberated person. Thus, for the mind—which is like a noble gem—there is a "being colored by that" (*tatsthatadañjanatā*) with respect to the perceiver, the perception, and the perceived, which consist of the person, the sense organ, and the object; that is, while abiding in them, it assumes their form. This is called "meditative absorption" (*samāpatti*).
[44,i] "In that regard, the attainment mixed with conceptualizations of word, object, and knowledge is *savitarka* (accompanied by applied thought) [Yoga-sūtra 1.42].

For example, the word "cow," the object "cow," and the cognition "cow" are perceived as undifferentiated, even though they are distinct. When analyzed, however, the properties of the word are one thing, the properties of the object another, and the properties of the cognition yet another; thus, their paths are separate. In that regard, when a yogin has attained meditative absorption (*samāpanna*), if the object such as a cow that has ascended into the wisdom of concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) returns accompanied by the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of word, object, and cognition, that is a mixed attainment and is called "with deliberation" (*savitarka*).

Furthermore, when the memory of linguistic conventions has been purified, and the object—abiding in its own essential nature alone within the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhi-prajñā*) that is devoid of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of knowledge derived from scripture or inference—is discerned solely through the form of its own nature, that is the "reflectionless" (*nirvitarka*) attainment. That is the supreme direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). And that is the seed of scripture and inference; from it, scripture and inference arise. Yet, that vision does not coexist with the knowledge of scripture or inference. Therefore, the vision born of the reflectionless attainment of the yogi is unmixed with other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). [46,i] "In the purification of mindfulness, when it is as if empty of its own form and there is the manifestation of the object alone, that is *nirvitarka* (1.43).

That wisdom (*prajñā*) which, when purified of conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*), recollection (*smṛti*), inference (*anumāna*), and the hearing of linguistic conventions (*śabdasaṃketaśruta*), is colored by the nature of the object of apprehension (*grāhyasvarūpoparakta*), abandons its own nature as an act of grasping—as if it were itself—, and becomes the mere nature of the thing itself, having as it were assumed the nature of the object of apprehension; that is then the *nirvitarka* attainment (*samāpatti*).

And thus it has been explained: "The object of a single cognition (*ekabuddhyupakrama*), such as a cow or a jar, consists in a specific aggregate of atoms (*aṇupracayaviśeṣātmā*) which constitutes the essence of the thing in the world."

And that particular configuration (*saṃsthānaviśeṣa*), which is a common property (*sādhāraṇadharma*) of the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*), being inherent (*ātma-bhūta*) to them, is inferred by its manifest effect; it appears when its own manifester (*svavyañjaka*) is applied, and it disappears upon the arising of another property, such as the potsherd. This very property is called the "whole" (*avayavin*). It is this which is one, large, minute, tangible, characterized by action, and impermanent; by means of this whole, worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*) are carried out.

Furthermore, for one for whom that specific accumulation (*pracaya-viśeṣa*) is without a real substrate (*avastuka*), and since its subtle cause is unperceivable and free from conceptual construction (*avikalpa*), there being no whole (*avayavin*), false knowledge (*mithyājñāna*) would be established as not having that [real object] as its form. Thus, it follows that almost all knowledge would be false. And in that case, what could even correct knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) be, given the absence of an object? Whatever is perceived is traditionally taught to be a whole. Therefore, the whole exists, which—having entered into the conventional usage of "largeness" and so forth—becomes the object of the non-conceptual (*nirvitarkā*) state of meditative attainment (*samāpatti*).
"By this very [explanation], the subtle-objected [samāpatti] with deliberation (*savicārā*) and without deliberation (*nirvicārā*) is explained" (Yogasūtra 1.44).

Therein, that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which has as its object the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*)—whose properties (*dharma*) are manifested, and which are delimited by experience of place, time, and cause—is called "with deliberation. Even there, it is the subtle element itself, characterized by the manifested property and perceivable by a single cognition, that presents itself as the objective support (*ālambana*) within the wisdom (*prajñā*) of samādhi.

[49,i] Furthermore, that meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) which occurs in relation to all things—things which are in every way and from every respect beyond description as either subsided, arisen, or indeterminable; which follow after all things; and which constitute the very nature of all things—is called "without deliberation" (*nirvicārā*). For the subtle element (*bhūtasūkṣma*), being of such a nature, when it becomes the object of focus in this very form, colors the nature of the wisdom (*prajñā*) of samādhi accordingly.

And when wisdom (*prajñā*) becomes as if empty of its own nature and consists of the object alone, it is then called "beyond-discursive-reflection" (*nirvicārā*). Among these, that which has gross objects as its domain is "with-discursive-thought" (*savitarkā*) and "without-discursive-thought" (*nirvitarkā*); that which has subtle objects as its domain is "with-discursive-reflection" (*savicārā*) and "without-discursive-reflection" (*nirvicārā*). Thus, by this very "without-discursive-thought" state, the abandonment of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) for both types is explained. [50,i] "And having subtle objects, it culminates in the unmanifest (*aliṅga*)" (YS 1.45).

[50,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in the perfection of giving. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift, and he does not perceive that gift as a gift, nor does he perceive himself as the giver, nor does he perceive the recipient as a recipient. This is called the perfection of giving of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of morality? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that morality as morality, nor does he perceive himself as one possessing morality, nor does he perceive any being as transgressing morality. This is called the perfection of morality of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that patience as patience, nor does he perceive himself as patient, nor does he perceive any being as an object of anger. This is called the perfection of patience of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of vigor? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that vigor as vigor, nor does he perceive himself as vigorous, nor does he perceive any being as lacking vigor. This is called the perfection of vigor of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of concentration? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that concentration as concentration, nor does he perceive himself as concentrated, nor does he perceive any being as distracted. This is called the perfection of concentration of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive that wisdom as wisdom, nor does he perceive himself as wise, nor does he perceive any being as lacking wisdom. This is called the perfection of wisdom of a bodhisattva mahāsattva who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in these six perfections, become irreversible from full enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva, having trained in these six perfections, does not perceive even the notion of irreversibility, then he is irreversible from full enlightenment.
