The subtle object of the earthy [tanmātra] is the subtle element of smell; that of the watery is the subtle element of taste; that of the fiery is the subtle element of form; that of the airy is the subtle element of touch; and that of the ethereal is the subtle element of sound. Of these, the ego (ahaṃkāra) is the subtle object. For this [ego] as well, the subtle object is the "mere-cause" (liṅgamātra). For the "mere-cause" also, the subtle object is the "uncaused" (aliṅga). There is nothing subtler than the uncaused. [Objection: But surely the Puruṣa is subtle? [Reply: True. However, the subtlety of the uncaused [Prakṛti] is in relation to the "mere-cause," whereas it is not so for the Puruṣa. Rather, the Puruṣa is not the inherent cause (anvayikāraṇa) of the "mere-cause," though he is its efficient cause (hetu). Therefore, the state of being without further limit (niratiśaya) regarding subtlety is explained as residing in the Pradhāna.
[50,iii] "Those very [attainments] are concentration with seed (sabīja-samādhi) [1.46].

Since those four attainments (*samāpatti*) have external objects as their seeds, concentration (*samādhi*) is also "with seed" (*sabīja*). Among these, concentration is enumerated as being of four types: with applied thought (*savitarka*) and without applied thought (*nirvitarka*) regarding a coarse object, and with sustained thought (*savicāra*) and without sustained thought (*nirvicāra*) regarding a subtle object.
[51,i] "When there is confidence (*vaiśāradya*) in the state without sustained thought, there is inner clarity (*adhyātmaprasāda*). (1.47)

[51,ii] For the *buddhi-sattva*, whose nature is luminosity, when it is freed from the impurities of the veil of impurity (*aśuddhy-āvaraṇa-mala*), its clear flow of stability—unoverpowered by *rajas* and *tamas*—is *vaiśāradya* (clarity). When this clarity of the *nirvicāra* samādhi arises, then for the yogin there occurs an internal serenity (*adhyātma-prasāda*), a vivid light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*) whose object is the reality of things (*bhūtārtha*), which does not follow a sequential order. And so it has been said:
"Having ascended to the clarity of wisdom, one who is beyond grief looks upon grieving people."
“As one standing on a mountain peak beholds all those on the ground, so does the wise man perceive everything.
[Yoga Sūtra 3.49] “In that state, wisdom is truth-bearing” (YS 1.48).

[51,iv] The wisdom that arises for one whose mind is concentrated in that state receives the designation "truth-bearing" (*ṛtaṃbhara*). This is a literal term, for it bears only truth; therein, not even a trace of erroneous cognition exists. And so it has been said:
“By means of scripture, inference, and the delight in the practice of meditation—
cultivating wisdom in these three ways— one attains the supreme yoga.
Thus it is said.
Furthermore, that—
"By means of the wisdom derived from scripture and inference, [the object of direct perception] has a different domain, because it concerns particulars" (1.49).

[52,iii] "Scripture" (*śruta*) refers to the knowledge of tradition (*āgama*); that has a universal (*sāmānya*) as its domain. For a particular (*viśeṣa*) cannot be expressed by means of scripture. Why? Because a word does not have a convention established for a particular. Likewise, inference also has only the universal as its domain. It has been stated: "Where there is attainment, there is movement; where there is non-attainment, there is no movement. And by means of inference, there is a synthesis (*upasaṃhāra*) through the universal. Therefore, there is no particular whatsoever that is the domain of scripture or inference.

Furthermore, there is no perception of this subtle, concealed, or remote object through worldly direct perception (*lokapratyakṣa*). Nor is there an absence of this particularity (*viśeṣa*) because it lacks a means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*); rather, that particularity—whether pertaining to the subtle elements (*bhūtasūkṣma*) or to the person (*puruṣa*)—is to be grasped solely by the wisdom of meditative concentration (*samādhiprajñā*). Therefore, that wisdom has a different object from the wisdoms of scripture (*śruta*) and inference (*anumāna*), because its purpose is the discernment of particularities.
Upon the attainment of concentration and wisdom, a new and ever-new formative impression produced by wisdom arises for the yogin—
[53,ii] "The formative impression born from that obstructs other formative impressions" (1.50).

[53,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred merchantmen and, by means of his supernormal power, transformed himself into a great sea monster (*mahāśuśumāra*). Having transformed himself into a great sea monster, he emerged from the great ocean and approached the ship where the five hundred merchantmen were. Upon seeing the great sea monster approaching, the five hundred merchantmen became terrified and cried out: “Sirs, do not be afraid! Do not be afraid! Then the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having manifested himself as a great sea monster, spoke these words to the five hundred merchantmen: “Sirs, do not be afraid! I shall carry you all across to the other shore. Having spoken thus, he took up all five hundred merchantmen upon his back and carried them across to the other shore. Having brought them safely across to the other shore, he returned once more to his own abode. This, Ānanda, is the second way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any woman who desires a son, and she, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, she will give birth to a son endowed with handsome features and a noble appearance. If she desires a daughter, she will give birth to a daughter endowed with handsome features and a noble appearance. This, Ānanda, is the third way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who, having committed an offense against the king, is bound in shackles, stocks, or fetters, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, those shackles, stocks, or fetters shall all fall away and be broken. This, Ānanda, is the fourth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by a multitude of enemies and intends to kill him, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the fifth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by robbers and intends to kill him, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the sixth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by water and is on the verge of drowning, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, he shall immediately find dry land. This, Ānanda, is the seventh way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by fire and is on the verge of being consumed, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, the fire shall be extinguished and he shall not be burned. This, Ānanda, is the eighth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by bandits and intends to kill him, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the ninth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by snakes and intends to kill him, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, the snakes shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the tenth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by spirits (*bhūta*), yakṣas, rākṣasas, kumbhāṇḍas, piśācas, pūtanas, kaṭapūtanas, or unhuman beings (*amanuṣya*), and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the eleventh way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is afflicted by various diseases—such as eye disease, ear disease, nose disease, tongue disease, body disease, or head disease—and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, all those afflictions shall be completely cured. This, Ānanda, is the twelfth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is afflicted by various poisons—whether snake venom, scorpion venom, centipede venom, or the venom of other such creatures—and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, all those poisons shall be neutralized. This, Ānanda, is the thirteenth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is afflicted by various weapons—whether swords, spears, arrows, clubs, or maces—and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, those weapons shall all turn into flowers. This, Ānanda, is the fourteenth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by a multitude of enemies and intends to kill him, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the fifteenth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by robbers and intends to kill him, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, they shall all become benevolent and compassionate toward one another. This, Ānanda, is the sixteenth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there should be any man who is surrounded by water and is on the verge of drowning, and if he, with single-minded devotion, pays homage to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by the power of that Bodhisattva’s majesty, he shall immediately find dry land. This, Ānanda, is the seventeenth way in which the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara bestows protection upon sentient beings. The formative force (*saṃskāra*) produced by concentration (*samādhi*) and wisdom (*prajñā*) obstructs the latent tendency toward the formative forces of emergence. Because the formative forces of emergence are overcome, the conditions (*pratyaya*) arising from them do not occur. When conditions cease, concentration is established. From that comes the wisdom born of concentration; from that come the formative forces produced by wisdom. Thus, a new and ever-fresh store of formative forces is generated. And from that comes wisdom, and from that, formative forces. How could this excellence of formative forces fail to render the mind free from further obligation (*sādhikāra*)? Those formative forces produced by wisdom do not make the mind characterized by obligation, because they are the cause for the destruction of the afflictions (*kleśa*). Indeed, they cause the mind to desist from its own activity, for the movement of the mind culminates in the realization of true knowledge (*khyāti*).
ii] And what happens to him?
"When that too is ceased, because of the cessation of everything, there is seedless concentration" (1.51).

This [cessation] is not only an adversary to concentration and wisdom, but it also acts as an obstacle to the formative forces (*saṃskāra*) produced by wisdom. Why? Because the formative force born of cessation subverts the formative forces born of concentration.

[55,ii] The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle. It is also called ‘The Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas,’ and it is also called ‘The Perfection of Wisdom. Why is it called ‘The Great Vehicle’? Ānanda, because it carries out the great vehicle of all sentient beings, it is therefore called ‘The Great Vehicle. Why is it called ‘The Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas’? Ānanda, because it brings forth the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas, it is therefore called ‘The Great Vehicle of the Bodhisattvas. Why is it called ‘The Perfection of Wisdom’? Ānanda, because it brings forth the perfection of wisdom, it is therefore called ‘The Perfection of Wisdom. Furthermore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is profound and difficult to understand; it is subtle and difficult to penetrate, and it is not easily grasped by ordinary people. It is not something that can be understood through mere logic or reasoning, nor is it within the sphere of the dialecticians. Only those who have practiced the holy life under the Buddhas of the past can understand it. Therefore, Ānanda, you should uphold, recite, and explain this Dharma-discourse to others. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Ānanda and the monks were delighted and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught. The existence of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) produced by the mind in cessation (*nirodha*) is to be inferred through the experience of the sequence of time during the state of cessation. Along with the latent impressions conducive to liberation (*kaivalyabhāgīya*), which arise from the meditative absorption of emergence and cessation, the mind dissolves into its own primordial nature (*prakṛti*). Therefore, those impressions are antagonistic to the mind’s functional mandate (*adhikāra*) and do not become causes for its continued persistence. Since the mind, having completed its mandate, ceases together with the impressions conducive to liberation, when that [mind] has ceased, the Person (*puruṣa*) is established in his own essential nature alone; thus he is called pure, isolated, and liberated.
[56,i] Thus ends the first chapter, the Samādhipāda, in the illustrious Patañjali’s Yogaśāstra, the Exposition of Sāṃkhya, with the commentary by the venerable Vyāsa.
<The Sadhanapāda>
[57,i] The yoga of one whose mind is concentrated has been taught. Now this is undertaken: how may one whose mind is emerged from concentration also be engaged in yoga?
"Austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord constitute the yoga of action" (2.1).

Yoga is not accomplished for one who lacks austerity. Impurity—which is variegated by the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of karma and afflictions (*kleśa*) from beginningless time and which presents a web of sense objects—does not undergo dissolution without austerity; thus, austerity is undertaken. And it is held that this [austerity] should be practiced so as not to obstruct the clarity of the mind.

[58,i] Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the recitation of purificatory mantras such as the *praṇava*, or the study of the scriptures on liberation. Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the offering of all actions to the Supreme Teacher, or the renunciation of their fruits.
For that is indeed the yoga of action (kriyāyoga):
"It is for the purpose of cultivating samādhi and for the purpose of attenuating the afflictions" (YS 2.2).

For when that [practice] is cultivated, it develops meditative concentration (*samādhi*) and attenuates the afflictions (*kleśa*). Having attenuated the afflictions, it will render them like burnt seeds—incapable of germination—by means of the fire of discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*). Because of their attenuation, the subtle wisdom (*sūkṣmā prajñā*), which is no longer touched by the afflictions and consists merely in the manifestation of the distinction between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, will have fulfilled its purpose and be ready for reabsorption (*pratiprasava*).
Now, as to what the afflictions are and how many there are:
"Ignorance, egoism, attachment, aversion, and clinging to life are the afflictions" (YS 2.3).

[59,iii] "Afflictions" (kleśa) means the five perversions. When they are in motion, they strengthen the sovereignty of the qualities (guṇa), establish their transformation (pariṇāma), and cause the stream of cause and effect to rise up; having become dependent on one another through mutual assistance, they bring about the ripening of karma (karmavipāka).
Ignorance is the field for the subsequent [afflictions], whether they be dormant, attenuated, interrupted, or active.

In this context, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the field, the ground of production, for the fourfold types of latent dispositions (*asmitā* and so forth)—namely, those that are dormant (*prasupta*), attenuated (*tanu*), interrupted (*vicchinna*), and active (*udāra*). What is dormancy? It is the state of having entered the condition of a seed, while remaining in the mind merely as a potentiality. Its awakening is its manifestation toward an object of perception (*ālambana*). For one who possesses discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, this [awakening] does not occur again even when an object is present; for how can there be sprouting from a burnt seed? Therefore, such a person is called "one whose afflictions are exhausted," "virtuous," and "in his final body. In that very state, there is a fifth stage of the afflictions consisting of the burnt state of the seeds, and not elsewhere. Since the capacity of the seeds of existing afflictions has been burnt at that time, their awakening does not occur even when an object is present; thus dormancy and the non-sprouting of burnt seeds have been explained.

[60,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of attachment (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependence (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfection (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of reality as it is (*tathatā-svabhāva*). Therein, Mahāmati, the self-nature of attachment is that which is characterized by the grasping of names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) based on the objects of the five sense-faculties. The self-nature of dependence is that which arises from the causal conditions of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination. The self-nature of perfection is that which is free from the two-fold grasping—that is, the absence of both the grasper and the grasped—and which is the suchness of the dependent nature. The self-nature of reality as it is is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is realized through the transformation of the basis (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*) and is not within the sphere of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or those who follow the teachings of externalists. Mahāmati, if one does not understand these four kinds of self-nature, one will fail to realize the non-existence of the three self-natures and will consequently fall into the view of nihilism. However, Mahāmati, when one thoroughly understands these four kinds of self-nature, one will transcend the views of existence and non-existence and enter the stage of a Bodhisattva. Therefore, Mahāmati, you and other Bodhisattvas should cultivate yourselves in the realization of the four kinds of self-nature.

"Attenuation" is explained as follows: the afflictions (*kleśa*), being struck down by the cultivation of their antidotes, become attenuated. Likewise, they are "interrupted" because they manifest again and again in various forms after having been repeatedly severed. How so? Because at the time of passion (*rāga*), anger (*krodha*) is not observed. Indeed, anger does not manifest at the time of passion. Furthermore, passion being observed in one place does not mean it is absent in other objects. It is not the case that Caitra is attached to one woman and therefore detached from other women; rather, in that instance, passion has attained its activity (*labdhavṛtti*), whereas elsewhere it is yet to attain its activity (*bhaviṣyadvṛtti*). Thus, at that time, it remains dormant, attenuated, or interrupted.

[61,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive feeling, perception, formations, or consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive forms as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the earth element as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive ignorance as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive generosity as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as existent or non-existent, nor does he perceive the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as existent or non-existent. Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as existent or non-existent. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as existent or non-existent, then how does he train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? How does he train in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? How does he train in the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path? How does he train in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he train in the knowledge of all modes? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he trains in the perfection of giving by means of the non-apprehension of a gift, a giver, or a recipient. He trains in the perfection of morality by means of the non-apprehension of transgression or non-transgression. He trains in the perfection of patience by means of the non-apprehension of an object of anger or a patient person. He trains in the perfection of vigor by means of the non-apprehension of laziness or diligence. He trains in the perfection of meditation by means of the non-apprehension of distraction or concentration. He trains in the perfection of wisdom by means of the non-apprehension of ignorance or knowledge. He trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment by means of the non-apprehension of those factors. He trains in the four applications of mindfulness by means of the non-apprehension of the body, feelings, mind, or dharmas. He trains in the four right efforts by means of the non-apprehension of the origination of unwholesome states or the abandonment thereof, and the non-origination of wholesome states or their cultivation. He trains in the four bases of psychic power by means of the non-apprehension of desire, vigor, mind, or investigation. He trains in the five faculties by means of the non-apprehension of faith, vigor, mindfulness, concentration, or wisdom. He trains in the five powers by means of the non-apprehension of those same powers. He trains in the seven factors of enlightenment by means of the non-apprehension of mindfulness, discrimination of dharmas, vigor, joy, pliancy, concentration, or equanimity. He trains in the eightfold noble path by means of the non-apprehension of right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, or right concentration. He trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata by means of the non-apprehension of those powers. He trains in the four fearlessnesses by means of the non-apprehension of those fearlessnesses. He trains in the four analytical knowledges by means of the non-apprehension of those knowledges. He trains in the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha by means of the non-apprehension of those qualities. He trains in great compassion by means of the non-apprehension of sentient beings. He trains in the knowledge of all modes by means of the non-apprehension of all dharmas. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom trains in the perfection of giving, trains in the perfection of morality, trains in the perfection of patience, trains in the perfection of vigor, trains in the perfection of meditation, and trains in the perfection of wisdom. It is in this way that he trains in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the four applications of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. It is in this way that he trains in the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion. It is in this way that he trains in the knowledge of all modes.”

That [affliction] which has acquired its functional activity toward an object is "intense" (*udāra*). All of these [four types of afflictions] do not transcend the state of being objects of the afflictions. What, then, is an "interrupted," "dormant," "subtle," or "intense" affliction? It is said: this is indeed true; however, the status of being "interrupted" and so forth applies only to these [afflictions] in their specific [manifested] forms. Just as they cease through the cultivation of the counteragent (*pratipakṣa-bhāvanā*), so too are they manifested by the application of their own manifesting conditions. All these afflictions are varieties of ignorance (*avidyā*). Why? Because ignorance alone pervades all of them. Whatever object is constructed by ignorance, it is precisely there that the afflictions adhere; they are perceived at the time of the cognition of error (*viparyāsa-pratyaya*), and they perish following the perishing of ignorance.
[61,ii] In this regard, the intrinsic nature of ignorance is stated—
"Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the perception of the permanent, the pure, the pleasant, and the self in what is impermanent, impure, painful, and non-self" (2.5).

[61, iv] It is the perception of permanence in what is impermanent, namely, an effect. For example: "The earth is eternal; the sky with its moon and stars is eternal; the inhabitants of heaven are immortal. Likewise, it is the perception of purity in the body, which is supremely loathsome—
“Because of its location, its seed, its support, its outflow, and also its end;
and because it requires purification to be inhabited, the wise indeed know the body to be impure.”

[62,ii] Thus, the perception of purity in the impure is observed. [One thinks: "This girl is like a fresh crescent moon; she is lovely, as if fashioned from the limbs of honey and nectar, as if known to have emerged after piercing the moon; her eyes are as long as the petals of a blue lotus, and with her eyes full of amorous gestures, she seems to comfort the world of the living. What connection is there between this and that? And yet, such a cognition of purity arises regarding the impure. By this, the cognition of merit in what is non-meritorious, and likewise the cognition of benefit in what is harmful, is explained.

Likewise, he will state that there is the perception of happiness in what is suffering: “To the discerning person, everything is indeed suffering because of the sufferings of transformation, anxiety, and latent impressions, and because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*. In that context, the perception of happiness is ignorance (*avidyā*). Similarly, the perception of a self in what is not-self—whether in external instruments, animate or inanimate, or in the body which is the locus of experience, or in the mind which is an instrument of the *puruṣa*—is the perception of a self in what is not-self. Thus it has been said here: “Having identified with the manifest or the unmanifest *sattva* as the self, one rejoices in its prosperity, thinking it to be the prosperity of the self, and grieves over its adversity, thinking it to be the adversity of the self; all such a person is unawakened. This four-footed ignorance is the root of this stream of afflictions and of the accumulation of karma along with its fruition.

And its ontological reality should be understood as being like that of a non-friend (*amitra*) or a non-cow-track (*agoṣpada*). Just as a "non-friend" is neither the absence of a friend nor merely a friend, but rather an adversary who is their opposite; or just as a "non-cow-track" is neither the absence of a cow-track nor merely a cow-track, but rather a distinct entity, namely the ground itself, different from those two—so too, ignorance (*avidyā*) is neither valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) nor the absence of valid cognition, but rather another kind of knowledge that is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*). Thus it is called ignorance.
"Asmitā is the apparent identity of the powers of the seer and the seen" (Yoga Sūtra 2.6).

The *puruṣa* is the power of seeing (*dṛk-śakti*), and the intellect (*buddhi*) is the power of seeing (*darśana-śakti*). The affliction called *asmitā* (egoism) is said to be the attainment, as it were, of a single nature by these two. When there is a state of non-differentiation, as it were, between the power of the enjoyer and the power of the object of enjoyment—which are absolutely distinct and absolutely unmixed—experience (*bhoga*) is possible. But when they regain their own true natures, there is only isolation (*kaivalya*); how then could there be experience? Thus it has been said: "Not perceiving the *puruṣa*, who is beyond the intellect and distinct from it by virtue of form, character, knowledge, and so forth, one might through delusion form the notion of 'self' with respect to that [intellect]. [64, iii]
"Attachment lies latent in pleasure" (2.7).
For one who has experienced pleasure, that greed, thirst, or covetousness which arises preceded by the recollection of pleasure, or toward pleasure or its means, is attachment (*rāga*).
"Hatred is that which lies latent within suffering" (2.8).

For one who has directly known suffering, that hostility, resentment, desire to strike, or anger directed toward suffering or its causes—which is preceded by the recollection of suffering—is hatred (*dveṣa*).
[65,iv] "A natural flow, deeply rooted even in the wise, is this clinging (*abhiniveśa*). (2.9)

[65,v] This self-cherishing wish—"May I not cease to exist; may I continue to be"—is constant for every living being. And such a wish for the self does not arise in one who has not experienced the nature of death. By this, the experience of a previous birth is inferred. Furthermore, this clinging is a defilement that flows by its own inherent force; even in a creature just born as a worm, there is a fear of death—unaccountable through perception, inference, or scripture—which consists of the view of annihilationism (ucchedadṛṣṭi) and leads one to infer the suffering of death experienced in a previous life.

Just as this affliction is seen among those who are utterly deluded, so too it is firmly rooted even in the wise person who has understood the prior and subsequent limits [of existence]. Why? Because this latent impression (*vāsanā*) arises from the experience of the suffering of death, which is common to both the virtuous and the non-virtuous. [66,ii] "Those subtle [afflictions] are to be abandoned through re-absorption" (2.10).
Those five afflictions, resembling burnt seeds, set together with that very mind when the mind's function of activity has dissolved for the yogin.
But for those that remain, having entered into the state of seeds— [67,i] "The fluctuations to be abandoned by meditative absorption are of that nature" (2.11).

[67,ii] Those coarse manifestations of the afflictions (*kleśa*) are thinned by the yoga of action (*kriyā-yoga*); once they have been thinned, they are to be abandoned through meditative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and dhyāna, until they are made subtle, that is, until they are like burnt seeds. Just as the coarse dirt on clothes is shaken off first, while the fine dirt is later removed with effort and skillful means, so too the coarse manifestations of the afflictions have few counteragents, whereas the subtle ones require great counteragents.
"The latent deposit of karma has its root in the afflictions; it is to be experienced in the seen or the unseen birth" (2.12).

In this regard, the latent deposit of meritorious and non-meritorious karma arises from desire, greed, delusion, and anger. It is both to be experienced in the present life and to be experienced in a future life. Among these, that which is accomplished through intense spiritual fervor (*saṃvega*) by means of mantras, austerities, and meditative absorption, or which is perfected through the propitiation of the Lord, deities, great seers, or those of great majesty—that deposit of meritorious karma ripens immediately. Likewise, a repeated injury inflicted with intense affliction upon those who are terrified, diseased, or pitiable, or upon those who have placed their trust in one, or upon those of great majesty or ascetics—that deposit of sinful karma also ripens immediately. For example, Kumāra Nandīśvara, having abandoned his human form, was transformed into a deity; likewise, Nahuṣa, the Indra of the gods, having abandoned his own form, was transformed into an animal. In this context, for those in hell there is no latent deposit of karma to be experienced in the present life; and for those whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted, there is no latent deposit of karma to be experienced in a future life.
"When the root exists, its maturation consists of birth, lifespan, and experience" (2.13).

When the afflictions (*kleśa*) exist, the latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*) becomes capable of initiating its fruition (*vipāka*), but not when the root of the afflictions has been severed. Just as rice grains covered by husks are capable of sprouting provided their seed-nature is not burnt, whereas those whose husks have been removed or whose seed-nature is burnt are not, so too the latent disposition of karma covered by afflictions leads to the sprouting of fruition, but not when the afflictions have been removed, nor when the seed-nature of the afflictions has been burnt away by higher knowledge (*prasaṃkhyāna*). And that fruition is threefold: birth, lifespan, and experience.

In this regard, the following is investigated: Is a single action the cause of a single birth, or does a single action project multiple births? The second investigation is: Do multiple actions bring about multiple births, or do multiple actions bring about a single birth? First of all, a single action is not the cause of a single birth. Why? Because, since there is an infinite accumulation of countless remaining actions from beginningless time, as well as present actions, there would follow a lack of certainty for the world regarding the sequence of their fruits; and that is undesirable. Nor is a single action the cause of multiple births. Why? Because, among the many actions, if only one single action were the cause of multiple births, it would follow that there is no time for the ripening of the remainder; and that too is undesirable. Nor are multiple actions the cause of multiple births. Why? Because those multiple births cannot occur simultaneously; thus, they must be said to occur only in succession. And in that case, the aforementioned defect persists.

Therefore, the diverse accumulation of latent impressions (*karmāśaya*) consisting of meritorious and non-meritorious actions, performed during the interval between birth and death, exists in a relationship of primary and secondary importance. Manifested at the time of death, it brings about death in a single stroke; having coalesced, it produces only one birth. That birth, through that very same karma, acquires its lifespan. During that lifespan, experience (*bhoga*) is accomplished by that very same karma. Because this latent impression of karma is the cause of birth, lifespan, and experience, it is designated as "having a threefold fruition" (*trivipāka*). Thus, it is called a "latent impression pertaining to a single existence" (*ekabhavika*).

[70,ii] Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was staying at Śrāvastī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍada’s monastery. There the Blessed One addressed the monks: “Monks! “Venerable sir,” those monks replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking a new existence. What four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the assistance of those seeking a new existence. Now, monks, from what source do these four nutriments arise? From what cause do they originate? By what are they produced? By what are they brought about? Physical food as nutriment, monks, has craving as its source, craving as its cause, craving as its producer, and craving as its bringer-about. Contact as nutriment has craving as its source... Mental volition as nutriment has craving as its source... Consciousness as nutriment has craving as its source, craving as its cause, craving as its producer, and craving as its bringer-about. And from what source, monks, does this craving arise? From what cause does it originate? By what is it produced? By what is it brought about? This craving, monks, has feeling as its source, feeling as its cause, feeling as its producer, and feeling as its bringer-about. And from what source, monks, does this feeling arise? From what cause does it originate? By what is it produced? By what is it brought about? This feeling, monks, has contact as its source, contact as its cause, contact as its producer, and contact as its bringer-about. And from what source, monks, does this contact arise? From what cause does it originate? By what is it produced? By what is it brought about? This contact, monks, has the six sense bases as its source, the six sense bases as its cause, the six sense bases as its producer, and the six sense bases as its bringer-about. And from what source, monks, do these six sense bases arise? From what cause do they originate? By what are they produced? By what are they brought about? These six sense bases, monks, have name-and-form as their source, name-and-form as their cause, name-and-form as their producer, and name-and-form as their bringer-about. And from what source, monks, does this name-and-form arise? From what cause does it originate? By what is it produced? By what is it brought about? This name-and-form, monks, has consciousness as its source, consciousness as its cause, consciousness as its producer, and consciousness as its bringer-about. And from what source, monks, does this consciousness arise? From what cause does it originate? By what is it produced? By what is it brought about? This consciousness, monks, has formations as its source, formations as its cause, formations as its producer, and formations as its bringer-about. And from what source, monks, do these formations arise? From what cause do they originate? By what are they produced? By what are they brought about? These formations, monks, have ignorance as their source, ignorance as their cause, ignorance as their producer, and ignorance as their bringer-about. Thus, monks, with ignorance as condition, formations come to be; with formations as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be; with name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases come to be; with the six sense bases as condition, contact comes to be; with contact as condition, feeling comes to be; with feeling as condition, craving comes to be; with craving as condition, clinging comes to be; with clinging as condition, existence comes to be; with existence as condition, birth comes to be; with birth as condition, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair come to be. Such is the origin of this entire mass of suffering. But from the complete fading away and cessation of that very ignorance, monks, comes the cessation of formations; with the cessation of formations, consciousness ceases; with the cessation of consciousness, name-and-form ceases; with the cessation of name-and-form, the six sense bases cease; with the cessation of the six sense bases, contact ceases; with the cessation of contact, feeling ceases; with the cessation of feeling, craving ceases; with the cessation of craving, clinging ceases; with the cessation of clinging, existence ceases; with the cessation of existence, birth ceases; with the cessation of birth, aging-and-death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, grief, and despair cease. Such is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir! It is marvelous, venerable sir! How well has this dependent origination been taught by the Blessed One in its forward order and its reverse order, with its many aspects and its many details! “It is wonderful, Ānanda! It is marvelous, Ānanda! That you, having been face-to-face with me, should say such things. For it is indeed wonderful, Ānanda, that this dependent origination has been taught by me in its forward order and its reverse order, with its many aspects and its many details. If, Ānanda, one were to point out the beginning of suffering, it would be possible to point to its beginning nowhere else than in ignorance. If, Ānanda, one were to point out the origin of suffering, it would be possible to point to its origin nowhere else than in craving. If, Ānanda, one were to point out the cessation of suffering, it would be possible to point to its cessation nowhere else than in the cessation of ignorance. If, Ānanda, one were to point out the path leading to the cessation of suffering, it would be possible to point to that path nowhere else than in this Noble Eightfold Path. Therefore, Ānanda, this dependent origination should be seen as profound and of profound meaning, appearing as though it were clear, yet being difficult to see and difficult to understand. It is by means of this that beings, becoming entangled, are unable to transcend the realm of death, the realm of Mara, the realm of Māra’s son. However, that which is to be experienced in the present life initiates a single fruition (*ekavipākārambhī*), because it is the cause of experience alone; or it may initiate two fruitions (*dvivipākārambhī*), because it is the cause of both experience and lifespan, as in the cases of Nandīśvara or Nahuṣa. But this mind, which has been coagulated since beginningless time by these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) produced through the experience of afflictions, karma, and fruition, is made variegated as if on all sides by a fish-net, or spread out like knots; these are the latent impressions belonging to many previous births. As for this store of karma (*karmāśaya*), it is said to belong to a single birth. Those formative forces (*saṃskāra*) which are the causes of memory are the latent impressions, and they are beginningless in time.

[71,i] That store of karma which pertains to a single birth is both of determinate fruition and of indeterminate fruition. Among these, this rule applies only to that which is to be experienced in the present life and has determinate fruition, but not to that which is to be experienced in a future life and has indeterminate fruition. Why? For that which is to be experienced in a future life and has indeterminate fruition has three possible courses: its destruction before it has ripened; its being cast into the background by a dominant karma; or its remaining for a long time, being suppressed by a dominant karma of determinate fruition. [71,ii]

In that regard, the destruction of what has been done but not yet ripened is as follows: through the arising of white karma, there is the destruction of black karma right here in this life. As it is said: "Two kinds of karma, indeed, are to be known; the single heap of the evil-doer's karma the doer of merit destroys. Therefore, desire to perform well-done deeds; for in this very world, the wise declare such karma to you. [72,i]

The "insertion" (āvāpa) occurs in the case of a primary action (*pradhānakarman*). Regarding this, it has been said: "There may be a slight confusion (*saṃkara*) that is remediable and tolerable; it is not sufficient to detract from one's merit (*kuśala*). Why? Because I possess much other merit into which this [confusion] has been inserted, so that even in heaven it will cause only a slight diminution.

Or, there may be a long-term persistence of [karma] that has been overwhelmed by a primary karma of certain fruition (*niyatavipāka*). How so? It has been stated that death is the manifesting cause (*abhivyaktikāraṇa*) specifically for karma that is to be experienced in an unseen birth (*adṛṣṭajanmavedanīya*) and whose fruition is certain; however, this does not apply to karma that is to be experienced in an unseen birth but whose fruition is uncertain (*aniyatavipāka*). As for that karma which is to be experienced in an unseen birth and whose fruition is uncertain, it may either perish, or it may enter into a state of being stored (*āvāpa*), or it may remain overwhelmed for a long time—until a similar karma acts as a manifesting condition and brings its fruition toward manifestation. Because the place, time, and conditions for its fruition cannot be determined, this course of karma is variegated and difficult to discern. Furthermore, the general rule is not set aside merely because of exceptions; thus, the *karmāśaya* (latent deposit of karma) pertaining to a single lifetime (*ekabhavika*) is acknowledged.

Since this experience of pleasure for everyone is permeated by passion (*rāga*) and depends upon means that are either conscious or unconscious, there exists therein a latent deposit of karma (*karmāśaya*) born of passion. Likewise, one hates the instruments of suffering and becomes deluded; thus, there also exists a latent deposit of karma produced by hatred (*dveṣa*) and delusion (*moha*). And so it has been said: "Since enjoyment is not possible without harming living beings, there also exists a bodily latent deposit of karma produced by violence. Furthermore, it has been stated that sensual pleasure is ignorance (*avidyā*).

That which is the subsiding of the thirst of the senses for objects of enjoyment is happiness; that which is the non-subsidance due to longing is suffering. Furthermore, it is not possible to effect the absence of thirst in the senses through the repeated practice of enjoyment. Why? Because, following the repeated practice of enjoyment, passions increase as well as the acuity of the senses. Therefore, the repeated practice of enjoyment is no means to happiness. Indeed, he who, seeking happiness, becomes habituated to sense-objects, is like one bitten by a venomous snake while fearing the poison of a scorpion; he is submerged in a great mire of suffering. This is what is called the "suffering inherent in transformation" (*pariṇāmaduḥkhatā*); it is adverse and afflicts the yogi alone, even during a state of pleasure.

The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are neither a bodhisattva nor a ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; the four noble truths are neither a bodhisattva nor a ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; the ten powers of a Tathāgata are neither a bodhisattva nor a ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation; the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion are neither a bodhisattva nor a ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation. All dharmas are neither a bodhisattva nor a ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, all these dharmas are empty of their own marks. Since they are empty, they cannot be apprehended. Because they cannot be apprehended, they cannot be known. Because they cannot be known, they cannot be fully understood. Because they cannot be fully understood, they cannot be realized. Because they cannot be realized, there is no attainment and no non-attainment. Therefore, Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who wishes to fully awaken to all dharmas in all their aspects should practice the perfection of wisdom. Now, what is the suffering of pain (*tāpa-duḥkhatā*)? It is the experience of pain, permeated by aversion, which depends upon means that are either conscious or unconscious; in this regard, there exists a latent deposit of karma born of aversion. Furthermore, desiring the means to pleasure, one exerts oneself through body, speech, and mind; thereafter, by favoring or harming others, one accumulates merit and demerit through those acts of favoring and paining others. That latent deposit of karma arises from greed and delusion; this is called the suffering of pain. What, then, is the suffering of mental impressions (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*)? From the experience of pleasure, there is a latent deposit of the impression of pleasure, and from the experience of pain, there is a latent deposit of the impression of pain. Thus, while the fruition of karma—whether pleasure or pain—is being experienced, there is again an accumulation of latent deposits of karma.

Thus, this beginningless stream of suffering, having spread forth, causes only the yogi to feel revulsion because its nature is contrary [to his state]. Why? Because "the wise man is like the eye-ball. Just as a thread of wool placed upon the eye-ball causes pain through touch but not on other parts of the body, so too these sufferings afflict only the yogi who is like the eye-ball, and not the other ordinary practitioner. But for the other person—who is driven by his own karma, who abandons each suffering once it is acquired and acquires each new one once it has been abandoned; who is pierced on all sides by mental fluctuations variegated by beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as if by ignorance (*avidyā*); who follows the notions of "I" and "mine" which are to be discarded; and who is born again and again—the three-jointed torments (arising from external, internal, and both) flow along with him. Thus, seeing himself and the aggregate of beings overwhelmed by this beginningless stream of suffering, the yogi takes refuge in right vision (*samyagdarśana*), which is the cause for the destruction of all suffering.
