He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive generosity as real, nor does he perceive morality, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Buddha as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the emptiness of the essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Buddha as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all aspects as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, how does he train in the perfection of wisdom? How does he progress toward omniscience? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive generosity as real, nor does he perceive morality, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a Buddha as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of morality, patience, diligence, concentration, or wisdom as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as real, nor does he perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of that which has neither beginning nor end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-existence and existence, the emptiness of the essential nature, or the emptiness of the essential nature of non-essential nature as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Buddha as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all aspects as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real. It is by means of this non-perception that he trains in the perfection of wisdom and progresses toward omniscience. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, how can he be said to be irreversible from full enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, Mara the Evil One comes to him, taking on the guise of a monk, and says: ‘What you have heard, son of good family, regarding the bodhisattva path, that is not the word of the Buddha; it is the work of Mara. Son of good family, do not practice this; for in this Dharma there is no bodhisattva path, nor is there any teaching of a bodhisattva. Subhūti, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva, hearing these words, does not become afraid, terrified, or fall into terror, but remains firm and does not waver, then, Subhūti, one should know that this bodhisattva mahāsattva is irreversible from full enlightenment. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, why Mara the Evil One exerts himself so much to create obstacles for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom will, in the future, turn the wheel of the Dharma, and having turned the wheel of the Dharma, he will establish many hundreds of thousands of living beings in the fruit of a stream-enterer, and likewise in the fruits of a once-returner, a non-returner, and arhatship; he will establish them in the fruit of a pratyekabuddha, and he will establish them in the state of a Buddha. Subhūti, it is for this reason that Mara the Evil One exerts himself so much to create obstacles for a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection

"And because of the conflict between the functions of the *guṇas*, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person. The qualities (*guṇas*) of the intellect (*buddhi*), whose forms are manifestation (*prakhyā*), activity (*pravṛtti*), and inertia (*sthiti*), being dependent on one another’s mutual assistance, produce only a threefold cognition—whether peaceful, terrible, or deluded. And since the function of the *guṇas* is mobile, the mind is said to be subject to rapid transformation. Distinctive forms (*rūpa-atiśaya*) and distinctive functions (*vṛtti-atiśaya*) are mutually contradictory, whereas generalities (*sāmānya*) operate together with the distinctive features. Thus, these *guṇas*, by depending on one another, produce cognitions of pleasure, pain, and delusion; consequently, all of them take on every form. However, their distinction is created by the state of being primary or secondary (*guṇa-pradhāna-bhāva*). Therefore, everything is indeed suffering for the discerning person."

[77,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a sentient being, a soul, or a person. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the element of water, nor does he perceive the element of fire, nor does he perceive the element of wind, nor does he perceive the element of space, nor does he perceive the element of consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena. He does not perceive the past, nor does he perceive the future, nor does he perceive the present. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, nor does he perceive the fruit of a non-returner, nor does he perceive arhatship, nor does he perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive the state of a buddha. Why is this? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor purified, neither increasing nor decreasing. Since they are thus, a bodhisattva mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom does not apprehend any dharma, and because he does not apprehend any dharma, he does not become attached to any dharma. Because he is not attached to any dharma, he transcends the world with its gods, humans, and asuras, and attains unsurpassed perfect enlightenment.”

Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the seed from which this great mass of suffering arises. And its cause of non-existence is right vision (*samyagdarśana*). Just as the science of medicine consists of four divisions—disease, the cause of disease, health, and the medicine—so too this treatise consists of exactly four divisions. Namely: saṃsāra, the cause of saṃsāra, liberation (*mokṣa*), and the means to liberation. Among these, saṃsāra, which abounds in suffering, is that which is to be abandoned. The conjunction of *pradhāna* and the *puruṣa* is the cause of what is to be abandoned. The absolute cessation of that conjunction is abandonment. The means to abandonment is right vision.

In this regard, the intrinsic nature of the agent cannot be something to be abandoned or something to be adopted. If it were abandoned, it would entail the consequence of nihilism; if it were adopted, it would entail the doctrine of causality. To reject both [extremes] constitutes the view of eternalism. This is right view.
Thus, this treatise is called the "Fourfold Array" (*caturvyūha*):
"[That which is to be abandoned is future suffering]" (2.16).

[79,i] Past suffering has already been exhausted through experience and thus does not belong to the category of what is to be abandoned (*heya*). Present suffering, being occupied with its own moment of experience, does not become something to be abandoned in any subsequent moment. Therefore, it is only future suffering that afflicts the yogi who is like a blind man holding a bowl, and not the other practitioner; that alone becomes the object of abandonment.
Therefore, regarding that which alone is said to be what is to be abandoned, its cause is specifically pointed out:
"The conjunction of the seer and the seen is the cause of what is to be abandoned" (2.17).

The Puruṣa is the seer and the experiencer of the intellect (*buddhi*). All phenomena (*dharma*) mounted upon the intellect are the objects of sight. This object of sight, which is like a magnet, assists merely by its proximity; it becomes "one's own" to the Puruṣa, who is of the nature of the seer and the master, because it has become the objective domain of the act of experience. Although it has acquired its own nature as something distinct [from the Puruṣa] and is independent, it is dependent on another because it exists for the sake of another.

The beginningless conjunction of these two—the power of seeing (*dṛk-śakti*) and the power of being seen (*darśana-śakti*)—which is brought about by their objects, is the cause of that which is to be abandoned; the meaning is that it is the cause of suffering. And so it has been said: "By the avoidance of the cause of that conjunction, there may be this absolute remedy for suffering. Why? Because a remedy is observed for a cause of suffering that is to be avoided. For example: the susceptibility to being pierced of the sole of the foot, the piercing nature of the thorn, and the avoidance [of the thorn], which consists in not placing the foot upon it or placing it while separated by a shoe—one who knows these three in the world, when undertaking a remedy therein, does not experience the suffering born of piercing. Why? Because of the efficacy of perceiving the triad. Here too, it is *sattva* alone that is tormented by *rajas*, the tormentor. Why? Because the action of tormenting resides in its object (*karman*); the action of tormenting occurs in the object, which is *sattva*, and not in the *kṣetrajña*, who is unchanging and inactive, because his field of perception has already been shown. But when *sattva* is being tormented, the *puruṣa* also suffers along with it, conforming to its form.
The nature of the object of perception is now described:
The object of perception (dṛśya), which consists of the elements and the senses, has the nature of illumination, activity, and inertia, and exists for the sake of experience and liberation.

Sattva is characterized by illumination; rajas is characterized by activity; and tamas is characterized by inertia. These *guṇas* have mutually colored distinctions, are subject to transformation, possess the properties of conjunction and disjunction, and have acquired their forms through mutual dependence. Although they function as limbs to one another, their powers remain undivided; they follow the differentiation of powers both homogeneous and heterogeneous. At the time of the *pradhāna*, they manifest their presence; and even while being subordinate (*guṇa*), their existence is inferred through their mere operation within the *pradhāna*. Their capacity is impelled by the duty to accomplish the purpose of the *puruṣa*; they assist by their mere proximity, like magnets. Without requiring a conscious agent, they follow the activity of whichever one among them predominates, and thus they become denotable by the term *pradhāna*. This is called the "visible" (*dṛśya*).

[83,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who courses in the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is called the great vehicle of the Bodhisattvas, the great beings. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is this ‘great vehicle’? What is the meaning of the term ‘great vehicle’? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, because it is immeasurable, it is called the ‘great vehicle. Furthermore, Subhūti, because it is infinite, it is called the ‘great vehicle. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, in what way is it immeasurable, and in what way is it infinite? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is immeasurable in terms of form, feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. It is infinite in terms of the emptiness of form, the emptiness of feeling, the emptiness of perception, the emptiness of mental formations, and the emptiness of consciousness. It is immeasurable in terms of the emptiness of the internal, the emptiness of the external, and the emptiness of both internal and external. It is infinite in terms of the emptiness of emptiness, the emptiness of the great, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of the conditioned, the emptiness of the unconditioned, the emptiness of the limitless, the emptiness of that which has no beginning or end, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all phenomena, the emptiness of characteristics, the emptiness of non-apprehension, the emptiness of essential nature, and the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature. It is immeasurable in terms of the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and the great compassion of a Buddha. It is infinite in terms of the knowledge of all aspects. Subhūti, it is for these reasons that it is called the great vehicle. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, is there anything whatsoever that is included in the great vehicle? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, there is not even the slightest thing that is included in the great vehicle. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if there is not even the slightest thing included in the great vehicle, how can it be called a ‘great vehicle’? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are non-existent and unapprehendable that it is called the great vehicle. Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty, signless, wishless, effortless, unproduced, unarisen, unceased, and without intrinsic nature that it is called the great vehicle. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, although all dharmas are empty, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment by means of skillful means. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, what is this ‘skillful means’ of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, practices the perfection of giving, yet he does not perceive a gift, a giver, or a recipient. He practices the perfection of morality, yet he does not perceive morality, a transgression, or one who observes morality. He practices the perfection of patience, yet he does not perceive anger, patience, or one who is patient. He practices the perfection of vigor, yet he does not perceive vigor, laziness, or one who is vigorous. He practices the perfection of concentration, yet he does not perceive distraction, concentration, or one who is concentrated. He practices the perfection of wisdom, yet he does not perceive ignorance, wisdom, or one who is wise. This, Subhūti, is the skillful means of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.”

This [Prakṛti], which consists of the elements and the senses, transforms through the state of the elements—whether subtle or gross, such as earth and so forth—and likewise transforms through the state of the senses—whether subtle or gross, such as the ear and so forth. Moreover, it does not proceed without a purpose; rather, it proceeds having taken up a purpose. For that object of perception exists for the sake of experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) for the Puruṣa. In this regard, experience is the determination of the nature of the qualities (*guṇa*), whether desirable or undesirable, when they have reached a state of non-discrimination; liberation is the determination of the true nature of the experiencer. There is no other vision (*darśana*) beyond these two. And thus it has been said: "But indeed, while the three *guṇas* are agents and the Puruṣa is a non-agent—though the latter is of a different class from them and is the fourth witness of their activity—one who perceives all objects presented to him, even though they have come into being, suspects another [vision] beyond that."

[83,ii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara beheld those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs who were practicing the practice of the bodhisattva, and he addressed them as follows: "Sisters, you must not harbor fear; you must not harbor terror; you must not fall into despair. Why is that? Because, sisters, the Tathāgata is your refuge, the Tathāgata is your protector, and the Tathāgata is your guide. [83,iii] Then, sisters, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having thus encouraged those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, spoke these verses: "O you who have set out for the sake of all beings, Do not be afraid, do not tremble, do not despair. The Protector, the Great Sage, the One with Vision, Is your refuge; he will deliver you from all suffering. He who has transcended birth and death, Who has reached the end of existence, The One with Ten Powers, the Lion of Men— He will lead you across the ocean of saṃsāra. He who has abandoned all afflictions, Who is free from the net of craving, The One with Great Compassion, the Self-Existent— He will bring you to the state of peace. He who has cut through the bonds of Māra, Who has shattered the mountain of pride, The One with Great Wisdom, the Unconquered— He will establish you in the state beyond fear. He who has attained the ten powers, Who possesses the four fearlessnesses, The One with Great Renown, the Bull of Men— He will grant you the supreme state of nirvāṇa. Having spoken these verses, sisters, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara then said to those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs: "Sisters, you must cultivate mindfulness of the Buddha, mindfulness of the Dharma, and mindfulness of the Saṅgha. By cultivating such mindfulness, sisters, you shall quickly attain the realization of the bodhisattva path. [83,iv] Then, sisters, the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs, having heard these words of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, were filled with joy and great faith. They rose from their seats, prostrated at his feet, and circumambulated him three times before departing. And so, sisters, by the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s compassionate vow, those five hundred bhikṣuṇīs were able to dwell in the forest hermitage without fear or dread, and they practiced the holy life with diligence until they attained the fruit of arhatship. Thus, sisters, the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great protector of all beings, a great savior from all suffering, and a great source of refuge for those who wander in the darkness of ignorance. [83,v] Therefore, sisters, you should always invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, for by doing so, you shall be delivered from all danger and attain the unsurpassed state of enlightenment. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the five hundred bhikṣuṇīs and the entire assembly praised what the Blessed One had said. Thus ends the chapter on the Five Hundred Bhikṣuṇīs in the Lotus Sūtra, the Dharma-discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma. [83,vi] Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the city of Rājagṛha, on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Ānanda: "Ānanda, go to the city of Rājagṛha and announce to the lay devotee Yaśodharā: 'Yaśodharā, the Tathāgata now dwells in the city of Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas. He wishes to see you. You should come quickly. [83,vii] Then the venerable Ānanda, having received these instructions from the Blessed One, went to the house of the lay devotee Yaśodharā and spoke to her as follows: "Yaśodharā, the Tathāgata now dwells in the city of Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas. He wishes to see you. You should come quickly. [83,viii] Then the lay devotee Yaśodharā, having heard these words of the venerable Ānanda, was filled with joy and great faith. She prepared a great offering of food and drink, and with a retinue of many women, she set out for Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa. Upon arriving at the presence of the Blessed One, she prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and sat down to one side. [83,ix] Then the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the lay devotee Yaśodharā, preached the Dharma to her, exhorting, encouraging, and delighting her with a discourse on the wonders of the bodhisattva path. Having heard this teaching, the lay devotee Yaśodharā attained the stage of non-retrogression and vowed to become a buddha. Thus, Ānanda, the lay devotee Yaśodharā, through the power of the Tathāgata’s grace, has attained the fruit of the bodhisattva path. [83,x] Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that the Tathāgata is a great benefactor to all beings, a great teacher of the Dharma, and a great source of light in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly praised what the Blessed One had said. Thus ends the chapter on the Lay Devotee Yaśodharā in the Lotus Sūtra, the Dharma-discourse of the Lotus of the True Dharma. [83,xi] Thus have I heard: At one time the Blessed One was dwelling in the city of Śrāvastī, in the Jeta Grove, in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the Blessed One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: "Śāriputra, go to the city of Śrāvastī and announce to the lay devotee Viśākhā: 'Viśākhā, the Tathāgata now dwells in the city of Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas. He wishes to see you. You should come quickly. [83,xii] Then the venerable Śāriputra, having received these instructions from the Blessed One, went to the house of the lay devotee Viśākhā and spoke to her as follows: "Viśākhā, the Tathāgata now dwells in the city of Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, in the Garden of Anāthapiṇḍada, surrounded by a great assembly of bhikṣus and bodhisattvas. He wishes to see you. You should come quickly. [83,xiii] Then the lay devotee Viśākhā, having heard these words of the venerable Śāriputra, was filled with joy and great faith. She prepared a great offering of food and drink, and with a retinue of many women, she set out for the Jeta Grove. Upon arriving at the presence of the Blessed One, she prostrated at his feet, circumambulated him three times, and sat down to one side. [83,xiv] Then the Blessed One, knowing the thoughts of the lay devotee Viśākhā, preached the Dharma to her, exhorting, encouraging, and delighting her with a discourse on the wonders of the bodhisattva path. Having heard this teaching, the lay devotee Viśākhā attained the stage of non-retrogression and vowed to become a buddha. Thus, Śāriputra, the lay devotee Viśākhā, through the power of the Tathāgata’s grace, has attained the fruit of the bodhisattva path. [83,xv] Therefore, Śāriputra, you should know that the Tathāgata is a great benefactor to all beings, a great teacher

How is it that these two—enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), which are produced by the intellect (*buddhi*) and reside in the intellect alone—are attributed to the *puruṣa*? Just as victory or defeat, though occurring among the warriors, is attributed to the master, because he is the enjoyer of its fruit; so too, bondage and liberation, though occurring in the intellect alone, are attributed to the *puruṣa*, because he is the enjoyer of their fruit. Bondage is the intellect’s failure to complete the purpose of the *puruṣa*; liberation is the completion of that purpose. By this [analogy], apprehension, retention, deliberation, rejection, knowledge of reality, and attachment, though residing in the intellect, have their existence superimposed upon the *puruṣa*, because he is the enjoyer of their fruit.
[84,i] This is commenced for the purpose of determining the specific distinctions in the essential natures of perceptible qualities—
"The stages of the *guṇas* consist of the specific (*viśeṣa*), the non-specific (*aviśeṣa*), the mere-indicators (*liṅgamātra*), and the indicatorless (*aliṅga*).

(2.19) [84,iii] Among these, the elements—ether, air, fire, water, and earth—are the specific manifestations of the non-specific subtle elements (*tanmātras*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Likewise, the sense organs of cognition—the ear, skin, eye, tongue, and nose—and the organs of action—the voice, hands, feet, anus, and genitals, with the mind as the eleventh which pertains to all objects—these are the specific manifestations of the non-specific ego-sense (*asmitā*). This sixteenfold transformation constitutes the specific evolution of the *guṇas*."

There are six non-specific (aviśeṣa) principles. They are as follows: the subtle element of sound, the subtle element of touch, the subtle element of form, the subtle element of taste, and the subtle element of smell—these five non-specific principles are sound and the others, characterized by one, two, three, four, and five attributes respectively; and the sixth non-specific principle is the mere state of "I-am-ness" (asmitāmātra). These are the six transformations of the Great Principle (mahat), which is the Self consisting of pure existence (sattāmātra). That Great Principle, the Great Element, which is the mere sign (liṅgamātra) beyond the non-specific principles, is the locus wherein these [six] abide within the Great Self of pure existence and experience the culmination of their growth.

And as they are being reabsorbed, having come to rest in that very Great Self which is mere existence, they proceed toward that Pradhāna—which is neither existence nor non-existence, neither being nor non-being, unmanifest, and signless. This is their transformation into the mere sign (liṅgamātra), and it is the signless transformation (aliṅgapariṇāma) that is neither existence nor non-existence.

In the state of the unmanifest (*aliṅga*), the purpose of the Spirit (*puruṣārtha*) is not the cause; nor does the purpose of the Spirit become the cause at the beginning of the state of the unmanifest. Thus, because the purpose of the Spirit is not its cause, that state is called "eternal" (*nitya*). However, for the three specific states [of the manifest], the purpose of the Spirit is the cause at their inception. Since that purpose serves as the motive, the sign, and the cause, they are called "non-eternal" (*anitya*). The *guṇas*, however, which follow all attributes, neither perish nor are they produced. It is only through the individual manifestations—which possess the passing away of the past and the arrival of the future—that the *guṇas*, though constant, appear as if they possessed the properties of arising and perishing. This is analogous to the case where it is said, "Devadatta is becoming poor because his cows are dying"; his poverty results from the death of the cows alone, not from any loss of his own essential nature. Such is the resolution.

[86,ii] The mere *liṅga* (the principle of intellect) is proximate to the *aliṅga* (the unmanifest); therein, that which was merged is distinguished through the transcendence of the sequence. Likewise, the six *aviśeṣas* (non-specific principles), being merged in the *liṅgamātra*, are distinguished according to the fixed rule of the sequence of transformation. Similarly, within those *aviśeṣas*, the elements (*bhūtas*) and the senses (*indriyas*) are distinguished as they were merged. And so it has been stated previously: since there is no other principle beyond the *viśeṣas* (specific principles), the *viśeṣas* do not undergo transformation into another principle. However, their transformations of quality (*dharma*), characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*) will be explained. [87,i]

The object of sight has been explained; now this is commenced for the purpose of determining the true nature of the seer: "The seer is pure consciousness alone; though pure, he beholds the mental modifications. (2.20)

"Pure seeing" (*dṛśimātra*) means that the power of vision alone is untouched by any qualifying attributes. That *puruṣa* is the perceiver of the intellect (*buddhi*). It is neither identical with the intellect nor entirely different from it. First of all, it is not identical; why? Because the intellect has objects both known and unknown, for the intellect is subject to transformation (*pariṇāminī*). By stating that its objects—such as cows or jars—are both known and unknown, he demonstrates its state of being subject to transformation.

The fact that the object is always known demonstrates the unchanging nature (*apariṇāmitva*) of the Puruṣa. Why? Because it is impossible for the intellect (*buddhi*) to be both the object of the Puruṣa and yet be simultaneously unperceived and perceived; thus, it is established that the object is always known to the Puruṣa, and from that, his unchanging nature follows. Furthermore, the intellect is for the sake of another because it acts through conjunction, whereas the Puruṣa is for his own sake. Likewise, the intellect consists of the three *guṇas* because it determines all objects, and because it consists of the three *guṇas*, it is insentient (*acetana*). The Puruṣa, however, is the witness of the *guṇas*; therefore, he is not of the same nature as them.

"Let it be, then, that [the Self] is dissimilar. Why is it not absolutely dissimilar? Because even though it is pure, it is a "perceiver of the mental modification" (*pratyayānupaśya*). It perceives the mental modification belonging to the intellect (*bauddha*); perceiving that, although it does not have that as its essence, it appears as if it were of that very nature. And so it has been said: "The power of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛśakti*) is indeed unchanging and non-transferrable, yet it appears as if transferred into the changing object; it follows the activity of that [object]. And because it merely imitates the activity of the intellect whose form has acquired the reflection of consciousness, the activity of knowledge is described as being indistinguishable from the activity of the intellect."
[89,i] "The very object for that purpose is the nature of the visible.

The object of sight (dṛśya) has attained the state of being an object for the Puruṣa, whose nature is seeing; thus, the very purpose of the object of sight becomes the self (ātman) of that [Puruṣa]. The meaning is that it becomes his own nature (svarūpa). However, when the purpose of experience and liberation has been accomplished by the Puruṣa, the object of sight—which had acquired its selfhood through the form of the other—is no longer seen by the Puruṣa. Because of this loss of its own nature (svarūpa), its destruction would follow, yet it does not perish.
Why? [90,i]
"Although it has perished for one who has accomplished his purpose, it has not perished, because it is common to others. (2.22)

For a single person whose purpose has been fulfilled, the object of sight (*dṛśya*), although it has perished—that is, although it has reached destruction—is not destroyed for others, because it is common to other persons. Even though it has reached destruction for a virtuous person, it has not fulfilled its purpose for non-virtuous persons; thus, it indeed attains the status of being an object of action for their vision, and by means of another's form, it obtains its own form. And therefore, because the powers of seeing and the seen are eternal, their conjunction is explained as being beginningless (*anādi*). Thus it has been said: "Because the substrates (*dharmin*) are in a beginningless conjunction, the conjunction of the mere attributes (*dharma*) is also beginningless."
[91,i] This sūtra was composed with the intention of explaining the essential nature of conjunction:
"Conjunction is the cause for the perception of the essential nature of both the self and the Lord" (2.23).

The Puruṣa, the master, is conjoined with the object of sight for the purpose of seeing. From that conjunction, whatever perception of the object occurs is experience (*bhoga*). However, the perception of the seer’s own true nature is liberation (*apavarga*). Since conjunction terminates with the completion of the act of seeing, seeing is said to be the cause of disjunction. Seeing is the adversary of non-seeing; thus, non-seeing is said to be the cause of conjunction. In this context, seeing is not the direct cause of liberation; rather, the absence of bondage results precisely from the absence of non-seeing—that is liberation. When seeing exists, non-seeing, which is the cause of bondage, is destroyed; therefore, seeing—meaning knowledge—is said to be the cause of isolation (*kaivalya*).

[92,i] Furthermore, what is this so-called "non-perception"? Is it the cessation of the activity of the *guṇas*, or rather the non-arising of the primary mind (*pradhānacitta*), which is the Lord whose nature is vision and who has already displayed the objects? It is the absence of perception while its own object of vision remains present.

Is it that the qualities (*guṇas*) possess purposefulness? Or is ignorance (*avidyā*), having ceased together with one's own mind, the seed for the arising of that very mind? Is it that when the formative forces of stability (*sthitisaṃskāra*) have perished, the formative forces of motion (*gatisaṃskāra*) become manifest? Regarding this, it has been said: "If the primary cause (*pradhāna*) were to exist solely through its state of stability, it would not be a primary cause because it would fail to produce transformations."

Likewise, if it were to exist solely through its own movement (*gati*), it would be subordinate (*apradhāna*) due to the impermanence of modification. Its activity (*vṛtti*) acquires the designation "Pradhāna" (the Primary Cause) only in both ways [through *gati* and *vikāra*], and not otherwise. An identical analysis applies even when other causes are postulated. Some maintain that non-perception (*adarśana*) is simply the power of perception (*darśana-śakti*), based on the scriptural statement: "The activity of the Pradhāna is for the sake of manifesting itself."

Prior to its engagement, the person, though capable of awakening to all objects of awakening, does not see; the object of vision, though capable of performing all functions, is not seen at that time. Some maintain that the non-perception of both is their inherent nature (*dharma*).

In this regard, although this vision is the very self-nature of the object of perception (*dṛśya*), it becomes a property of the object of perception by depending upon the mental faculty (*pratyaya*) of the Puruṣa. Likewise, although non-vision is not the self-nature of the Puruṣa, it appears as if it were a property of the Puruṣa by depending upon the mental faculty of the object of perception. Some declare that non-vision is simply knowledge (*jñāna*) itself. These are the various conceptual constructions found in the treatises. Among these, this multiplicity of conceptual constructions concerns the common objects resulting from the conjunction of the Guṇas with all Puruṣas. However, as for the conjunction of the individual conscious being with its own intellect (*buddhi*)—
[94,iii] "Its cause is ignorance" (2.24) [95,i]

The meaning is "the latent impression (*vāsanā*) of erroneous cognition. Furthermore, a *buddhi* permeated by the latent impressions of erroneous cognition does not reach the culmination of its task, which is the discernment of the *puruṣa*; it returns again, still possessing its functional mandate (*sādhikārā*). But that [other *buddhi*] reaches the culmination of its task, which terminates in the discernment of the *puruṣa*; having fulfilled its mandate, with non-perception having ceased and due to the absence of the cause of bondage, it does not return again.

On this point, someone introduces the story of the eunuch (*paṇḍaka*): A foolish wife says to him, "Noble son, my sister has offspring; why is it that I do not? He replies to her, "I am dead; how shall I produce offspring for you? Likewise, this existing knowledge does not bring about the cessation of the mind; what hope is there that it will do so once it has perished? Regarding this, one who is like a teacher says: "Is not liberation simply the cessation of the intellect (*buddhi*), since the cessation of the intellect occurs due to the absence of the cause of non-perception (*adarśana*)? And that non-perception, which is the cause of bondage, ceases through perception (*darśana*). Therefore, liberation is indeed the cessation of the mind (*citta*); why then is there this misplaced confusion of his mind?"

That which is to be abandoned— suffering— and the cause of that which is to be abandoned, known as conjunction along with its instrumental cause, have been explained; hereafter, abandonment (hāna) must be discussed.
"From the absence of that, there is the absence of conjunction; this is cessation, which is the isolation of the Seer" (2.25).

The meaning is that from the absence of that non-perception (*adarśana*), there is the absolute absence of the conjunction between the intellect (*buddhi*) and the person (*puruṣa*), which is the end of bondage. This is cessation (*hāna*). "Isolation of the Seer" means the person's state of non-mixture, i.e., non-conjunction again with the *guṇas*. When the cause of suffering has ceased, the cessation of suffering is cessation; at that time, it is said that the person is established in its own nature.
[96,iv] Now, what is the means for attaining abandonment?
"Uninterrupted discriminative discernment is the means to liberation" (2.26).

The discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the cognition of the distinctness between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*. However, as long as false knowledge has not been ceased, that discernment fluctuates. When false knowledge becomes like a burnt seed—rendered incapable of producing further results—then for the *sattva* whose impurity of afflictions (*kleśa-rajas*) has been shaken off, and which abides in supreme clarity and the highest consciousness of mastery, the flow of discriminative cognition becomes stainless. That undisturbed discriminative discernment is the means for the removal [of suffering]. Thereupon, false knowledge reaches the state of a burnt seed and no longer produces [results]; this is the path to liberation, the means for its removal.
[97,ii] "His wisdom is sevenfold, reaching the ultimate stage.

The word "of him" (tasya) is a reference back to one for whom discriminative knowledge has arisen. "Sevenfold" means that, due to the removal of the impurities of the veil of impurity and the non-arising of other mental modifications, the wisdom of the discerning one becomes sevenfold.

That is to say: that which was to be abandoned has been fully known; there is nothing further for him to know. The causes of what is to be abandoned have been exhausted; there is nothing further to be exhausted for them. Abandonment has been realized through the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*). The means of abandonment, consisting of discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), has been cultivated. This fourfold result belongs to wisdom (*prajñā*). As for the liberation of the mind (*cittavimukti*), it is the intellect (*buddhi*) whose functional mandate has been fulfilled. Like stones fallen from the slope of a mountain peak, the *guṇas*—having no further station and tending toward dissolution—set along with their cause. Once dissolved, there is no further arising of these *guṇas*, because of the absence of any purpose. In this state, the *puruṣa* is one who has transcended the connection with the *guṇas*, a stainless light consisting of its own nature alone, the *kevalī*. One who contemplates this sevenfold wisdom of the final stage is called "skilled. Even upon the re-absorption of the mind, he remains liberated and skilled precisely because he has transcended the *guṇas*.

[98,i] It has been established that discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*) is the means to liberation; and since no accomplishment is possible without a means of achievement (*sādhana*), this [section] is now commenced:
"From the practice of the limbs of yoga, upon the destruction of impurity, there is the illumination of knowledge up to discriminative discernment.

The eight limbs of yoga are about to be described. From their practice comes the destruction—that is, the cessation—of the five-fold error which consists of impurity. Upon that destruction, right knowledge becomes manifest. To the extent that the means are practiced, to that same extent does impurity undergo attenuation. And to the extent that it is diminished, to that same extent the radiance of knowledge increases, following the sequence of that diminution. This very increase reaches its culmination up until discriminative discernment (*vivekakhyāti*), meaning up until the specific realization of the true nature of the *guṇas* and the *puruṣa*. The practice of the limbs of yoga is the cause of separation from impurity, just as an axe is the cause of cutting what is to be cut. But it is the cause of the attainment of discriminative discernment, just as merit (*dharma*) is the cause of happiness; it is not otherwise a cause. How many such causes are there in the treatise? He says: "There are exactly nine. They are as follows: [the list of nine causes follows].
“Arising, persistence, manifestation, transformation, acquisition, separation, change, support, and attainment— these are remembered as the ninefold causes.”

Thus it is said. [99,iii] In this regard, the mind (*manas*) is the cause of the arising (*utpatti-kāraṇa*) of consciousness; the purpose of the person (*puruṣārthatā*) is the cause of the subsistence (*sthiti-kāraṇa*) of the mind, just as food is for the body. The cause of manifestation (*abhivyakti-kāraṇa*) is, for example, light for a visible form, and likewise the cognition of form for the form itself. The cause of modification (*vikāra-kāraṇa*) is another object for the mind, just as fire is for that which is to be cooked. The cause of conviction (*pratyaya-kāraṇa*) is the cognition of smoke for the cognition of fire. The cause of attainment (*prāpti-kāraṇa*) is the practice of the limbs of yoga for discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*).

[100,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is established as a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is established as the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them. Because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. Not being attached, he does not tremble; being unafraid, he has transcended all error and dwells having attained the ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Subhūti, this is the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great beings. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the reason, what is the cause, why the bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive a dharma that is established as a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is established as the perfection of wisdom? Why does he not apprehend them, and because he does not apprehend them, why is he not attached? Why, not being attached, does he not tremble, and being unafraid, does he transcend all error and dwell having attained the ultimate *nirvāṇa*? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature. Subhūti, since all dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature, a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is established as a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma that is established as the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them. Because he does not apprehend them, he is not attached. Not being attached, he does not tremble; being unafraid, he transcends all error and dwells having attained the ultimate *nirvāṇa*. Subhūti, this is the great vehicle of the bodhisattvas, the great beings.”

That very [cause] is the cause of disjunction from impurity. The cause of otherness is, for example, the goldsmith in relation to gold. Likewise, for a single objective condition (strī-pratyaya), ignorance is the cause of delusion, hatred of its state as suffering, passion of its state as pleasure, and knowledge of reality of its state as neutrality. The body is the cause of support for the senses, and they [the senses] are [the cause of support] for that [body]. The great elements are the cause of support for bodies, and they are [the cause of support] for one another; and all those belonging to the animal, human, and divine realms are so because they serve each other’s purposes. Thus, there are nine causes. These are to be applied to other categories of objects as well, according to their possibility. However, the practice of the limbs of yoga obtains causality in only two ways.
[101,i] In this regard, the limbs of yoga are now determined—
"Restraints, observances, postures, breath-control, withdrawal of the senses, concentration, meditation, and absorption are the eight limbs" (2.29).
We shall explain their performance and their essential nature in due order.
In that regard— [102,iii]
Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, and non-possession are the restraints (Yamas).

In this context, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of malice toward all living beings in every way and at all times. The subsequent restraints (*yama*) and observances (*niyama*) are rooted in it; they are taught solely for the purpose of its accomplishment and are adopted specifically to purify its form. Thus it has been said: "Indeed, as this Brahmin undertakes more and more vows, so he turns away from the causes of violence committed through negligence, thereby making that very non-violence pure in form.

Truth consists of speech and thought that accord with reality; that is, speech and mind should correspond exactly to what has been seen and what has been inferred. Speech is uttered for the sake of transferring one's own understanding to another, provided that it is not deceptive, erroneous, or barren of comprehension. This [truth] is intended for the benefit of all beings, not for their injury. Even if spoken in this manner, if it were solely intent upon injuring a being, it would not be truth; it would be a sin. Through that semblance of merit, that counterfeit of virtue, one would fall into terrible darkness. Therefore, having investigated, one should speak a truth that is beneficial to all beings.

[103,i] Theft is the unauthorized appropriation of another's property not in accordance with the scriptures; its prohibition, moreover, is non-stealing, which consists of the absence of desire for such things. Celibacy is the restraint of the organ of generation through the guarding of the senses. Non-possessiveness is the refusal to accept objects due to perceiving the faults in their acquisition, preservation, loss, attachment, and destruction—these are the restraints (yamās).
But they— [104,ii] "Unrestricted by birth, place, time, or circumstance, universal in scope, constitute the Great Vow (2.31)."

[104,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘bodhisattva’ as a designation. He does not perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom’ as a designation. He does not perceive the six perfections, nor does he perceive ‘six perfections’ as a designation. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, nor does he perceive ‘thirty-seven factors of enlightenment’ as a designation. He does not perceive the four noble truths, nor does he perceive ‘four noble truths’ as a designation. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive ‘ten powers of a Tathāgata’ as a designation. He does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, nor does he perceive ‘four grounds of self-confidence’ as a designation. He does not perceive the four analytical knowledges, nor does he perceive ‘four analytical knowledges’ as a designation. He does not perceive the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, nor does he perceive ‘eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha’ as a designation. He does not perceive omniscience, nor does he perceive ‘omniscience’ as a designation. He does not perceive the level of a śrāvaka, nor does he perceive ‘level of a śrāvaka’ as a designation. He does not perceive the level of a pratyekabuddha, nor does he perceive ‘level of a pratyekabuddha’ as a designation. He does not perceive the level of a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘level of a bodhisattva’ as a designation. He does not perceive the level of a Tathāgata, nor does he perceive ‘level of a Tathāgata’ as a designation. Why is that? Because, Subhūti, these dharmas are all empty; they are non-existent, unapprehendable, and without intrinsic nature.”

In this regard, non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) delimited by species is when a fisherman practices violence only toward fish and not toward others. That same [non-violence] delimited by place is "I shall not kill at a sacred ford (*tīrtha*). That same [non-violence] delimited by time is "I shall not kill on the fourteenth day, nor on an auspicious day. That same [non-violence] delimited by occasion for one who has desisted from the three [previous delimiters] is "I shall not kill for the sake of gods or Brahmins, but not otherwise. And just as for Kṣatriyas, violence is restricted to battle alone and not elsewhere; non-violence and the other [virtues] must be observed in every way without being delimited by such species, place, time, or occasion. When they are practiced across all grounds, regarding all objects, and are entirely free from deviation, they are called the "Universal Great Vows" (*sārvabhauma-mahāvratam*).
"Purity, contentment, austerity, self-study, and devotion to the Lord are the observances (YS 2.32)."

In this context, purity (*śauca*) consists of external purification produced by earth, water, and so forth, as well as the consumption of pure substances; internal purification is the washing away of the impurities of the mind. Contentment (*saṃtoṣa*) is the lack of desire for more than the means currently at hand. Austerity (*tapas*) is the endurance of the pairs of opposites (*dvaṃdva*). These pairs are hunger and thirst, cold and heat, standing and sitting, and both silence like a log (*kāṣṭhamauna*) and silence through gesture (*ākāramauna*). Their observances (*vrata*) are, as appropriate, the *kṛcchra*, *cāndrāyaṇa*, *sāṃtapana*, and other such penances. Self-study (*svādhyāya*) is the study of the treatises on liberation or the recitation of the *praṇava*. Devotion to the Lord (*īśvarapraṇidhāna*) is the dedication of all actions to Him, the Supreme Teacher.
Whether staying in a bed or a seat, or walking on a path, being composed and with the web of discursive thoughts exhausted,
one who perceives the destruction of the seed of saṃsāra will, through constant application, partake in the enjoyment of the deathless.
Regarding this,
it has been stated: "From that, there is the realization of the inward-turned consciousness, as well as the absence of obstacles."
Regarding these restraints and observances:
"When there is obstruction by discursive thoughts, one should cultivate the counter-measures" (Yoga Sūtra 2.33).

[105,v] The mind is not produced by itself, nor is it produced by another; it is not produced by both, nor is it produced without cause. How could that which is thus unproduced ever arise? It is like a flower in the sky. Since it does not exist, how can there be a cessation of it? Therefore, the mind is empty of intrinsic nature. Because it is empty, it is without arising or cessation. Because it is without arising or cessation, it is quiescent from the very beginning. Because it is quiescent from the very beginning, it is naturally extinguished.
