When such thoughts of violence and the like arise in this brahmin—such as, "I shall kill the wrongdoer," "I shall speak even untruth," "I shall take his property," "I shall commit adultery with his wife," or "I shall become the master of his possessions"—and when he is afflicted by the intensely blazing fever of thoughts inclined toward the wrong path, he should cultivate their antidotes. He should reflect: "The yoga-dharma consists in granting fearlessness to all beings; it has been adopted as a refuge by me while I was being cooked in the terrible embers of *saṃsāra*. Indeed, if I were to abandon these thoughts and then take them up again, I would be equal to one who lives like a dog. Just as a dog licks what has been vomited, so too is he who takes back what has been abandoned. This and other such [reflections] should also be applied to other sūtras.

"Discursive thoughts such as violence and so forth—whether performed, caused to be performed, or approved; whether preceded by greed, anger, or delusion; whether mild, middling, or intense—have suffering and infinite ignorance as their results; thus one should cultivate the counteractive measures.

In this regard, violence (*hiṃsā*) first of all is threefold: committed, caused to be committed, and consented to. Each of these is again threefold: by greed—for the sake of meat or skin; by anger—thinking "this person has done me harm"; and by delusion—thinking "this will be my merit. Greed, anger, and delusion are further divided into three types: mild, moderate, and intense. Thus, there are twenty-seven varieties of violence. These mild, moderate, and intense types are each again threefold: mild-mild, moderate-mild, and intense-mild; likewise, mild-moderate, moderate-moderate, and intense-moderate; and likewise, mild-intense, moderate-intense, and intense-intense. In this way, violence consists of eighty-one varieties. Furthermore, through the distinctions of restriction, option, and combination, it becomes innumerable, because the varieties of living beings are incalculable. This same principle should be applied to falsehood and the other [non-virtues] as well.

[106,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend that form is permanent, nor does he apprehend that it is impermanent; he does not apprehend that feeling is permanent, nor does he apprehend that it is impermanent; he does not apprehend that perception is permanent, nor does he apprehend that it is impermanent; he does not apprehend that formations are permanent, nor does he apprehend that they are impermanent; he does not apprehend that consciousness is permanent, nor does he apprehend that it is impermanent. He does not apprehend that form is pleasant, nor does he apprehend that it is painful; he does not apprehend that feeling is pleasant, nor does he apprehend that it is painful; he does not apprehend that perception is pleasant, nor does he apprehend that it is painful; he does not apprehend that formations are pleasant, nor does he apprehend that they are painful; he does not apprehend that consciousness is pleasant, nor does he apprehend that it is painful. He does not apprehend that form is self, nor does he apprehend that it is non-self; he does not apprehend that feeling is self, nor does he apprehend that it is non-self; he does not apprehend that perception is self, nor does he apprehend that it is non-self; he does not apprehend that formations are self, nor does he apprehend that they are non-self; he does not apprehend that consciousness is self, nor does he apprehend that it is non-self. He does not apprehend that form is empty, nor does he apprehend that it is not empty; he does not apprehend that feeling is empty, nor does he apprehend that it is not empty; he does not apprehend that perception is empty, nor does he apprehend that it is not empty; he does not apprehend that formations are empty, nor does he apprehend that they are not empty; he does not apprehend that consciousness is empty, nor does he apprehend that it is not empty. He does not apprehend that form is signless, nor does he apprehend that it is signless; he does not apprehend that feeling is signless, nor does he apprehend that it is signless; he does not apprehend that perception is signless, nor does he apprehend that it is signless; he does not apprehend that formations are signless, nor does he apprehend that they are signless; he does not apprehend that consciousness is signless, nor does he apprehend that it is signless. He does not apprehend that form is wishless, nor does he apprehend that it is wishless; he does not apprehend that feeling is wishless, nor does he apprehend that it is wishless; he does not apprehend that perception is wishless, nor does he apprehend that it is wishless; he does not apprehend that formations are wishless, nor does he apprehend that they are wishless; he does not apprehend that consciousness is wishless, nor does he apprehend that it is wishless. He does not apprehend that form is calm, nor does he apprehend that it is not calm; he does not apprehend that feeling is calm, nor does he apprehend that it is not calm; he does not apprehend that perception is calm, nor does he apprehend that it is not calm; he does not apprehend that formations are calm, nor does he apprehend that they are not calm; he does not apprehend that consciousness is calm, nor does he apprehend that it is not calm. He does not apprehend that form is sublime, nor does he apprehend that it is not sublime; he does not apprehend that feeling is sublime, nor does he apprehend that it is not sublime; he does not apprehend that perception is sublime, nor does he apprehend that it is not sublime; he does not apprehend that formations are sublime, nor does he apprehend that they are not sublime; he does not apprehend that consciousness is sublime, nor does he apprehend that it is not sublime. He does not apprehend that form is void, nor does he apprehend that it is not void; he does not apprehend that feeling is void, nor does he apprehend that it is not void; he does not apprehend that perception is void, nor does he apprehend that it is not void; he does not apprehend that formations are void, nor does he apprehend that they are not void; he does not apprehend that consciousness is void, nor does he apprehend that it is not void. He does not apprehend that form is unconditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is conditioned; he does not apprehend that feeling is unconditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is conditioned; he does not apprehend that perception is unconditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is conditioned; he does not apprehend that formations are unconditioned, nor does he apprehend that they are conditioned; he does not apprehend that consciousness is unconditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is conditioned. He does not apprehend that form is transcendent, nor does he apprehend that it is mundane; he does not apprehend that feeling is transcendent, nor does he apprehend that it is mundane; he does not apprehend that perception is transcendent, nor does he apprehend that it is mundane; he does not apprehend that formations are transcendent, nor does he apprehend that they are mundane; he does not apprehend that consciousness is transcendent, nor does he apprehend that it is mundane. He does not apprehend that form is past, nor does he apprehend that it is future, nor does he apprehend that it is present; he does not apprehend that feeling is past, nor does he apprehend that it is future, nor does he apprehend that it is present; he does not apprehend that perception is past, nor does he apprehend that it is future, nor does he apprehend that it is present; he does not apprehend that formations are past, nor does he apprehend that they are future, nor does he apprehend that they are present; he does not apprehend that consciousness is past, nor does he apprehend that it is future, nor does he apprehend that it is present. He does not apprehend that form is produced, nor does he apprehend that it is ceased; he does not apprehend that feeling is produced, nor does he apprehend that it is ceased; he does not apprehend that perception is produced, nor does he apprehend that it is ceased; he does not apprehend that formations are produced, nor does he apprehend that they are ceased; he does not apprehend that consciousness is produced, nor does he apprehend that it is ceased. He does not apprehend that form is defiled, nor does he apprehend that it is purified; he does not apprehend that feeling is defiled, nor does he apprehend that it is purified; he does not apprehend that perception is defiled, nor does he apprehend that it is purified; he does not apprehend that formations are defiled, nor does he apprehend that they are purified; he does not apprehend that consciousness is defiled, nor does he apprehend that it is purified. He does not apprehend that form is inferior, nor does he apprehend that it is superior; he does not apprehend that feeling is inferior, nor does he apprehend that it is superior; he does not apprehend that perception is inferior, nor does he apprehend that it is superior; he does not apprehend that formations are inferior, nor does he apprehend that they are superior; he does not apprehend that consciousness is inferior, nor does he apprehend that it is superior. He does not apprehend that form is with outflows, nor does he apprehend that it is without outflows; he does not apprehend that feeling is with outflows, nor does he apprehend that it is without outflows; he does not apprehend that perception is with outflows, nor does he apprehend that it is without outflows; he does not apprehend that formations are with outflows, nor does he apprehend that they are without outflows; he does not apprehend that consciousness is with outflows, nor does he apprehend that it is without outflows. He does not apprehend that form is conditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is unconditioned; he does not apprehend that feeling is conditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is unconditioned; he does not apprehend that perception is conditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is unconditioned; he does not apprehend that formations are conditioned, nor does he apprehend that they are unconditioned; he does not apprehend that consciousness is conditioned, nor does he apprehend that it is unconditioned. He does not apprehend that form is compounded, nor does he apprehend that it is uncompounded; he does not apprehend that feeling is compounded, nor does he apprehend that it is uncompounded; he does not apprehend that perception is compounded, nor does he apprehend that it is uncompounded; he does not apprehend that formations are compounded, nor does he apprehend that they are uncompounded; he does not apprehend that consciousness is compounded, nor does he apprehend that it is uncompounded. He does not apprehend that form is afflicted, nor does he apprehend that it is purified; he does not apprehend that feeling is afflicted, nor does he apprehend that it is purified; he does not apprehend that perception is afflicted, nor does he appreh

Indeed, these thoughts have suffering and ignorance as their infinite fruit; thus is the cultivation of the antidote. That is to say, the cultivation of the antidote consists in [recognizing] those whose fruit is infinite suffering and ignorance. For instance, first of all, the injurer deprives the victim of his vitality (*vīrya*). Then, by the falling of weapons and the like, he causes him pain. Thereafter, he even deprives him of life. From the deprivation of vitality, his conscious and unconscious implements become exhausted in their power. From the production of suffering, he experiences pain in the hells, among animals, hungry ghosts, and so forth. Because of the taking of life, existing at every moment on the brink of death, even though he desires death, he somehow barely breathes, because the ripening of that suffering must necessarily be experienced. And if, by some chance, the injury were accompanied by merit, then upon the attainment of happiness there would be shortness of life. In this same way, it should be applied to falsehood and the other [non-virtues] as far as possible. Thus, contemplating this very undesirable ripening that follows upon such thoughts, one should not direct the mind toward them.
[107,i] When,

due to the cultivation of the counteractive measures (*pratipakṣa*), his discursive thoughts (*vitarka*) become subject to abandonment and no longer have the nature of arising, then the mastery (*aiśvarya*) produced thereby becomes an indicator of accomplishment (*siddhi*) for the yogin. For example—
"When non-violence is firmly established, there occurs the abandonment of enmity in its presence by all living beings" (2.35).
This happens for all creatures.
[107,iv] “Upon the establishment of the truths, there is the state of being the locus for the fruit of action” (2.36).
Thinking, "May he become righteous," he becomes righteous; thinking, "May you attain heaven," he attains heaven; his speech becomes unfailing.
[108,i] "When established in non-stealing, there is the provision of all jewels" (2.37).
Precious jewels from all directions attend upon him.

"When one is established in the holy life (*brahmacarya*), there is the attainment of vigor (*vīrya*). (2.38) Through the attainment of which, one causes unimpeded qualities to flourish; and having achieved this, one becomes capable of instilling knowledge in those to be trained (*vineya*).
"When non-appropriation is stabilized, there is the awakening to the manner of one's births" (2.39).

The inquiry regarding the nature of one's own self—such as "Who was I? How was I? What indeed is this? How indeed is this? Or who shall we become? Or how shall we become?"—arises in him with respect to the past, the future, and the middle [present] states. These are the perfections (*siddhis*) resulting from steadiness in *yama*.
We shall discuss them further under the *niyamas*.
[109,ii] "From purity comes disgust for one's own body and non-association with others" (2.40).

One who undertakes purification out of disgust for one's own limbs becomes an ascetic who perceives the body as faulty and is free from attachment to the body. Furthermore, being unassociated with others, observing the true nature of the body, and desiring to abandon even his own body, how could he—seeing no purity in the body even while washing it with earth, water, and so forth—ever associate with the bodies of others, which are utterly impure?
Moreover—
[109,v] "Purity of being, cheerfulness, one-pointedness, mastery over the faculties, and fitness for the vision of the self" (2.41).

"they come to be" is the completion of the sentence. From purity comes purification of the *sattva*; from that, cheerfulness; from that, one-pointedness; from that, mastery over the senses; and from that, the fitness of the *buddhi-sattva* for the perception of the Self—this is attained through the steadiness of purity.
"From contentment comes the attainment of unsurpassed happiness" (2.42).
And so it has been said: [109,ix]
“Whatever sensual pleasure there is in the world, and whatever great divine pleasure there is—
these are not worth even a sixteenth part of the bliss that comes from the exhaustion of craving.
Thus it is said.
"The perfection of the sense-organ of the body results from the destruction of impurity through austerity. (2.43)

As the austerity (*tapas*) is being accomplished, it destroys the impurity of the veil; from the removal of that veiling impurity, there arises the perfection of the body (*kāyasiddhi*), such as the powers of *aṇimā* and so forth. Likewise, there is the perfection of the senses (*indriyasiddhi*), such as hearing and seeing from a distance.
[2.43] "From the study of one's own sacred texts (*svādhyāya*), there is communion with the chosen deity" (2.44).
Gods, seers, and perfected beings come into the sight of one who is devoted to the practice of private recitation, and they assist him in his undertakings.
"Success in samādhi comes from devotion to Īśvara" (2.45).

For one who has surrendered all states of being to Īśvara, there is success in samādhi by which he knows everything desired—unerringly—in another place, another body, and another time. Consequently, his wisdom perceives things as they truly are.
The restraints (yama) and observances (niyama), together with their attainments (siddhi), have been explained; we shall now describe the postures (āsana) and the others therein.
[110.viii]
"A posture is steady and comfortable" (2.46).

For example: the lotus posture (*padmāsana*), the auspicious posture (*bhadrāsana*), the cross-legged posture (*svastika*), the staff posture (*daṇḍāsana*), the supported posture (*sopāśraya*), the couch posture (*paryaṅka*), the crane's seat (*krauñcaniṣadana*), the elephant's seat (*hastiniṣadana*), the camel's seat (*uṣṭraniṣadana*), the balanced stance (*samasaṃsthāna*), the steady and comfortable posture, and the posture as one pleases, and so forth.
[111,ii] "By means of relaxation of effort and meditative absorption on the infinite" (2.47) [111,iii]

The ellipsis of the sentence is "it comes to be. Through the cessation of effort, the posture is perfected, by which one does not experience trembling of the limbs. Alternatively, the mind, when absorbed in the Infinite (*ananta*), brings about the perfection of the posture.
[Yoga Sūtra 2.47] "From that, there is no affliction by the pairs of opposites" (2.48).
Through mastery of the posture, one is not overcome by the pairs of opposites, such as cold and heat.
"When that [posture] exists, the cessation of the flow of inhalation and exhalation is breath control (prāṇāyāma) (2.49).

When mastery of posture has been attained, the drawing in of external air is inhalation (śvāsa), and the expulsion of internal air is exhalation (praśvāsa); the cessation of their flow, the absence of both, is breath control.
But that—
"The flow of the breath, whether external or internal, which is regulated by place, time, and number, becomes long and subtle.

Where there is an absence of movement preceded by exhalation, that is the external [breath]. Where there is an absence of movement preceded by inhalation, that is the internal [breath]. The third is the state of suspension (*stambha-vṛtti*), where both cease simultaneously through a single effort; just as water placed on a heated stone undergoes contraction on all sides, so too do both movements cease at once. These three are "observed by space" (*deśa-paridṛṣṭa*) in the sense that their range is defined, such that one knows, "this is the extent of its domain. They are "observed by time" (*kāla-paridṛṣṭa*) in the sense that they are delimited by the determination of the number of moments (*kṣaṇa*). They are "observed by number" (*saṃkhyā-paridṛṣṭa*) in the sense that the first upward surge (*udghāta*) occurs after this many inhalations and exhalations, and likewise the second and third surges occur when the breath is similarly restrained for that many counts. Thus, they are observed by number as being mild, moderate, or intense. Indeed, when practiced in this way, it becomes long and subtle.
"The fourth [dhyāna] projects external and internal objects" (2.51).

[The third type of breath control] is that which is observed with respect to external objects and is projected by means of place, time, and number; likewise, [the fourth] is that which is observed with respect to internal objects and is projected. In both cases, it is long and subtle. Preceded by that [third type], the fourth breath control is the absence of movement in both [inhalation and exhalation] through the gradual mastery of the stages. However, the third is the absence of movement not yet observed with respect to objects, which, having been undertaken once, is observed by means of place, time, and number as being long and subtle. But the fourth breath control is the absence of movement preceded by the projection of both [breaths] through the gradual mastery of the stages, resulting from the determination of the limits of the objects of inhalation and exhalation; this is the distinction.
[114,i] "Thereupon, the obscuration of the light is destroyed" (2.52) [114,ii]

For this yogin who practices *prāṇāyāma*, that karma which veils discriminative knowledge (*vivekajñāna*) is destroyed. Regarding that, they say: "By means of a magical net consisting of great delusion (*mahāmoha*), it veils *sattva*—which is by nature luminous—and yokes it to what ought not to be done. This karma, which veils luminosity and binds one to *saṃsāra*, becomes weakened through the practice of *prāṇāyāma* and is destroyed moment by moment. And so it has been said: "There is no austerity higher than *prāṇāyāma*; from it comes the purification of impurities and the radiance of knowledge. Furthermore—
"And fitness of the mind for the concentrations" (2.53).
It is through the practice of breath control (*prāṇāyāma*) alone, according to the statement: "Or by means of exhalation and retention of the breath.
Now, what is withdrawal (*pratyāhāra*)?
"Pratyāhāra is, as it were, the imitation by the senses of the nature of the mind when they are not in contact with their own objects" (Yoga Sūtra 2.54).

In the absence of contact with their own objects, the senses appear as if they were conforming to the very nature of the mind; thus, when the mind is restrained, the senses are restrained along with it and do not require any other means, as is the case in the conquest of the other senses. Just as bees fly up after the king bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too the senses are restrained when the mind is restrained—this is *pratyāhāra*.
From that follows the supreme mastery over the senses. (2.55)

[116,ii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend form as real, nor does he apprehend feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not apprehend the eye as real, nor does he apprehend the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not apprehend forms as real, nor does he apprehend sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not apprehend eye-consciousness as real, nor does he apprehend ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not apprehend eye-contact as real, nor does he apprehend ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not apprehend feeling born of eye-contact as real, nor does he apprehend feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not apprehend the element of earth as real, nor does he apprehend the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not apprehend the realm of desire as real, nor does he apprehend the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not apprehend ignorance as real, nor does he apprehend volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as real. He does not apprehend the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he apprehend the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or arhatship as real. He does not apprehend the fruit of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he apprehend the state of a Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha as real. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not apprehend anything at all as real. The Venerable Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, train in the perfection of giving? How does he train in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, gives a gift without apprehending a recipient, without apprehending a giver, and without apprehending a gift. Thus he trains in the perfection of giving. He observes morality without apprehending transgression or non-transgression; he practices patience without apprehending anger or non-anger; he exerts vigor without apprehending laziness or diligence; he enters meditative concentration without apprehending distraction or concentration; and he practices wisdom without apprehending ignorance or knowledge. Thus he trains in the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, and the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, trains in the six perfections.”

Some maintain that mastery over the senses (*indriyajaya*) consists in not being addicted to sound and the other objects of sense. Addiction (*vyasana*) is attachment; it casts one away from the highest good. A practice that is not contradictory [to dharma] is the proper course. Others hold that it is the engagement with sound and the rest according to one’s own will. Some say that mastery over the senses is the cognition of sound and so forth that is devoid of pleasure and pain due to the absence of passion and hatred. Jaigīṣavya maintains that it is simply non-engagement [with objects] through one-pointedness of mind. And thus, this is the supreme form of control: when the mind is restrained, the senses are also restrained, and they do not require any other effortful means as is the case in other forms of mastery over the senses for the yogin.
[117,i] Thus ends the second chapter, the Sādhanapāda, in the illustrious Pātañjala Yogaśāstra, the Exposition of Sāṃkhya, the commentary by the venerable Vyāsa. [The Third Chapter: The Vibhūtipāda.
The five external means of accomplishment have been explained. Now, dhāraṇā must be discussed.
"Concentration (*dhāraṇā*) is the binding of the mind to a place" (Yoga Sūtra 3.1).

Binding the mind by means of its mere activity to such internal locations as the navel-center, the lotus of the heart, the crown of the head, the light, the tip of the nose, or the tip of the tongue, or to an external object, is concentration.
In that regard:
"Concentration (*dhyāna*) is the one-pointedness of the mental modification (*pratyaya*) upon that object of meditation" (Yoga Sūtra 3.2).

In that location, the one-pointedness of the mental modification directed toward the object of meditation— a continuous flow of similar modifications untouched by other mental modifications— is concentration.
"That very [state] in which there is the appearance of the object alone, as if devoid of its own nature, is meditative concentration (samādhi).

When meditation itself, through the penetration of the nature of the object of meditation, becomes as if empty of its own nature as a mental state— no longer manifesting in the form of the object to be meditated upon— it is then called *samādhi*.
[120,i] "The three together in one place constitute *saṃyama* (3.4)."

[120, ii] This triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* together constitutes *saṃyama*. These three means of accomplishment directed toward a single object are called *saṃyama*. Thus, "saṃyama" is the technical term for this triad according to the system.
"From the mastery of that, there is the light of wisdom" (3.5).

From the mastery of that restraint (*saṃyama*), there arises the light of the wisdom of meditative absorption (*samādhi*). To the extent that the restraint becomes firmly established, to that same extent the wisdom of meditative absorption becomes confident and clear.
[120,v] "Its application to the stages" (3.6) [120,vi]

The application of that *saṃyama* is to the stage immediately following the stage already mastered. For one who has not conquered a lower stage cannot attain *saṃyama* regarding the final stages by skipping over the immediately succeeding stage. And in the absence of that [lower mastery], how could there be for him the light of wisdom (*prajñāloka*)? Furthermore, for one who has conquered a higher stage through the grace of Īśvara, it is not appropriate to apply *saṃyama* toward lower stages, such as the knowledge of others' minds and so forth. Why? Because the object of those [lower stages] is already understood from another source. Regarding which stage is immediately followed by this stage, Yoga alone is the teacher. For how has it been stated thus?
“Yoga must be understood through yoga; yoga proceeds from yoga.
He who is heedful by means of yoga will delight in yoga for a long time.
Thus [it is said].
[121,i] "The triad is internal compared to the preceding ones" (3.7) [121,ii]
Thus, this triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* is internal to cognitive (*saṃprajñāta*) concentration, as compared to the five previous means beginning with the *yamas*.
"Even that is external to the seedless (*nirbīja*) [concentration]. (3.8)
Even that triad of means, though internal, becomes external to yoga that is seedless; why? Because [the seedless state] exists even in the absence of those [means].
Now, since the functioning of the qualities (*guṇa*) is mobile, what kind of transformation of consciousness (*citta-pariṇāma*) occurs at the moments of cessation?
[Yoga Sūtra 3.9]:

"The transformation of cessation (*nirodha-pariṇāma*) is the sequence of the moments of consciousness during cessation, consisting in the suppression of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence and the manifestation of the latent impressions of cessation."

[123,i] The mental factors (*cittadharma*) that constitute the formative impressions (*saṃskāra*) of emergence are not themselves of the nature of causal conditions; thus, when the conditions cease, they are not ceased. The formative impressions of cessation are also mental factors. Through the suppression of the former and the manifestation of the latter, the formative impressions of emergence are discarded and the formative impressions of cessation are established. The mind follows the moment of cessation; this alteration of the formative impressions of a single mind at every moment is the transformation of cessation (*nirodhapariṇāma*). At that time, the mind has only formative impressions remaining; this was explained in the context of the concentration of cessation (*nirodhasamādhi*). [123,ii]
"From that, there is a tranquil flow due to the latent impressions" (3.10).

A tranquil flow of the mind occurs in dependence on the proficiency gained through the practice of the latent impressions of cessation. When those impressions weaken, the impression characterized by cessation is overcome by the impression whose nature is emergence.
"The transformation of the mind as meditative concentration (*samādhi*) consists in the waning of its state directed toward all objects and the arising of its one-pointedness. (3.11)

The state of being directed toward all objects (*sarvārthatā*) is a property of the mind (*cittadharma*). One-pointedness (*ekāgratā*) is also a property of the mind. The "destruction" (*kṣaya*) of the state of being directed toward all objects means its disappearance; the "arising" (*udaya*) of one-pointedness means its manifestation. The mind is that which persists as the substrate (*dharmin*) for these two. Thus, this very mind, persisting through these two properties—which constitute its own essence—undergoes concentration (*samādhīyate*); this is the transformation of the mind into concentration (*samādhipariṇāma*). Thereafter, furthermore:
"The transformation of one-pointedness of mind consists in the subsided and the arisen having equal cognitive content" (3.12).

For one whose mind is concentrated, the preceding cognition is calm; the succeeding one, similar to it, arises. The mind in samādhi follows both, and thus remains just as it was, provided there is no lapse from concentration. This, indeed, is the transformation of the mind—the subject—into one-pointedness.
By this, the transformations of properties (*dharma*), characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and states (*avasthā*) in the elements and the sense organs are explained. (3.13)

[124,v] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is a bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a dharma called ‘the perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive these dharmas, he does not apprehend them; and because he does not apprehend them, he does not become attached to them. He does not think, ‘I am practicing the perfection of wisdom,’ nor does he think, ‘I am a bodhisattva. Subhūti, this is the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom.”

By this aforementioned transformation of the mind, consisting of the forms of dharma, characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and state (*avasthā*), one should understand that the transformation of dharma, the transformation of characteristic, and the transformation of state have been described with respect to the elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*). In that regard, the suppression of emergence (*vyutthāna*) and the manifestation of cessation (*nirodha*) constitute the transformation of dharma within the substrate (*dharmin*). Furthermore, the transformation of characteristic consists in cessation possessing three characteristics and being endowed with the three time-periods (*adhvan*). Indeed, having first abandoned its future characteristic, yet not having transcended its essential nature (*dharmatva*), it enters into the present characteristic, wherein its own form becomes manifest. This is its second time-period. And it is not separated from the past and future characteristics.

[125,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive the perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive that which is called ‘Bodhisattva. Subhūti, because he does not perceive these things, he is neither apprehended nor grasped; and because he is neither apprehended nor grasped, he is not terrified, nor does he tremble, nor does he fall into fear. Subhūti, this is the supreme perfection of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, is neither apprehended nor grasped? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is because form is empty of its own intrinsic nature, and feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty of their own intrinsic nature. Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom is neither apprehended nor grasped. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature, what dharma is there that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should train in? What dharma is there that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should fully awaken to? And by means of what dharma would a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva demonstrate the Dharma to sentient beings? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is precisely because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom. It is precisely because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment. It is precisely because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva demonstrates the Dharma to sentient beings. Subhūti, if all dharmas were not empty of their own intrinsic nature, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva would not train in the perfection of wisdom, nor would he fully awaken to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, nor would he demonstrate the Dharma to sentient beings. Subhūti, because all dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva trains in the perfection of wisdom, fully awakens to unsurpassed, perfect enlightenment, and demonstrates the Dharma to sentient beings. Subhūti, this is the supreme perfection of a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva.”

Likewise, emergence (*vyutthāna*) possesses three characteristics and is endowed with the three time-periods (*adhvan*). Having abandoned the present characteristic while not transcending its essential nature (*dharmatva*), it has entered the past characteristic; this is its third time-period. Yet, it is not devoid of the future and present characteristics. Similarly, when emergence again attains [its state], having abandoned the future characteristic while not transcending its essential nature, it has entered the present characteristic—that is, that wherein its own form is manifested and its activity occurs; this is its second time-period. And it is not devoid of the past and future characteristics. Thus, again there is cessation (*nirodha*), and thus again there is emergence.

[126,i] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivered all suffering beings. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or object of mind; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and also no non-attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear; having transcended delusion, one ultimately attains *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It relieves all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* should be proclaimed: *Tadyathā—gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.* Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, including the bodhisattvas, śrāvakas, and the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught. Likewise, there is the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*). In that regard, during the moments of cessation, the latent impressions of cessation (*nirodha-saṃskāra*) become powerful, while the latent impressions of emergence (*vyutthāna-saṃskāra*) become weak. This is the transformation of state of phenomena (*dharma*). In this context, the substrate (*dharmin*) undergoes transformation through its properties (*dharma*); the properties belonging to the three times undergo transformation through their characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*); and the characteristics themselves undergo transformation through their states (*avasthā*). Thus, due to these transformations of property, characteristic, and state, the activity of the *guṇas* does not remain devoid of them even for a single moment. And the activity of the *guṇas* is mobile. It has been stated that the inherent nature of the *guṇas* is the cause of their activity. By this, it should be understood that in the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the sense organs (*indriya*), there is a threefold transformation based on the distinction between the property and the substrate.

[126,ii] From the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārthataḥ*), however, there is only one transformation (*pariṇāma*). For a property (*dharma*) is merely the essential nature of the substratum (*dharmisvarūpamātra*); it is precisely this modification of the substratum that is elaborated through the medium of its properties. In this regard, while a property remains within its substratum, there occurs a change in the state (*bhāvānyathātva*)—namely, its existence in the past, future, and present time-periods (*adhvan*)—but not a change in the substance (*dravyānyathātva*). Just as when a golden vessel is broken and fashioned into something else, there is a change in its state, but no change in the gold itself.

Another says: "The substrate (dharmin) is not distinct from its properties (dharmas), because it does not transcend its prior reality. If it were a persisting entity (anvayin), it would revolve with absolute immutability, not falling into the distinction between prior and subsequent states. This is no fault. Why? Because we do not accept an absolute [position]. Thus, this triple world departs from manifestation, because permanence is denied; yet even when departed, it exists, because destruction is denied. And through association, it attains subtlety; and due to subtlety, it is unperceived.

[128,i] The transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*) is as follows: a dharma existing in the time-periods (*adhvan*), when past, is endowed with the characteristic of the past, yet it is not dissociated from the two characteristics of the future and the present. Likewise, when future, it is endowed with the characteristic of the future, yet it is not dissociated from the two characteristics of the present and the past. Likewise, when present, it is endowed with the characteristic of the present, yet it is not dissociated from the two characteristics of the past and the future. It is just as a man who is attached to one woman is not thereby dispassionate toward the others.

Regarding this transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇapariṇāma*), opponents raise the objection that because everything would be joined with every characteristic, there would result a confusion of the time-periods (*adhvasaṃkara*). The rebuttal to this is as follows: the "dharma-nature" (*dharmatva*) of phenomena is not something to be established [arbitrarily]. And since dharma-nature exists, a distinction between characteristics must also be stated; it is not the case that the dharma-nature of a phenomenon belongs only to its present moment. For if it were so, the mind would not possess the nature of passion (*rāga*), because passion does not manifest at the time of anger.

Furthermore, the three characteristics cannot exist simultaneously in a single individual; rather, their manifestation occurs sequentially through their respective manifesting conditions. And it has been said: "The specific intensifications of form and the specific intensifications of activity are mutually exclusive, whereas universals function together with those intensifications. Therefore, there is no confusion. Just as when passion (*rāga*) is active in a particular instance, it does not mean that it is absent elsewhere at that time; rather, it simply coexists with its universal. Thus, its existence in that place at that time is established by way of the universal; so it is with the characteristic. [130,i]

The substratum (dharmin) does not belong to the three times; rather, it is the dharmas that belong to the three times. These are characterized as being either manifested or unmanifested. Among these, those that are manifested, while attaining various states, are designated as different on account of their change of state, not on account of a change in substance. Just as a single line is called "one hundred" in the hundreds place, "ten" in the tens place, and "one" in the units place; and just as a woman, though being one and the same, is called a mother, a daughter, and a sister.

Regarding the transformation of state (*avasthā-pariṇāma*), some have raised the objection that it leads to the fallacy of immutability (*kauṭasthya*). How so? Because the time-periods (*adhvan*) are separated by their respective functions. When a property (*dharma*) does not perform its own function, it is "future"; when it performs it, it is "present"; and when, having performed it, it has ceased, it is "past. Thus, they argue, the properties (*dharma*), the substratum (*dharmin*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and the states (*avasthā*) would all become immutable; this is the objection stated by others. [131,i]

This is not a fault. Why? Because, even though the qualities (*guṇa*) are eternal, there is a variety of their mutual suppression. Just as *saṃsthāna* (configuration) is a beginningless property (*dharmamātra*) of the qualities such as sound—which are both perishable and imperishable—so too the *liṅga* (the manifest world) is a beginningless property of the qualities such as *sattva*, which are both perishable and imperishable; this is what is designated as "transformation" (*vikāra*).

In this regard, there is this illustration: the substance (dharmin), clay, undergoing a transition from one state (dharma) characterized by the form of a lump to another state characterized by the form of a jar, undergoes transformation according to its nature (*dharmataḥ pariṇamate*). The form of the jar, having abandoned the future characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) and attained the present characteristic, undergoes transformation according to its characteristic (*lakṣaṇataḥ pariṇamate*). The jar, experiencing newness and antiquity at every moment, undergoes transformation of its condition (*avasthāpariṇāma*). Thus, the "condition" is a further state of the substance, and the "state" is a further characteristic of that [substance's] characteristic; therefore, the single transformation of the substance is presented through these distinctions. This same principle should be applied to other categories as well. These transformations of state, characteristic, and condition do not transcend the essential nature of the substance; thus, there is only one transformation that encompasses all these particularities. Now, what is this transformation? Transformation is the emergence of a different property (*dharmāntara*) upon the cessation of a previous property of a persisting substance.
In that regard—
"The substratum (*dharmī*) conforms to attributes (*dharma*) that are subsided, arisen, or indeterminable" (3.14).

[132, iii] An attribute is simply the power of the substratum as delimited by its capacity (*yogyatā*). And that [power], inferred from the diversity of the production of results, is observed as one thing at one time and another at another, even though it belongs to a single [substratum]. In that regard, when the substratum is present and undergoing its own operation, it is distinguished from other attributes—namely, those that are subsided or indeterminable. But when it is endowed with [the attribute] in a general sense, then, because it consists of nothing but the essential nature of the substratum itself, what could it be, and by what would it be distinguished?

[133,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: (1) the self-nature of attachment to words; (2) the self-nature of discrimination according to the characteristics of objects; (3) the self-nature of discrimination according to the characteristics of one's own mind; and (4) the perfectly accomplished self-nature. These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of self-nature. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvana. What are these four? They are: (1) the nirvana of the extinction of the particular and general characteristics of all things; (2) the nirvana of the non-existence of the self-nature of all things; (3) the nirvana of the discrimination of the characteristics of one's own mind; and (4) the nirvana of the entrance into the realm of reality (*dharmadhātu*) through the non-duality of grasper and grasped. These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of nirvana. This is a summary of the section on the four kinds of self-nature and the four kinds of nirvana from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. It explains that the Buddha taught these categories to refute the views of external philosophers and to clarify the true nature of reality for his disciples. The four kinds of self-nature refer to the way phenomena appear through language, the way they are perceived as external objects, the way they are projected by one's own mind, and their ultimate perfected state. The four kinds of nirvana describe different levels of realization, ranging from the cessation of conceptual characteristics to the entry into the non-dual realm of reality. In that regard, the properties (*dharma*) of a substrate (*dharmin*) are indeed those that are subsided (*śānta*), arisen (*udita*), and indeterminable (*avyapadeśya*). Among these, the subsided are those which, having performed their functions, have ceased; the arisen are those still performing their functions. These [arisen ones] are immediately followed by the future characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and the past ones are immediately preceded by the present. Why are the past ones not immediately followed by the present? Because there is no priority or posteriority (*pūrvapaścimatā*) in the case of the past, as there is between the future and the present. Therefore, the past has no immediate successor; rather, it is the future alone that constitutes the immediate predecessor of the present.

[133, ii] Now, as for those who maintain that the indefinable consists in "everything being of the nature of everything": it has been stated that the transformative variety of tastes and so forth belonging to water and earth is observed in stationary things; likewise, the qualities of stationary things are found in moving things, and those of moving things in stationary things. Thus, through the non-interruption of their respective classes, everything is of the nature of everything.

"Indeed, because of the constraints of place, time, form, and cause, there is no simultaneous manifestation of [all] selves. That which persists through these qualities (dharmas), whether manifested or unmanifested, having the nature of both the universal and the particular, is the persisting substratum (dharmin). For one who holds that this is merely a collection of qualities without persistence, there can be no experience [of the fruits of action]. Why? Because how could one consciousness be entitled to the status of an experiencer for an action performed by another consciousness? Furthermore, there would be an absence of memory; for one person does not remember what was seen by another. And because of the recognition of objects, the persisting substratum is established—that which is recognized as having undergone a change in its qualities. Therefore, this is not merely a collection of qualities without persistence."
"A difference in sequence is the cause for a difference in transformation" (3.15).

Since it follows that there is only one transformation for a single substratum (*dharmī*), the difference in sequence serves as the cause for the difference in transformation. For example, the sequence is: powdered clay, lump of clay, clay, jar, shards, and clay-dust. That which is the immediate successor to a given state is its sequence. The sequence of the transformation of states (*dharma-pariṇāma*) is such that the lump ceases and the jar arises. The sequence of the transformation of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-pariṇāma*) is the transition of the jar from its future state to its present state; likewise, the transition of the lump from its present state to its past state is the sequence. There is no sequence for what is past. Why? Because immediate succession exists only when there is a relation of priority and posteriority, but that does not exist for the past; therefore, sequence belongs only to two characteristics [the present and the future]. Similarly, the sequence of the transformation of conditions (*avasthā-pariṇāma*) is also observed: in a new jar, oldness is seen at the end. And that [oldness], being manifested through a sequence following a succession of moments, reaches its ultimate manifestation. Thus, this third transformation is distinguished by both state and characteristic.

These sequences have their own specific natures established when there is a distinction between the property (*dharma*) and the property-possessor (*dharmī*). Furthermore, even a property becomes a property-possessor in relation to the nature of another property. However, when—in ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*)—there is a metaphorical treatment of non-difference within the property-possessor, and that very [property-possessor] is designated as the property by means of that [non-difference], then this sequence appears precisely as a unity.

Regarding the mind, there are two kinds of phenomena: those that are perceived and those that are unperceived. Among these, those consisting of conditions (*pratyaya*) are perceived, while those consisting of mere entities (*vastumātra*) are unperceived. These latter ones are precisely seven in number, whose existence as mere entities is established through inference:
“Cessation, phenomena, formations, transformation, and life;”
“Movement and power are properties of the mind, devoid of perception.
Therefore, for the yogin who has acquired all the necessary means, the object of *saṃyama* for the sake of attaining knowledge of the desired object is introduced:
"From *saṃyama* upon the three transformations, there is knowledge of the past and the future" (3.16).

[137,iii] Through *saṃyama* upon the transformations of the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the states (*avasthā*), and the essential nature (*pariṇāma*) of things, knowledge of the past and future arises for yogins. The triad of *dhāraṇā*, *dhyāna*, and *samādhi* is called *saṃyama* when applied to a single object. By means of that, the threefold transformation being directly perceived brings about knowledge of the past and future regarding those objects.
"Due to the mutual superimposition of word, object, and cognition, there is a confusion; by performing *saṃyama* on their distinction, knowledge of the cries of all beings arises" (Yogasūtra 3.17).

In this regard, speech is meaningful only with respect to the phonemes (*varṇa*). The auditory organ, moreover, has as its object only the transformation of sound (*dhvani*). A word (*pada*), however, is to be grasped by the intellect through the synthesis of sounds (*nāda*). Since phonemes cannot exist simultaneously and are therefore incapable of assisting one another, they do not touch upon or present a word; appearing and disappearing individually, they are said to be each of the nature of non-words.

Furthermore, each individual phoneme (*varṇa*), being the essence of a word, is accumulated with the capacity for all denotations; having attained a state of manifoldness (*vaiśvarūpya*) due to its relation to other cooperating phonemes, the preceding one is established in a specific distinction by the following one, and the following one by the preceding one. Thus, many phonemes, following a specific sequence and delimited by convention (*saṃketa*) regarding the object, such as the phonemes *ga*, *au*, and the visarga (*visarjanīya*),—all of them enveloped by the capacity for all denotations—illuminate the object characterized by a dewlap and so forth.

Thus, that single mental image (*buddhi-nirbhāsa*) which arises from these [phonemes]—which are delimited by the convention of meaning and whose sequential order of sounds has been withdrawn—is designated as the *pada* (word), the signifier of the signified. That single word is the object of a single cognition; it is projected by a single effort, partless, without sequence, and devoid of phonemes (*avarṇa*). It is a mental entity brought forth by the operation of the cognition of the final phoneme. With the desire to communicate it to another, it is perceived by listeners through the very phonemes being uttered and heard, by means of a worldly cognition permeated by the beginningless latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of linguistic usage, as if it were an established reality.

[141,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are these four? They are: (1) the self-nature of attachment to words; (2) the self-nature of the attachment to the signs of things; (3) the self-nature of the attachment to the discrimination of the nature of things; and (4) the perfected self-nature. Now, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of attachment to words? It is the habit-energy accumulated from beginningless time through the attachment to various names and words, which gives rise to the manifestation of objects even though they do not exist. This is called the self-nature of attachment to words. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the attachment to the signs of things? It is the appearance of forms, characteristics, and marks that manifest according to the habit-energy of the attachment to words, appearing as if they were external objects. This is called the self-nature of the attachment to the signs of things. Next, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of the attachment to the discrimination of the nature of things? It is the grasping of the internal and external dharmas as having a self-nature established by their own characteristics, such as the elements, the sense-fields, and the aggregates. This is called the self-nature of the attachment to the discrimination of the nature of things. And finally, Mahāmati, what is the perfected self-nature? It is the state where one realizes that all dharmas are devoid of the two-fold grasping—that is, free from the grasping of the subject and the grasping of the object—and it is the attainment of the Tathāgata-knowledge through the realization of the non-existence of the imagined nature within the dependent nature. This is called the perfected self-nature. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the attachment to the self-nature of words and the signs of things, and instead cultivate the wisdom that penetrates the perfected self-nature. Thus it is said: The self-nature of words, the signs of things, The nature of the imagined, and the perfected— These four kinds of self-nature Are taught by the Buddhas for the sake of beings. Thus ends the fourteenth chapter, "On the Four Kinds of Self-Nature," from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

The distinction of that [convention] arises from the cognition of convention; the synthesis of this many [elements] is such that they denote a single object. Convention, however, consists of the mutual superimposition (*itaretarādhyāsa*) between word and object, having the nature of memory: "this word is this object" and "this object is this word. Thus, convention takes the form of mutual superimposition. In this way, these—word, object, and cognition—are confounded through mutual superimposition: "cow" is the word, "cow" is the object, and "cow" is the cognition. He who knows their distinction is all-knowing.

[142,i] In all words, there is the power of the sentence; when "tree" is uttered, "exists" is understood. This is because the meaning of a word does not deviate from existence (*sattā*). Likewise, there is no action without a means of accomplishment (*sādhana*).

And likewise, when "he cooks" (*pacati*) is uttered, there is an implication of all the factors of action (*kārakas*); this is a restatement for the sake of restriction regarding the agent, instrument, and object—namely, Caitra, fire, and rice-grains. Furthermore, we observe the arrangement of words within the meaning of a sentence, as in "the Vedic scholar studies the meters" (*śrotriyaś chando 'dhīte*) or "he lives, he sustains his vital breaths" (*jīvati prāṇān dhārayati*). In that sentence, the word-meanings are manifested; therefore, having analyzed the word, it must be grammatically explained, whether it expresses an action or a factor of action. Otherwise, in cases such as *bhavati*, *aśvaḥ*, or *ajāpayaḥ*, since these resemble both nouns and verbs, how could they be explained if their status as an action or a factor of action were not determined?

[143,i] This is the distinction between those three: the word, the object, and the cognition. For example, in the expression "the palace is white" (*śvetate prāsādaḥ*), the meaning is that of the action (*kriyārtha*). In the expression "the white palace" (*śvetaḥ prāsādaḥ*), the word has the meaning of the agent (*kārakārtha*). The meaning of that [word] and the cognition consist of both the action and the agent. Why is this so? Because through the connection "this is that," the cognition and the convention (*saṃketa*) take on a single form.

But that object which is white is the objective support for both the word and the cognition. For that [object], while undergoing modification through its own states, is not accompanied by the word, nor is it accompanied by the cognition. Thus, the word is one way, the cognition is another, and they are not mutually concomitant; hence there is a distinction: the word is one thing, the object is another, and the cognition is yet another. Through *saṃyama* on this distinction, the knowledge of the cries of all living beings is attained by the yogi. "From the direct realization of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge of previous births arises. (YS 3.18)

[144,iii] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive the perfection of generosity as a real entity, nor does he perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as a real entity. He does not perceive form as a real entity, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as a real entity. He does not perceive the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as a real entity. He does not perceive forms as real entities, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real entities. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as a real entity, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real entities. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as a real entity, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real entities. He does not perceive the earth element as a real entity, nor does he perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as real entities. He does not perceive the door of the Dharma called ‘emptiness’ as a real entity, nor does he perceive the doors of the Dharma called ‘signlessness,’ ‘wishlessness,’ ‘the unconditioned,’ ‘non-arising,’ ‘non-cessation,’ ‘non-defilement,’ ‘non-purification,’ ‘nonduality,’ ‘non-differentiation,’ ‘the absence of intrinsic nature,’ ‘the absence of characteristics,’ ‘the absence of production,’ ‘the absence of cessation,’ ‘the absence of birth,’ ‘the absence of aging,’ ‘the absence of death,’ ‘the absence of sorrow,’ ‘the absence of lamentation,’ ‘the absence of suffering,’ ‘the absence of dejection,’ or ‘the absence of mental disturbance’ as real entities. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as real entities, nor does he perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path as real entities. He does not perceive the four dhyānas as real entities, nor does he perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen emptinesses, the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment, the three gateways to liberation, the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as real entities. Subhūti, it is thus: when the bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as a real entity.”

Indeed, these *saṃskāras* are of two kinds: those which are the causes of memory and affliction (*kleśa*) in the form of latent impressions (*vāsanā*), and those which are the causes of maturation (*vipāka*) in the form of merit and demerit (*dharma-adharma*). These, having been formed by the previous existence, are mental factors (*cittadharma*) that are imperceptible, like transformation, effort, cessation, power, and the property of life-force. Mastery (*saṃyama*) over them is capable of bringing about the direct perception of those *saṃskāras*. And there can be no direct perception of them without [the knowledge of] place, time, cause, and experience. Thus, from the direct perception of *saṃskāras*, the knowledge of past births arises for the yogin. Likewise, in another case as well, from the direct perception of *saṃskāras*, there is the awareness of future births.

[145,i] The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. Which four? They are: physical food as nutriment, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. These, monks, are the four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence."

In this regard, the following narrative is heard: As the venerable Jaigīṣavya was observing the sequence of births and transformations throughout ten great cosmic cycles (*mahāsarga*) through the direct realization of his latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) arose within him. Then the venerable Āvaṭya, assuming a subtle body, said to him: "Since you have been born again and again among gods and humans during ten great cosmic cycles, having possessed a sattvic intellect that was not overwhelmed due to your auspicious nature, and having clearly perceived the suffering inherent in birth as hell-beings, animals, or embryos, which of the two—pleasure or pain—did you experience more? Jaigīṣavya said to the venerable Āvaṭya: "During those ten great cosmic cycles, because my intellect was not overwhelmed by virtue of my auspicious nature, and because I clearly perceived the suffering of existence as hell-beings and animals while being born again and again among gods and humans, I realized that whatever was experienced was nothing but suffering. The venerable Āvaṭya said: "This supreme mastery over primordial matter (*pradhāna*) and this unsurpassed happiness of contentment belonging to your long-lived self—must even these be cast into the category of suffering? The venerable Jaigīṣavya said: "This unsurpassed happiness of contentment was spoken of only in comparison with the pleasure derived from sense objects. In comparison with the bliss of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*), it is indeed suffering. This quality belongs to the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*), and since the intellect consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), its corresponding cognition is placed on the side of what is to be abandoned (*heya*). It is a thread of craving whose very form is suffering. However, because of the departure of the torment of the suffering of craving, this happiness is described as serene, unassailable, and favorable to all."
[146,i] "The knowledge of others' minds is conditioned" (3.19) [146,ii]
Through *saṃyama* on the mental modification (*pratyaya*), by means of the direct realization of that modification, there arises knowledge of another's mind.
[Yogasūtra 3.19] "And that [knowledge] does not have an object-support (*sālambana*), because that [other person's mind] has not become its object" (3.20).

[146,iv] He knows the other person’s cognition as being "attached," yet he does not know it as being attached to such-and-such an object. This is because the object of that other person’s cognition has not been taken as an object by the yogi’s mind; rather, it is merely the other person’s cognition itself that has become the object of the yogi’s mind.
"By *saṃyama* on the form of the body, when the power of its being perceived is suppressed and there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility occurs" (3.21).

Through *saṃyama* on the form of the body, one suppresses that power of the form which consists in its being perceived. When the power of being perceived is suppressed, and there is no contact with the light of the eye, invisibility arises for the yogin. By this, it should be understood that invisibility regarding sound and so forth is also stated.
"Action is both with and without onset; from mastery over it, or from portents, there is knowledge of the future.

Karma that results in the maturation of lifespan (*āyur-vipāka*) is of two kinds: with an onset (*sopakrama*) and without an onset (*nirupakrama*). In this regard, just as a wet cloth spread out would dry in a shorter time, so it is with that which has an onset; and just as that same cloth, when folded up, would take a long time to dry, so it is with that which has no onset. Or again, just as a fire set upon dry undergrowth and joined by wind on all sides would burn it in the shortest time, so it is with that which has an onset; and just as that same fire, placed gradually upon the parts of a heap of grass, would burn it after a long time, so it is with that which has no onset. Thus, the karma that produces the lifespan for a single existence is twofold: with an onset and without an onset. Through *saṃyama* directed toward that [lifespan], there arises knowledge of the future limit, that is, of death.

[147, iii] Or, "from the signs of death" (*ariṣṭa*); there are three kinds of signs of death: internal (*ādhyātmika*), external (*ādhibhautika*), and celestial (*ādhidaivika*). Among these, the internal sign is when one does not hear sounds within one's own body even with the ears covered, or does not see light even when the eyes are pressed. Likewise, the external sign is when one sees the messengers of Yama, or suddenly sees deceased ancestors. Likewise, the celestial sign is when one suddenly sees heaven or the *siddhas*. Or, conversely, all things appear inverted; by this, one knows that the end of life has arrived. [148, i]
The powers regarding loving-kindness and the other [immeasurables] (3.23).

There are three meditative cultivations: loving-kindness (*maitrī*), compassion (*karuṇā*), and sympathetic joy (*muditā*). Among these, by cultivating loving-kindness toward beings who are happy, one attains the power of loving-kindness. By cultivating compassion toward those who are suffering, one attains the power of compassion. By cultivating sympathetic joy toward those who possess merit and virtue, one attains the power of sympathetic joy. The concentration that arises from cultivation is "restraint" (*saṃyama*); from that, powers arise whose vigor is not in vain. Toward those of evil character, however, there is equanimity (*upekṣā*) but no cultivation. Consequently, because there is no concentration therein, there is no power derived from equanimity, due to the absence of restraint in that case.

"Regarding powers, such as the power of an elephant" (3.24): through *saṃyama* upon the power of an elephant, one becomes possessed of the power of an elephant; through *saṃyama* upon the power of Vainateya (Garuḍa), one becomes possessed of the power of Vainateya; through *saṃyama* upon the power of the wind, one becomes possessed of the power of the wind—and so forth.
"By directing the light of the mind toward the process of activity, there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, and the remote.
The activity of the mind has been described as luminous; by fixing its light upon an object—whether subtle, concealed, or distant—the yogi perceives that object.
[149,i] "Knowledge of the worlds arises from *saṃyama* on the sun" (3.26).

[149, ii] Its expansion consists of the seven worlds. Among them, from the Avīci hell up to the summit of Mount Meru is the world of the earth (bhūrloka). Beginning from the summit of Mount Meru up to the Pole Star (Dhruva), the world of the atmosphere (antarikṣaloka) is variegated with planets, lunar mansions, and stars. Beyond that is the heavenly world (svarloka), the third world, which is fivefold and belongs to Mahendra. The fourth is the world of Prajāpati, Maharloka. The Brahma-world is threefold, namely: Janaloka, Tapoloka, and Satyaloka. [149, iii]

“The world of Brahmā consists of three levels; beyond that is the world of Prajāpati, then the world of Mahendra; and ‘Svar’ is said to be the heavens, where the stars are in the sky and living beings are on earth.
This is the summary verse.

[149,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, should train in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, train in all the dharmas of a buddha? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in the dharma of giving, but he does not perceive that gift, nor the giver, nor the recipient. He trains in the dharma of morality, but he does not perceive that morality, nor the one who observes it, nor the field of merit. He trains in the dharma of patience, but he does not perceive that patience, nor the one who is patient, nor the object of patience. He trains in the dharma of vigor, but he does not perceive that vigor, nor the one who exerts it, nor the basis for exertion. He trains in the dharma of concentration, but he does not perceive that concentration, nor the one who concentrates, nor the object of concentration. He trains in the dharma of wisdom, but he does not perceive that wisdom, nor the one who possesses wisdom, nor the object of wisdom. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of the internal, but he does not perceive that internal emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of the external, but he does not perceive that external emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of the internal and external, but he does not perceive that internal and external emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of emptiness, but he does not perceive that emptiness of emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the great emptiness, but he does not perceive that great emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of the ultimate, but he does not perceive that ultimate emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the conditioned emptiness, but he does not perceive that conditioned emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the unconditioned emptiness, but he does not perceive that unconditioned emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the limitless emptiness, but he does not perceive that limitless emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the dispersion emptiness, but he does not perceive that dispersion emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the essential nature emptiness, but he does not perceive that essential nature emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of all dharmas, but he does not perceive that emptiness of all dharmas, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of own-marks, but he does not perceive that emptiness of own-marks, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the unattainable emptiness, but he does not perceive that unattainable emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the non-dispersal emptiness, but he does not perceive that non-dispersal emptiness, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of nature, but he does not perceive that emptiness of nature, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of all natures, but he does not perceive that emptiness of all natures, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the emptiness of characteristics, but he does not perceive that emptiness of characteristics, nor the one who contemplates it, nor the object of that contemplation. He trains in the dharma of the ten powers, but he does not perceive those ten powers, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the four grounds of self-confidence, but he does not perceive those four grounds of self-confidence, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the four analytical knowledges, but he does not perceive those four analytical knowledges, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, but he does not perceive those eighteen unique qualities of a buddha, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the great compassion, but he does not perceive that great compassion, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the thirty-two marks of a great man, but he does not perceive those thirty-two marks of a great man, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the eighty minor marks, but he does not perceive those eighty minor marks, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the dharanis, but he does not perceive those dharanis, nor the one who realizes them, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the path of vision, but he does not perceive that path of vision, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization.
