He trains in the dharma of the path of cultivation, but he does not perceive that path of cultivation, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the fruit of a stream-enterer, but he does not perceive that fruit of a stream-enterer, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the fruit of a once-returner, but he does not perceive that fruit of a once-returner, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the fruit of a non-returner, but he does not perceive that fruit of a non-returner, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of arhatship, but he does not perceive that arhatship, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of pratyekabuddhahood, but he does not perceive that pratyekabuddhahood, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. He trains in the dharma of the knowledge of all modes, but he does not perceive that knowledge of all modes, nor the one who realizes it, nor the object of that realization. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, coursing in the perfection of wisdom, trains in all the dharmas of a buddha. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive a gift, nor a giver, nor a recipient; if he does not perceive morality, nor one who observes it, nor a field of merit; if he does not perceive patience, nor one who is patient, nor an object of patience; if he does not perceive vigor, nor one who exerts it, nor a basis for exertion; if he does not perceive concentration, nor one who concentrates, nor an object of concentration; if he does not perceive wisdom, nor one who possesses wisdom, nor an object of wisdom; if he does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the emptiness of the internal and external, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the great emptiness, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the emptiness of the ultimate, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the conditioned emptiness, nor one who contemplates it, nor an object of that contemplation; if he does not perceive the unconditioned emptiness

There, situated one above the other, are the grounds of the six great hells—Avīci, Ghanodaka, Ghanāgni, Ghanavāyu, Tamas, and Mahātamas—which rest respectively upon water, fire, wind, space, and darkness; these are Mahākāla, Ambarīṣa, Raurava, Maharaurava, Kālasūtra, and Andhatāmisra. Therein, living beings who have experienced suffering earned by their own karma are born, having drawn out a miserable and long lifespan. Below that are the seven subterranean realms (pātālas) known as Mahātala, Rasātala, Atala, Sutala, Vitala, Talātala, and Pātāla. This is the eighth level, the earth consisting of seven continents, in the center of which stands Sumeru, the golden king of mountains. Its peaks are composed of silver, lapis lazuli, crystal, gold, and jewels. There, due to the coloring of the light from the lapis lazuli, the southern side of the sky appears dark like the petal of a blue lotus, the eastern side white, the western side transparent, and the northern side the color of the *kuraṇṭaka* flower. On its southern flank stands the Jambū tree, from which this continent is called Jambūdvīpa. Due to the movement of the sun across it, day and night proceed as if attached to it. To the north of it are three mountains with blue and white peaks, each two thousand [yojanas] in extent. Between them are three regions, each nine thousand yojanas in size: Ramaṇaka, Hiraṇmaya, and Uttarakuru. To the south are the Niṣadha, Hemakūṭa, and Himavat mountains, each two thousand yojanas in extent. Between them are three regions, each nine thousand yojanas in size: Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣa, and Bhārata. To the east of Sumeru are the boundaries of Bhadrāśva and Mālyavat; to the west are the boundaries of Ketumāla and Gandhamādana. In the middle is the region of Ilāvṛta. Thus, this [Jambūdvīpa] extends for a hundred thousand yojanas, arranged at half that distance in every direction from Sumeru.

[150,i] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas who, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, will not be afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror—Subhūti, it is because they have practiced for a long time that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas will hear this profound perfection of wisdom and not be afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, how long has it been since those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have practiced? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have practiced for as many hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of aeons as there are grains of sand in the river Gaṅgā. Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, what kind of roots of merit do those bodhisattva mahāsattvas possess? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have planted roots of merit under the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones equal in number to the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have honored, served, and attended upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, and have made offerings to them with robes, alms-food, bedding, seats, medicinal requisites for the sick, and various necessities. Subhūti, those bodhisattva mahāsattvas have also questioned those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones regarding the profound Dharma, and they have understood its meaning. Subhūti, it is because they have planted such roots of merit, and because they have honored, served, and attended upon those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones, that these bodhisattva mahāsattvas, having heard this profound perfection of wisdom, will not be afraid, nor terrified, nor fall into terror."

This Jambūdvīpa, which is indeed one hundred thousand [yojanas] in extent, is surrounded by the Salt Ocean, which is twice its size and shaped like a ring. Beyond that, the islands of Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, Śālmala, Gomedha (Plakṣa), and Puṣkara are each double the size of the preceding one; and the oceans are like heaps of mustard seeds, adorned with various mountain ornaments, containing sugarcane juice, wine, clarified butter, whey, milk, and sweet water. These seven oceans, surrounding the islands in a circular form, are encircled by the Lokāloka mountain range and are numbered at fifty koṭis of yojanas. All this is arranged within the center of the Cosmic Egg (*aṇḍa*), which is a minute part of Pradhāna, just as a firefly is in the sky.

There, in Pātāla, in the ocean, and upon these mountains, dwell the hosts of gods, as well as asuras, gandharvas, kiṃnaras, kimpuruṣas, yakṣas, rākṣasas, bhūtas, pretas, piśācas, apasmārakas, apsarases, brahmarākṣasas, kūṣmāṇḍas, and vināyakas. In all the continents dwell meritorious beings, both gods and humans.

Sumeru is the pleasure garden of the Thirty-three gods; there are the gardens known as Miśravana, Nandana, Caitraratha, and Sumānasa. Sudharmā is the assembly hall of the gods, Sudarśana is the city, and Vaijayanta is the palace. The planets, lunar mansions, and stars, however, are bound to Dhruva and, their movements characterized by the regulation of wind-currents, revolve in the sky, situated one above the other over Sumeru.

There are six classes of gods residing in the realm of Mahendra: the Tridaśas, the Agniṣvāttas, the Yāmyas, the Tuṣitas, the Aparinirmitavaśavartins, and the Parinirmitavaśavartins. All of them have their intentions fulfilled, are endowed with sovereign powers such as *aṇimā*, live for the duration of a kalpa, are venerable deities who enjoy sensual pleasures, possess spontaneously born bodies, and are attended by Apsarases who are most excellent and compliant.

In the great world of Prajāpati, there are five classes of gods: the Kumudas, the Ṛbhus, the Pratardanas, the Añjanābhas, and the Pracitābhas. These have mastery over the gross elements, subsist on meditation, and have a lifespan of a thousand kalpas. In the first world of Brahmā, Janaloka, there are four classes of gods: the Brahmapurohitas, the Brahmakāyikas, the Brahmamahākāyikas, and the Amaras. They have mastery over the elements and the sense faculties, and their lifespans increase twofold at each successive level.

In the second *tapas* world, there are three classes of deities: the Ābhāsvaras, the Mahābhāsvaras, and the Satyamahābhāsvaras. They have mastery over the elements (*bhūta*), the senses (*indriya*), and primordial nature (*prakṛti*); their lifespans increase twofold at each successive level; they all subsist on meditative absorption (*dhyāna-āhāra*); their vital seed flows upward (*ūrdhvaretas*); their knowledge is unimpeded above; and the objects of their knowledge are not obstructed by the lower levels. In the third, Brahmā’s Satyaloka, there are four classes of deities who do not construct physical abodes, who are self-supported, situated one above the other, who have mastery over primordial matter (*pradhāna*), and whose lifespan lasts as long as the period of creation (*sarga*).

Among them, the *acyuta*s possess the bliss of *dhyāna* accompanied by *vitarka*; the *śuddhanivāsa*s possess the bliss of *dhyāna* accompanied by *vicāra*; the *satyābhā*s possess the bliss of *dhyāna* consisting of mere *ānanda*; and the *saṃjñāsaṃjñin*s possess the bliss of *dhyāna* consisting of mere *asmitā*. They too are situated within the three worlds (*trailokya*). These seven worlds are all indeed the worlds of Brahmā (*brahmaloka*). However, those who have attained dissolution into the bodyless state (*videha*) or dissolution into primordial nature (*prakṛtilaya*) abide in the state of liberation; thus, they are not included among the worlds. This [state] is to be directly realized by the yogi after performing *saṃyama* on the gate of the sun; then he should likewise practice elsewhere until all this has been seen.
[153,i] “The knowledge of the array of stars in the moon” (3.27) [153,ii]
Having practiced *saṃyama* on the moon, one should know the arrangement of the stars. "By means of the pole star (*dhruva*), there is knowledge of their motion" (3.28).
Then, having practiced mastery over the Pole Star (Dhruva), one should discern the movement of the stars; having practiced mastery over the celestial palaces above, one should discern them.
"Knowledge of the arrangement of the body through the navel-center" (3.29).

Having performed *saṃyama* on the navel-center, one should know the arrangement of the body. There are three humors (*doṣas*): wind, bile, and phlegm. There are seven constituents (*dhātus*): skin, blood, flesh, sinews, bone, marrow, and semen. Among these, each preceding one is external to the following; such is their arrangement.
"In the throat-pit, there is the cessation of hunger and thirst" (3.30).
Below the tongue is the thread; below the thread is the throat; below that is the well. By restraint there, hunger and thirst do not afflict one. [153,ix] "Stability in the tortoise-channel" (3.31).
[153,x] Below the well, in the chest, there is a channel shaped like a tortoise; by practicing restraint upon it, one attains a steady state, just as a snake or a lizard does.
"Vision of the Siddhas in the light of the crown" (3.32):
within the aperture in the skull, there is a luminous light; by performing *saṃyama* upon that, one gains vision of the Siddhas who move between heaven and earth.
"Or, everything [is known] through intuition.

The so-called *prātibha* [intuition] is the deliverer; it is the precursor of the knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*), just as the light precedes the rising of the sun. Or rather, by means of that, the yogi knows everything upon the arising of *prātibha*-knowledge.
[3.34cd] "In the heart, there is the consciousness of the mind. (3.34)
In this city of Brahman, there is a small lotus-palace; therein is consciousness. Through *saṃyama* upon that, there is knowledge of the mind.

Experience is the non-differentiation of the cognitions of the sattva and the puruṣa, which are absolutely distinct; through saṃyama upon that which is for its own sake, there arises knowledge of the puruṣa, distinct from that which is for the sake of another.

The *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi-sattva*), whose nature is luminosity, having brought under control *rajas* and *tamas* through its connection with a similar *sattva*, undergoes transformation by means of the cognition of the distinction between the *sattva* and the Puruṣa. And from that *sattva*, which is subject to transformation, the Puruṣa is absolutely different—possessing contrary properties, being pure, and consisting solely of the nature of consciousness. Since these two are absolutely unmixed, the non-distinction of their cognitions constitutes experience for the Puruṣa; because its object has been presented [to it], that cognitive state of experience belongs to the *sattva*. Being for the sake of another, that *sattva* is the object of perception.

But that other, distinct, conscious, and spiritual cognition which is superior to that [intellectual reflection], by practicing *saṃyama* upon it, there arises wisdom whose object is the Puruṣa. And the Puruṣa is not perceived by means of the cognition of the Puruṣa—which is essentially the *buddhi-sattva*—but rather the Puruṣa itself perceives that cognition as having itself as its support. For thus it has been said: "By what, O Maitreyī, could one know the knower? [Yājñavalkya Upaniṣad 2.4.14].
"From that, there arise intuitive insight, supernormal hearing, feeling, seeing, tasting, and the sense of touch" (YS 3.36).

[156,ii] Through *prātibha* (intuitive insight), there arises knowledge of the subtle, the concealed, the distant, the past, and the future. Through *śrāvaṇa* (the power of hearing), there is the hearing of divine sounds. Through *vedana* (the power of feeling), there is the attainment of divine touch. Through *ādarśa* (the power of vision), there is the perception of divine forms; through *āsvāda* (the power of taste), there is the perception of divine tastes; and through *vārtā* (the power of smell), there is the cognition of divine odors—these arise constantly. [156,iii]
"These are obstacles in concentration and accomplishments in the emergent state" (3.37).

These, such as intuitive insight (*prātibha*) and the rest, are obstacles when arising for one whose mind is in a state of concentration (*samāhita*), because they are contrary to that vision; however, when arising for one whose mind has emerged from concentration (*vyutthita*), they are accomplishments (*siddhi*).
"Entry into another's body occurs through the loosening of the cause of bondage and through the awareness of the movement of the mind.

The meaning is that for the mind which has become liquefied (*lolībhūta*) and is otherwise without a fixed support within the body, its "fixation" (*pratiṣṭhā*) consists in bondage through the force of the latent impressions of karma (*karmāśaya*). The loosening of that karma, which is the cause of bondage, occurs by the power of *samādhi*. Furthermore, the perception of the movement of the mind arises precisely from *samādhi*. Through the destruction of the bondage of karma and through the perception of the movement of one's own mind, the yogi draws the mind out from his own body and deposits it into other bodies. And once the mind is deposited, the sense organs follow it; just as bees fly up after the king-bee when he flies up, and settle down after him when he settles down, so too do the sense organs conform to the mind during the entry into another body.
"From mastery over the udāna breath, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and so forth, as well as the power of upward departure. (3.39)

The functioning of all the senses, characterized by *prāṇa* and the others, constitutes life. Its activity is fivefold: *prāṇa* is the movement through the mouth and nose, with its function reaching to the heart; *samāna* is so called because it equalizes, and its function reaches to the navel; *apāna* is so called because it carries away, with its function reaching down to the soles of the feet; *udāna* is so called because it leads upward, with its function reaching to the head; and *vyāna* is pervasive. Among these, *prāṇa* is the primary one. Through mastery over *udāna*, there is non-attachment to water, mud, thorns, and the like, and at the time of death, the soul's departure occurs; this [departure] he attains through mastery. [158,i] "From mastery over *samāna*, there is radiance" (3.40).
Having conquered his pride and applied his vital energy, he blazes forth.
"By *saṃyama* on the connection between the auditory organ and space, there arises divine hearing" (YS 3.41).

Space is the support of all auditory organs and of all sounds, as it has been stated: "For all [beings], despite having ears located in the same place, the quality of hearing occurs in one and the same location; and this is the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of space."

And it has been stated that there is no obstruction. Likewise, because that which is formless is seen without obstruction, the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of space is also made known. The auditory organ is inferred from the perception of sound. Since, between a deaf person and one who is not deaf, one perceives sound while the other does not, it follows that the auditory organ alone is the locus of the object sound. For the yogi who has practiced *saṃyama* upon the connection between the auditory organ and space, the divine ear (*divya-śrotra*) comes forth.
"By *saṃyama* on the connection between the body and space, and through mastery over lightness like that of cotton, one attains the power of moving through space.

Wherever there is a body, there is space, because space provides room for the body; thus, there is a connection (*saṃbandha*) with it, which is to say, an attainment (*prāpti*). Having practiced *saṃyama* upon that connection and having mastered it, or having attained meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) in light things such as cotton down, down to the level of atoms, one becomes light by having conquered that connection. And due to this lightness, one walks upon water with the feet; then, having walked upon a mere thread from a spider's web, one walks upon rays of light; thereafter, one gains the power of moving through space at will.
"Then, the external non-conceptualized state is Mahāvideha; from that follows the destruction of the veil of obscuration. (3.43) [160,iv]

The acquisition of the mind’s functioning outside the body is the *dhāraṇā* known as "bodiless" (*videhā*). If this occurs merely through the external functioning of the mind while it remains established within the body, it is called "imagined" (*kalpitā*). However, that which is the external functioning of the mind itself when it has actually become external, independent of the body, is indeed "unimagined" (*akalpitā*). By means of the imagined [form], they accomplish the unimagined "great bodiless" (*mahāvidehā*) state. Through this, yogis enter the bodies of others; and from that *dhāraṇā*, there occurs the destruction of the veil of the luminous *buddhi-sattva*—namely, the triad of afflictions, karma, and their fruition—which is rooted in *rajas* and *tamas*.
"Through *saṃyama* upon the gross form, the subtle essence, and the inherence of the purposefulness [of the elements], mastery over the elements is attained. (3.44)

In this context, the specific qualities such as sound and so forth, which belong to earth and the other elements, together with their attributes such as shape and so on, are designated by the term "gross" (*sthūla*); this is the first form of the elements. The second form is their own commonality (*svasāmānya*), which is expressed by the term "essential nature" (*svarūpa*): solidity is earth, moisture is water, heat is fire, mobility is air, and all-pervadingness is space.

Sound and the other qualities are the specific instances (*viśeṣa*) of this commonality; and thus it has been said: "For these things, which are endowed with a single genus, there is a differentiation consisting merely of their respective attributes."

[162,ii] Here, a substance (*dravya*) is a collection of generalities and particularities. For a collection exists in two ways: that in which the distinctness of its parts has subsided, such as "body," "tree," "herd," or "forest.

A collection that follows parts whose distinctions are conveyed by a word—such as "both gods and humans"—is designated by those two very parts themselves; for in such a collection, the gods constitute one part and the humans constitute the second part.

And this [collection] is intended to be expressed in terms of both difference and non-difference, as in "an orchard of mangoes" (*āmrāṇāṃ vanaṃ*) or "a community of brahmins" (*brāhmaṇānāṃ saṃghaḥ*), which are called "mango-orchard" (*āmravana*) and "brahmin-community" (*brāhmaṇasaṃgha*).

Furthermore, that [substance] is of two kinds: that whose parts are separately established (*yutasiddhāvayava*) and that whose parts are inseparably established (*ayutasiddhāvayava*). A collection whose parts are separately established is, for example, a forest or an assembly; a collection whose parts are inseparably established is, for example, a body, a tree, or an atom. Patañjali stated that a collection which follows the distinctions of its inseparably established parts is a substance (*dravya*); this has been described as its essential nature.

Now, what is their subtle form? It is the *tanmātra*, the cause of the elements (*bhūta*). A single part of that is the atom (*paramāṇu*), which consists of both the universal and the particular, and which follows from the distinction of inseparable parts; such a collection is [the subtle form]. In this way, all the *tanmātras* constitute this third [form]. Now, the fourth form of the elements is the *guṇas*, whose nature is manifestation, activity, and inertia, which follow the nature of their effects, and which are expressed by the term "concomitance" (*anvaya*). Now, their fifth form is "possessing purpose" (*arthavattva*); the fact that they have the purpose of experience and liberation resides in the *guṇas* themselves, and since the *guṇas* reside in the *tanmātras*, the elements, and the elemental products, everything possesses purpose. Now, through *saṃyama* upon these five elements, each having these five forms, there arises for each respective form both the perception of its true nature and mastery over it. Therein, having mastered the five essential natures of the elements, one becomes a conqueror of the elements. Through that conquest, the primary constituents of the elements become obedient to his will, like cows following after their calves.
"From that, there arises the manifestation of the powers such as *aṇiman*, the perfection of the body, and non-obstruction by its qualities. (3.45)

In this regard, *aṇimā* is the state of being minute; *laghimā* is the state of being light; *mahimā* is the state of being large. *Prāpti* is that by which one touches even the moon with the tip of a finger. *Prākāmya* is non-obstruction by desire; one emerges from and sinks into the earth as if in water. *Vaśitva* is mastery over the elements and elemental products, whereby one becomes their controller and others become subject to one's will. *Īśitṛtva* is lordship over their origin, dissolution, and arrangement. *Yatra-kāmāvasāyitva* is the power of true resolve, whereby the fundamental natures of the elements abide exactly according to one's intention. Even though capable of it, one does not effect a reversal of the nature of things; why? Because another who has previously attained the power of resolving at will already exercises such a resolve over those elements. These are the eight sovereign powers (*aiśvarya*).

The perfection of the body will be described later; it includes non-obstruction by the qualities of those elements. The earth does not obstruct the yogi’s bodily movements and so forth with its material form, for he can even pass through solid rock. Water, though moist, does not wet him; fire, though hot, does not burn him; and wind, though moving, does not carry him away. Even in space, which is by nature unobstructive, his body becomes obstructed [by will], and he becomes invisible even to perfected beings (*siddhas*).
"The perfection of the body consists of beauty, loveliness, strength, and adamantine firmness" (3.46);
that is to say, he is handsome, radiant, possessed of extraordinary strength, and has a body as firm as a diamond.
"From saṃyama on the essential nature of perception, on egoism, on the sequence, and on purposefulness, mastery over the senses [is attained].

Sound and the other objects of sense are composed of both the universal and the particular; the operation of the senses upon them is "grasping. This grasping does not take the form of apprehending the universal alone; for if that specific object were not perceived by the sense organ, how could it be subsequently determined by the mind? Furthermore, the intrinsic nature of the sense organ is the substance (*dravya*), which is the aggregate of the *sattva* of the intellect (*buddhi*)—which is luminous in nature—consisting of parts that are inseparably established as both universal and particular. The third form of these [senses] is the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), characterized by the notion of "I-ness" (*asmitā*). Of that [ego-sense], the senses are the particulars. The fourth form consists of the *guṇas*, whose nature is determination and whose characteristics are illumination, activity, and stability, of which the senses together with the ego-sense are the transformation. The fifth form is the state of being directed toward the purpose of the *puruṣa* which inheres in the *guṇas*. By practicing *saṃyama* in sequence upon these five forms of the senses, and having achieved mastery over each, mastery over the senses arises for the yogin through mastery over these five forms.
[167,i] "From that, [arise] swiftness like thought, the state of being without organs, and mastery over the primary matter (pradhāna).

The attainment of supreme speed of movement for the body is *manojava* (mind-swiftness). The state of possessing *vikaraṇa* (transformational faculties) is the acquisition of the functioning of the sense organs without a body, depending upon the desired place, time, and object. Mastery over all primary causes (*prakṛti*) and their modifications is the conquest of *pradhāna*. These three perfections (*siddhis*) are called the "Honey-like" (*madhupratīkā*), and they are attained through mastery over the five forms of the instruments (*karaṇa*).

"For one who possesses the mere discriminative discernment (*khyāti*) of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is sovereignty over all states of being and omniscience" (Yoga Sūtra 3.49).

[167,iv] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive ‘Bodhisattva,’ nor does he perceive ‘perfection of wisdom. Since he does not perceive them, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell with the thought, ‘I am practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, this is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva. Subhūti asked: “Blessed One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom become one who has set out correctly? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, here a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, while practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive form, nor does he perceive the arising of form, nor does he perceive the cessation of form. He does not perceive feeling, nor does he perceive the arising of feeling, nor does he perceive the cessation of feeling. He does not perceive perception, nor does he perceive the arising of perception, nor does he perceive the cessation of perception. He does not perceive formations, nor does he perceive the arising of formations, nor does he perceive the cessation of formations. He does not perceive consciousness, nor does he perceive the arising of consciousness, nor does he perceive the cessation of consciousness. Subhūti, since he does not perceive these, he does not apprehend them; because he does not apprehend them, he does not dwell with the thought, ‘I am practicing the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti, it is in this way that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva who practices the perfection of wisdom becomes one who has set out correctly.”

For one whose *buddhisattva* has shaken off the impurities of *rajas* and *tamas*, who abides in supreme clarity and in the highest state known as "mastery," and who is established in the form of the mere discernment of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there arises the presiding over all states of being. This means that all the *guṇas*, which consist of both the determining (*vyavasāya*) and the determined (*vya-vaseya*), present themselves to the Lord, the Knower of the Field (*kṣetrajña*), as the totality of all objects of perception. Omniscience is the knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) that has ascended without succession; it is the knowledge of all the *guṇas* in their entirety, as they exist in the form of past (*śānta*), present (*udita*), and unmanifest (*avyapadeśya*) attributes. This is the perfection called "Freedom from Sorrow" (*viśokā*), having attained which the yogi dwells as an omniscient master, his afflictions and bonds extinguished.
"From detachment even from that, upon the destruction of the seeds of defects, there is isolation. (3.50)

When it occurs to him thus: "This dharma of discriminative discernment exists for the sake of the being's destruction of afflictions and karma; yet the *sattva* (the intellect) is placed among the things to be abandoned, while the *puruṣa* is immutable, pure, and distinct from *sattva*," then, as he becomes dispassionate toward that [intellect], those seeds of affliction—which are like burnt rice seeds and incapable of germination—perish along with the mind (*manas*). When they have dissolved, the *puruṣa* no longer experiences these three types of suffering. Thus, when there is the reversion (*pratiprasava*) of these *guṇas*—which had manifested in the mind in the form of the fruition of karma and afflictions and had thereby fulfilled their purpose—there is for the *puruṣa* an absolute separation from the *guṇas*, which is *kaivalya*. At that time, the *puruṣa* is simply the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) established in its own nature.
[168,iii] "Upon being invited by those in higher realms, one should avoid attachment and pride, lest undesirable consequences follow.

There are indeed these four types of yogis: the beginner (*prāthamakalpika*), the one who has reached the stage of honey (*madhubhūmika*), the one whose light of wisdom is kindled (*prajñājyotis*), and the one who has transcended the need for cultivation (*atikrāntabhāvanīya*). Among them, the first is the practitioner in whom the light has merely begun to function; the second is the one whose wisdom bears the truth (*ṛtaṃbharaprajña*); the third is the one who has conquered the elements and the senses; and the fourth is the one who has transcended all that is to be cultivated, having performed the protective binding regarding everything already cultivated and yet to be cultivated, and having accomplished what was to be done. For the one who has transcended cultivation, the sole purpose is the dissolution of the mind (*cittapratisarga*); his wisdom on the final stages (*prāntabhūmi*) is sevenfold.

In that regard, when a brahmin realizes the stage known as Madhumatī, the resident deities, perceiving his purity of being, invite him to their realms, saying: "O, sit here! Delight yourself here! This enjoyment is desirable; this maiden is desirable; this elixir wards off old age and death; this vehicle travels through the air; these are the wish-fulfilling trees; there is the holy Mandākinī river; the perfected great ṛṣis are most favorable; the apsarases are compliant; divine hearing and sight are yours; your body is like a diamond; all this has been acquired by you, long-lived one, through your own virtues. Accept this imperishable, ageless, immortal station, beloved of the gods. Being addressed in this way, he should contemplate the faults of attachment: "By me, who was being cooked in the terrible embers of saṃsāra and wandering in the darkness of birth and death, this lamp of yoga—which destroys the cataracts of the afflictions—has somehow been obtained. Yet these winds of sense objects are its adversaries, arising from the womb of craving. Having gained this light, how could I, deceived by this mirage of sense objects, once again make myself fuel for that very same blazing fire of saṃsāra? Thinking, "Farewell to you, sense objects, which are like dreams and sought after by wretched people," he should cultivate meditative concentration (*samādhi*) with a mind thus resolved.

Without forming attachments, one should not even harbor pride, thinking, "In this way, I am worthy of being entreated even by the gods. Through such pride, one will fail to contemplate oneself as being seized by the hair by Death due to a sense of self-complacency. Consequently, heedlessness—which constantly watches for a vulnerability, requires constant effort to guard, and seizes any opening it finds—will cause the afflictions (*kleśa*) to surge forth. From that, there will again follow undesirable consequences. Thus, for one who avoids attachment and pride, the goal already cultivated will become firm, and the goal yet to be cultivated will come into manifestation.
"From *saṃyama* upon the moment (*kṣaṇa*) and its sequence (*tatkrama*), knowledge born of discrimination arises" (3.52).

Just as the atom (*paramāṇu*) is the ultimate limit of the reduction of substance, so too the moment (*kṣaṇa*) is the ultimate limit of the reduction of time; or rather, that duration of time in which a moving atom leaves its former location and reaches the subsequent location is a moment. The succession (*krama*), however, is the non-interruption of that flow. There is no real aggregate of moments and their succession; rather, aggregates such as a *muhūrta*, a day, or a night are mental constructs. Indeed, although this time is devoid of objective reality and is a mental construction following upon verbal cognition, it appears to ordinary people of worldly perception as if it were the nature of a real entity.

[171,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent. Subhūti, this is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s practice of the perfection of wisdom. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how is it that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a dharma that is either existent or non-existent? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive forms as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive eye-contact as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the feeling arisen from eye-contact as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the feeling arisen from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the earth element as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive ignorance as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the perfection of giving as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-observation, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the four foundations of mindfulness as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the four meditative concentrations as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen emptinesses, the eight liberations, the nine successive absorptions, the ten spheres of totality, the ten spheres of mastery, or the twelve links of dependent origination in forward or reverse order as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of arhatship as existent or non-existent. He does not perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as existent or non-existent; he does not perceive the state of a bodhisattva or the state of a Tathāgata as existent or non-existent. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as either existent or non-existent. Subhūti said to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive any dharma as existent or non-existent, then how does he train in the perfection of wisdom? How does he progress toward unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, a bodhisattva mahāsattva training in the perfection of wisdom does not train in form, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of form. He does not train in feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of consciousness. He does not train in the eye, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the eye. He does not train in the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the mind. He does not train in forms, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of forms. He does not train in sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of mental phenomena. He does not train in eye-consciousness, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of eye-consciousness. He does not train in ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of mind-consciousness. He does not train in eye-contact, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of eye-contact. He does not train in ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of mind-contact. He does not train in the feeling arisen from eye-contact, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the feeling arisen from eye-contact. He does not train in the feeling arisen from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the feeling arisen from mind-contact. He does not train in the earth element, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the earth element. He does not train in the water element, fire element, wind element, space element, or consciousness element, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the consciousness element. He does not train in ignorance, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of ignorance. He does not train in volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of aging-and-death. He does not train in the perfection of giving, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the perfection of giving. He does not train in the perfection of ethical discipline, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the perfection of wisdom. He does not train in the emptiness of the internal, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the emptiness of the internal. He does not train in the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of the ultimate, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of dispersion, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of self-characteristic, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of non-observation, the emptiness of essential nature, or the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the emptiness of the nature of non-essential nature. He does not train in the four foundations of mindfulness, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the four foundations of mindfulness. He does not train in the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the eightfold noble path, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the eightfold noble path. He does not train in the four meditative concentrations, nor does he train in the attainment of the cessation of the four meditative concentrations. He does not train in the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen emptinesses, the eight liberations, the nine successive absorptions, the ten spheres of totality, the ten spheres of mastery, or the twelve links of dependent orig

A *kṣaṇa* (moment) is that which falls within the objective reality and serves as the basis for succession; and succession (*krama*) consists in the immediate sequence of moments. Those yogis who know time call this "time. Two moments do not exist simultaneously, nor is there succession between two co-existent things, because such a thing is impossible. Succession is the immediate sequence of a moment arising from what precedes it. Therefore, only the single present moment exists; past and future moments do not exist. Consequently, there is no collection (*samāhāra*) of them. However, those moments that have passed or are yet to come must be explained as being endowed with transformation (*pariṇāma*). Thus, by means of that single moment, the entire world undergoes transformation. Indeed, all these phenomena (*dharmas*) are mounted upon that moment. Through *saṃyama* on both that moment and its succession, there is direct perception of them. And from that, knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*) manifests.
A specific object for that [consciousness] is proposed:
"Because difference is not delimited by genus, characteristic, or location, there is therefore a cognition of two things as equal.

When two things are similar in their location (*deśa*) and characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the difference in genus (*jāti-bheda*) is the cause of their distinctness, as in "this is a cow" and "this is a mare. When they are of the same genus and in the same location, the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) is what creates the distinction, as in "the spotted cow Kālākṣī" and "the healthy cow Svastimatī. When there are two *āmalaka* fruits, because they are similar in genus and characteristics, the difference in location is the cause of their distinctness, as in "this is the one in front" and "this is the one behind. However, when the fruit that was in front is moved to the position behind while the knower is distracted by something else, then, since they occupy the same location, the distinction "this is the former" and "this is the latter" would be impossible. And yet, there must be an unerring knowledge of reality; therefore, this was said: "From that [distinction], comprehension arises from knowledge born of discrimination (*viveka-jñāna*)."

How so? A location co-existent with a preceding *āmalaka* fruit is distinct from a location co-existent with a subsequent *āmalaka* fruit, and those two *āmalaka* fruits are distinct due to their experience of their own respective locations and moments. Furthermore, the experience of a different location and moment is the cause of their difference. By this analogy, in the case of an atom whose genus, characteristic, and location are identical, because it directly perceives the location and moment co-existent with a preceding atom, that location is not possible for a subsequent atom; thus, the subsequent atom’s experience of that location is distinct due to the difference in its co-existent moment. Consequently, for Īśvara or a yogin, there arises the cognition of the difference between the two.

Others, however, explain it thus: those which are ultimate particulars (*antyaviśeṣa*) produce the cognition of difference. Even in that case, the cause of difference consists in the distinction of spatial location, the distinction of form, obstruction, and genus. But the distinction of moments is accessible only to the intellect of yogins; therefore, Vārṣagaṇya stated that because there is an absence of distinctions in form, obstruction, and genus, there is no fundamental separateness (*mūlapṛthaktva*).
"Saving, having all things as its object, having no objects at all, and being timeless—such is the knowledge born of discrimination.

"Star-like" (*tāraka*) means that which arises from one's own intuition (*svapratibhā*), being non-instructional (*anaupadeśika*). "Universal object" (*sarvaviṣaya*) means that there is nothing whatsoever that has not become its object. "In every way" (*sarvathā*) means that it knows everything—past, future, and present—in all its modes and through all its synonyms. "Simultaneous" (*akrama*) means that it grasps everything in every way as it arises in a single moment. This is the complete knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*); a portion of this very knowledge is the "lamp of yoga," beginning from the stage of "Honeyed" (*madhumatī-bhūmi*) until its final completion.
Whether one has attained the knowledge born of discrimination or has not yet attained it—
"When there is equality of purity between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, there is isolation (*kaivalya*)."

[175,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when the perfection of wisdom is being taught, those who do not become discouraged, do not become cowed, do not tremble, do not fear, and do not fall into terror—these are the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have set out for a long time. Subhūti said: “Blessed One, how long has it been since those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have set out? The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: suppose there were a man who, having gone to the eastern direction, would travel for a hundred years, and at the end of each hundred years he would turn back toward the western direction and travel for another hundred years; and suppose he were to continue in this manner, traveling back and forth between the two directions for hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of years. Subhūti, what do you think? Would that man, by means of such a course, ever reach the end of the eastern direction or the end of the western direction? Subhūti said: “No indeed, Blessed One. That man, Blessed One, would not reach the end of the eastern direction nor the end of the western direction, even though he were to travel for such a vast number of years. The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, I tell you, I declare to you: even more difficult than that is the task performed by those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, having heard this perfection of wisdom being taught, do not become discouraged, do not become cowed, do not tremble, do not fear, and do not fall into terror. Subhūti, it is because these bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have practiced for a long time, have served many Buddhas, and have planted roots of merit under many Buddhas. Subhūti, it is because they have been taken hold of by the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, and have been sustained by the power of the Buddhas, the Blessed Ones, that these bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, when this perfection of wisdom is being taught, do not become discouraged, do not become cowed, do not tremble, do not fear, and do not fall into terror.”

When the *buddhi-sattva*—its stains of *rajas* and *tamas* having been shaken off, its task consisting merely in the cognition of the distinctness from the *puruṣa*, and the seeds of the afflictions (*kleśa*) having been burnt away—becomes as if it has attained a state of similarity in purity with the *puruṣa*, then the absence of imputed experience for the *puruṣa* is his purity. In this state, there is isolation (*kaivalya*) for one who possesses knowledge born of discrimination, whether they be a Lord (*īśvara*) or not a Lord, or anyone else. For one whose seeds of affliction have been burnt, there is no further need for knowledge. This sovereignty and knowledge born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) were introduced by way of the purification of *sattva*. But in the ultimate sense, through knowledge, non-vision (*adarśana*) ceases; when that has ceased, the subsequent afflictions do not exist. Due to the absence of afflictions, there is an absence of the ripening of karma. In this state, the *guṇas*, having fulfilled their office, no longer present themselves to the *puruṣa* as objects of perception. That is the isolation of the *puruṣa*; then the *puruṣa* becomes solitary (*kevalī*), stainless, and a light consisting solely of his own essential nature.
[175,ii] Thus ends the third chapter, the Chapter on Supernatural Powers (*vibhūtipāda*), in the *Yogaśāstra*, the *Sāṃkhyapravacana* of the venerable Patañjali, with the commentary by Vyāsa.
[Now begins] the Chapter on Isolation (*kaivalyapāda*).
"Attainments are born of birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative concentration. (4.1)

Success through birth is that which is separated from the body, such as [attaining success] through herbs in the abodes of the Asuras, or through elixirs (*rasāyana*), and so forth. Through mantras, there is the attainment of traveling through the sky, the powers of *aṇimā* and the rest. Through austerity (*tapas*), there is the fulfillment of one's intentions (*saṃkalpasiddhi*), such as being able to take any form at will and going wherever one desires; these successes born of meditative absorption (*samādhi*) have been explained.
In that regard, when the body and the sense organs have undergone transformation into another species—
"Transformation into another state occurs through the natural influx [of new elements].

The disappearance of the previous transformation and the arising of the subsequent transformation occur through the entry of new constituent parts (*avayava*). Furthermore, the fundamental natures (*prakṛti*) of the body and the sense organs sustain their respective modifications by means of replenishment, depending upon causes such as merit (*dharma*) and so forth.
"The efficient cause (*nimitta*) does not impel the primal natures (*prakṛti*); rather, it effects the removal of obstacles from them, like a farmer. (Sāṃkhyakārikā 4.3)

[177,v] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive that which arises from eye-contact as real, nor does he perceive that which arises from ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact as real. He does not perceive the element of earth as real, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the realm of desire as real, nor does he perceive the realm of form or the formless realm as real. He does not perceive conditioned phenomena as real, nor does he perceive unconditioned phenomena as real. He does not perceive the fruit of a stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of a once-returner, the fruit of a non-returner, or the fruit of an arhat as real. He does not perceive the state of a pratyekabuddha as real, nor does he perceive the state of a buddha as real. He does not perceive all-knowledge as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all modes as real. Why is this so? Subhūti, it is because form is empty of the intrinsic nature of form; feeling is empty of the intrinsic nature of feeling; perception is empty of the intrinsic nature of perception; mental formations are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental formations; and consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of consciousness. The eye is empty of the intrinsic nature of the eye; the ear is empty of the intrinsic nature of the ear; the nose is empty of the intrinsic nature of the nose; the tongue is empty of the intrinsic nature of the tongue; the body is empty of the intrinsic nature of the body; and the mind is empty of the intrinsic nature of the mind. Forms are empty of the intrinsic nature of forms; sounds are empty of the intrinsic nature of sounds; odors are empty of the intrinsic nature of odors; tastes are empty of the intrinsic nature of tastes; tangibles are empty of the intrinsic nature of tangibles; and mental phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of mental phenomena. Eye-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-consciousness; ear-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-consciousness; nose-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of nose-consciousness; tongue-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of tongue-consciousness; body-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of body-consciousness; and mind-consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-consciousness. Eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of eye-contact; ear-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of ear-contact; nose-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of nose-contact; tongue-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of tongue-contact; body-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of body-contact; and mind-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of mind-contact. That which arises from eye-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from eye-contact; that which arises from ear-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from ear-contact; that which arises from nose-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from nose-contact; that which arises from tongue-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from tongue-contact; that which arises from body-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from body-contact; and that which arises from mind-contact is empty of the intrinsic nature of that which arises from mind-contact. The element of earth is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of earth; the element of water is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of water; the element of fire is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of fire; the element of wind is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of wind; the element of space is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of space; and the element of consciousness is empty of the intrinsic nature of the element of consciousness. The realm of desire is empty of the intrinsic nature of the realm of desire; the realm of form is empty of the intrinsic nature of the realm of form; and the formless realm is empty of the intrinsic nature of the formless realm. Conditioned phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of conditioned phenomena; unconditioned phenomena are empty of the intrinsic nature of unconditioned phenomena. The fruit of a stream-enterer is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of a stream-enterer; the fruit of a once-returner is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of a once-returner; the fruit of a non-returner is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of a non-returner; and the fruit of an arhat is empty of the intrinsic nature of the fruit of an arhat. The state of a pratyekabuddha is empty of the intrinsic nature of the state of a pratyekabuddha; the state of a buddha is empty of the intrinsic nature of the state of a buddha. All-knowledge is empty of the intrinsic nature of all-knowledge; and the knowledge of all modes is empty of the intrinsic nature of the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti, it is because these dharmas are empty of their own intrinsic nature that a bodhisattva mahāsattva, practicing the perfection of wisdom, does not perceive them as real."

For merit (*dharma*) and so forth do not act as the motive force for the primary constituents (*prakṛti*); a cause is not set in motion by its effect. How then [does it function]? "But from that [merit] comes the breaking of the obstruction, like a farmer. Just as a farmer, wishing to flood another field from a field full of water, does not draw out the water with his hand—whether the [new field] be level, low, or lower—but rather breaks the barrier to the water; when that is broken, the waters themselves flood the other field—so too, merit breaks the obstructive quality of the primary constituents. When that is broken, the primary constituents themselves flood their respective transformations. Or again, just as that same farmer is not able to make the watery or earthy juices enter the roots of the grain in that very field, but rather removes the mudga-beans, gavedhuka-grass, śyāmāka-grain, and so forth from there; when those have been removed, the juices themselves enter the roots of the grain—so too, merit is the cause merely for the cessation of demerit (*adharma*), because purity and impurity are absolutely contradictory; but merit does not become the cause for the activity of the primary constituents. In this regard, Nandīśvara and others are to be cited as examples. Conversely, demerit also subverts merit. From that, there is a transformation toward impurity. In that case as well, Nahuṣa becoming a serpent and others are to be cited as examples.
But when a yogi emanates many bodies, are they then possessed of a single mind or multiple minds?
"Created minds [arise] from the mere sense of 'I-am-ness' (4.4).
Taking the mere sense of "I-am-ness" as the cause of the mind, one produces created minds; therefore, they become possessed of mind.
"The single mind is the motivator for the various activities of many.

How is it that the activity of many minds proceeds preceded by the intention of a single mind? [The Buddha] creates a single motivating mind for all those minds; from that, the differentiation of their activity arises.
Regarding this, it is said: "Therein, that which is born of meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) is without latent disposition (*anāśaya*). (4.6)

There are five kinds of transformative mind (*nirmāṇacitta*): those born of birth, herbs, mantras, austerity, and meditative absorption (*samādhi*). Among these, that very mind which is born of meditative absorption is without latent disposition (*anāśaya*); for it has no latent disposition, meaning there is no activity of passion and so forth, and thus there is no connection with merit or demerit for the yogin because his afflictions have been exhausted. However, for others, there does exist a latent disposition of karma (*karmāśaya*).
For it is said:
"The karma of the yogi is neither white nor black; for others, it is of three kinds. (4.7)

[180,iii] The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding those sentient beings suffering such torments, was moved by great compassion and resolved to deliver them from their distress. He then entered into meditative concentration and, through his supernormal power, caused the entire assembly of monks to behold him. At that moment, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, do you see this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara standing before us? “I see him, World-Honored One,” he replied. The Buddha said: “Ānanda, this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great majesty; he is able to bring deliverance to all sentient beings. If there are those who, with single-minded devotion, take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall immediately be freed from all calamities. If there are those who, during times of fire, water, sword, or poison, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall not suffer harm. If there are those who, during times of bandits or imprisonment, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall be released from their bonds. If there are those who, during times of execution, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the swords shall break and the executioners shall be unable to strike them. If there are women who, desiring a son or a daughter, invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they shall give birth to a child of noble character and virtue, as they wish. For these reasons, Ānanda, one should always take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Having spoken thus, the World-Honored One further addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there are those who, for the sake of seeking merit, wish to make offerings to the Buddhas of the ten directions, they should first offer to the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to bestow upon all sentient beings the roots of goodness of the Buddhas of the three times. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are those who wish to practice the Bodhisattva path, they should first learn from the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara has already perfected the practices of all Bodhisattvas and is able to guide and instruct all sentient beings. Thus did the Buddha speak. Having heard the Buddha’s words, the venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly were filled with joy and faithfully practiced what they had been taught. Thus ends the chapter on the Universal Gateway of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, the eighteenth. [180,iv] Chapter Nineteen: The Chapter on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, it is marvelous how the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara delivers sentient beings from such various perils. World-Honored One, how does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Akṣayamati cultivate the practice of the Bodhisattva path? The Buddha told the venerable Śāriputra: “Excellent, excellent! Śāriputra, you have asked well. Listen attentively and I will explain for you.
