This class of action is indeed fourfold: black, white-and-black, white, and neither-white-nor-black. Among these, the black belongs to the wicked; the white-and-black is that which is accomplished by external means. In that regard, the accumulation of the latent deposit of action (*karmāśaya*) occurs solely through the gate of harming or favoring others. The white belongs to those devoted to austerity (*tapas*), self-study (*svādhyāya*), and meditation (*dhyāna*); for since it depends solely on the mind, it does not require external means and does not come about by harming others. The neither-white-nor-black belongs to renunciants (*saṃnyāsins*) whose afflictions (*kleśa*) have been exhausted and who are in their final bodies. In this context, it is "white" for the yogi because of the renunciation of fruits, and "not black" because of the absence of new undertakings; however, for other beings, it is already threefold as previously described.
"Therefore, there is the manifestation only of those latent impressions (*vāsanā*) that are conducive to that specific maturation" (4.8).

"From that" means from the threefold karma. "Only those [latencies] which are conducive to its maturation" means that only those latencies (*vāsanā*) which conform to the maturation of whichever type of karma it is—those latencies that underlie the maturation of karma—are manifested. For a divine karma undergoing maturation cannot possibly be the cause for the manifestation of the latencies of hell-beings, animals, or humans; rather, only those latencies of his that are conducive to a divine state are manifested. The same analysis applies equally to the cases of hell-beings, animals, and humans.
"Even for those separated by birth, place, and time, there is immediate succession because memory and its latent impressions are of a single nature.

The fruition of a cat [experienced in a previous life] arises when it is manifested by its own manifesting agent, such as collyrium. Even if that fruition were separated by a hundred births, or by distance in space, or by a hundred eons, and were to arise again through its own manifesting agent—collyrium—it would immediately manifest by drawing upon the latent impression (*vāsanā*) conditioned by the previously experienced fruition of being a cat. Why? Because even for those [fruits] that are separated, a similar action serves as the manifesting cause and thus constitutes immediate succession. Furthermore, because memory and latent impressions are of the same nature—the impressions correspond to the experiences, they conform to the latent impressions of karma, and the memory corresponds to the impressions—memory arises from impressions separated by birth, space, and time. From memory, in turn, new impressions arise; thus, these memories and impressions are manifested by virtue of the activity of the storehouse of karma (*karmāśaya*). Therefore, even for those [fruits] that are separated, immediate succession is established because the relationship between cause and effect is never interrupted.
[182,i] "And their beginninglessness is due to the eternity of the aspiration" (4.10).

Because these latent impressions (*vāsanā*) are based on desires that are eternal, they are beginningless. This desire for self, expressed as "May I not cease to be; may I continue to exist," is observed in everyone; yet it is not inherent (*svābhāvikī*). Why? Because how could a newborn creature, who has never experienced the nature of death, feel fear of death caused by the recollection of the suffering associated with aversion? Furthermore, an inherent entity does not depend upon a cause. Therefore, this mind, permeated by beginningless latent impressions, acquires only certain impressions through the power of external objects and turns toward the experience of the *puruṣa*.

Others maintain that the mind, which contracts and expands like a lamp within a jar or a palace, has a form corresponding exactly to the dimensions of the body; and thus, both the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) and cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*) are logically established.

The Teacher [Vyāsa] maintains that the very mode of existence (*vṛtti*) of this all-pervading mind is what causes its contraction and expansion, and that this mode depends upon causal factors such as merit (*dharma*). These causal factors are of two kinds: external and internal. The external depends on instruments such as the body, consisting of praise, giving, salutation, and so forth; the internal, consisting of faith and the like, depends solely upon the mind. Thus it has been said: "These states of abiding in loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and the rest for meditators, which do not require the assistance of external instruments, bring about preeminent merit (*dharma*). Of these two, the mental is more powerful. How so? By what could knowledge and dispassion be surpassed? And who would venture to empty the Daṇḍaka forest by physical action alone, without the power of the mind, or drink up the ocean like Agastya?
"Because these are comprised of causes, fruits, bases, and objects, in their absence, those are absent. (4.11)

From *dharma* comes happiness; from *adharma*, suffering. From happiness arises passion (*rāga*); from suffering, hatred (*dveṣa*). From that [hatred] arises effort (*prayatna*), by which, through mind, speech, or body, one in motion either benefits or harms another. Therefrom again arise *dharma* and *adharma*, happiness and suffering, and passion and hatred. Thus this six-spoked wheel of saṃsāra revolves. And for this wheel, which turns at every moment, ignorance (*avidyā*) is the guide and the root of all afflictions (*kleśa*); such is its cause. As for the fruit, however, it is that which, depending upon something else, becomes present—such as *dharma* and so forth; for there is no production of what was previously non-existent. The mind, however, is the basis (*āśraya*) of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) as long as it possesses functional authority (*sādhikāra*). For when the mind has ceased its authority, latent impressions are unable to remain without a basis. Whatever object comes before it manifests whichever latent impression, that object is the objective support (*ālambana*) of that [impression]. Thus, all latent impressions are subsumed by these four: cause, fruit, basis, and objective support. In the absence of these, there is also the absence of the latent impressions that depend upon them.

There is no arising of what is non-existent, nor is there destruction of what is existent; therefore, since these latent predispositions (*vāsanā*) arise as substantial entities, how can they ever cease?
"The past and the future exist in their own nature, due to the distinction of the temporal paths of phenomena.

The future is that whose manifestation is yet to be; the past is that whose manifestation has been experienced; and the present is that which is engaged in its own activity. These three objects constitute the knowable for cognition. If these did not exist by way of their own nature (*svarūpataḥ*), this cognition would not have arisen as being devoid of an object. Therefore, the past and the future exist by way of their own nature. Furthermore, if the fruit of karma—whether conducive to experience or conducive to liberation—were about to arise and were non-existent (*nirupākhyam*), then the performance of virtuous acts for the sake of that [fruit] or with it as a motive would be illogical. A cause is capable of bringing an existing fruit into the present state, but not of producing something previously non-existent. An established cause effects a specific favor upon the effect (*naimittika*) that already exists; it does not produce what was previously non-existent.

[187,i] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of imagined characteristics (*parikalpita-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha (*tathāgatagarbha-svabhāva*). Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of imagined characteristics? It is the attachment to names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) regarding objects that have no intrinsic nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the self-nature of imagined characteristics. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the manifestation of various phenomena based on causes and conditions, devoid of the grasping of names and signs. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfected reality? It is the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is free from the duality of grasped and grasper, and is eternally quiescent. This is called the self-nature of perfected reality. What is the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha? It is the realm of the Tathāgatas, which is the locus of the three bodies (*trikāya*), the storehouse of all Buddha-qualities, and the source of the transformation-bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) that appear according to the dispositions of sentient beings. This is called the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the views of the self-nature of imagined characteristics and to realize the self-natures of dependent origination, perfected reality, and the Tathāgata-garbha. Thus it is said: The imagined is the grasping of names and signs; Dependent origination is the arising from causes and conditions; Perfected reality is the absence of duality therein; The Tathāgata-garbha is the realm of the Buddhas.

The substratum (dharmin) possesses a nature consisting of multiple attributes (dharma), and these attributes are established according to the distinction of the time-periods (adhvan). However, the past and the future do not exist substantially (dravyataḥ) in the same way that the present exists as having attained a specific manifestation. How then? The future exists by its own essential nature (svarūpa) which is yet to be manifested; the past exists by its own essential nature whose manifestation has already been experienced. Thus, the manifestation of the essential nature belongs only to the present time-period; it does not occur for the past and future time-periods. Furthermore, at the time of one time-period, the other two time-periods necessarily remain associated with the substratum. Therefore, the three time-periods do not come into being after having previously not existed.
[187,ii] "Those manifest and subtle entities have the *guṇas* as their essence. (4.13)" [187,iii]

Indeed, these phenomena (*dharma*) of the three times are manifest in nature when present, and subtle in nature when past or future, existing in six non-specific forms (*aviśeṣa*). All this is merely a particular arrangement of the *guṇas*; thus, in the ultimate sense, they have the *guṇas* as their essence. And so it is taught in the scripture:
“The supreme form of the *guṇas* does not come within the range of vision.”
But that which has come within the range of vision is utterly void, like an illusion.
But when it is asked how all the *guṇas* can be a single sound or a single sense organ, [the answer is:
"The reality of the thing is due to the unity of its transformation" (4.14).

[188,iii] The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom not perceive a self, nor perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel? The Blessed One replied: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness as real. He does not perceive the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the feeling born of the contact of the eye as real, nor does he perceive the feeling born of the contact of the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive the earth element as real, nor does he perceive the water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness elements as real. He does not perceive ignorance as real, nor does he perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death as real. He does not perceive the conditioned as real, nor does he perceive the unconditioned as real. He does not perceive the world as real, nor does he perceive the transcendence of the world as real. He does not perceive the past as real, nor does he perceive the future or the present as real. He does not perceive the stream-enterer as real, nor does he perceive the fruit of stream-entry, the once-returner, the fruit of once-returning, the non-returner, the fruit of non-returning, the arhat, the fruit of arhatship, the pratyekabuddha, or the state of a pratyekabuddha as real. He does not perceive the bodhisattva as real, nor does he perceive the perfection of giving, the perfection of morality, the perfection of patience, the perfection of vigor, the perfection of meditation, or the perfection of wisdom as real. He does not perceive the first dhyāna as real, nor does he perceive the second, third, or fourth dhyāna as real. He does not perceive the emptiness of emptiness as real, nor does he perceive the great compassion as real. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata as real, nor does he perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion as real. He does not perceive omniscience as real, nor does he perceive the knowledge of all aspects as real. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel, then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the thought of awakening? How does he train in the perfections? How does he enter into the stages? How does he purify the lineage of the buddhas? How does he fulfill the marks and signs of a great man? How does he fulfill the dharmas of a buddha? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he purify the buddha-field? How does he approach the seat of awakening? How does he defeat the hosts of Māra? How does he turn the wheel of Dharma? How does he demonstrate the passing away into parinirvāṇa? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is because a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel, that he generates the thought of awakening. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he trains in the perfections. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he enters into the stages. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he purifies the lineage of the buddhas. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he fulfills the marks and signs of a great man. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he fulfills the dharmas of a buddha. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he matures sentient beings. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he purifies the buddha-field. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he approaches the seat of awakening. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he defeats the hosts of Māra. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he turns the wheel of Dharma. It is for the sake of sentient beings who do not perceive a self, who do not perceive one who acts, who do not perceive one who causes to act, who do not perceive one who feels, and who do not perceive one who causes to feel, that he demonstrates the passing away into parinirvāṇa. Subhūti, it is in this way that a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel. Subhūti said: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive a self, nor perceive one who acts, one who causes to act, one who feels, or one who causes to feel, then, Blessed One, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? How does he practice the perfection of giving? How does he practice the perfection of morality? How does he practice the perfection of patience? How does he practice the perfection of vigor? How does he practice the perfection of meditation? How does he practice the perfection of wisdom? The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, here a bodhisattva mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom does not perceive form as real, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness as real. He does not perceive the eye as real, nor does he perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind as real. He does not perceive forms as real, nor does he perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena as real. He does not perceive eye-consciousness as real, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness,

The single transformation of the qualities (*guṇas*)—which have the natures of manifestation, activity, and stability, and which consist of grasping—is the sense organ, the ear, acting as an instrument; the single transformation of those [qualities] consisting of being grasped is the object, sound, in the form of the subtle element of sound (*śabda-tanmātra*). Of sound and the others, which are of the same genus as material form (*mūrti*), the single transformation is the earth atom, which is a constituent part of the subtle elements; and the single transformation of those [atoms] is earth, such as a cow, a tree, or a mountain. In the case of the other elements as well, one should understand that there is a commonality in the commencement of a single modification, taking up their respective functions: cohesion, heat, motility, and the providing of space.

There is no object that exists apart from consciousness; however, there is cognition that occurs without an object, as is imagined in dreams and the like. Following this line of reasoning, those who deny the intrinsic nature of things—claiming that a thing is merely a mental construction (*parikalpanā*) like an object in a dream and does not exist in ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)—are correct. How can those who, by the power of conceptual cognition which lacks the nature of valid means of knowledge (*apramāṇa*), reject the very nature of a thing that has appeared through its own majesty, and then deny that very thing, be considered credible in their speech?
And why is this unreasonable?
Because: "Since there is a difference of mind despite the identity of the object, the paths of these two are distinct" (4.15).

[191,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive that form is permanent, nor does he perceive that it is impermanent; he does not perceive that feeling is permanent, nor does he perceive that it is impermanent; he does not perceive that perception is permanent, nor does he perceive that it is impermanent; he does not perceive that formations are permanent, nor does he perceive that they are impermanent; he does not perceive that consciousness is permanent, nor does he perceive that it is impermanent. He does not perceive that form is pleasant, nor does he perceive that it is painful; he does not perceive that feeling is pleasant, nor does he perceive that it is painful; he does not perceive that perception is pleasant, nor does he perceive that it is painful; he does not perceive that formations are pleasant, nor does he perceive that they are painful; he does not perceive that consciousness is pleasant, nor does he perceive that it is painful. He does not perceive that form is self, nor does he perceive that it is non-self; he does not perceive that feeling is self, nor does he perceive that it is non-self; he does not perceive that perception is self, nor does he perceive that it is non-self; he does not perceive that formations are self, nor does he perceive that they are non-self; he does not perceive that consciousness is self, nor does he perceive that it is non-self. He does not perceive that form is empty, nor does he perceive that it is non-empty; he does not perceive that feeling is empty, nor does he perceive that it is non-empty; he does not perceive that perception is empty, nor does he perceive that it is non-empty; he does not perceive that formations are empty, nor does he perceive that they are non-empty; he does not perceive that consciousness is empty, nor does he perceive that it is non-empty. He does not perceive that form is signless, nor does he perceive that it is signless; he does not perceive that feeling is signless, nor does he perceive that it is signless; he does not perceive that perception is signless, nor does he perceive that it is signless; he does not perceive that formations are signless, nor does he perceive that they are signless; he does not perceive that consciousness is signless, nor does he perceive that it is signless. He does not perceive that form is wishless, nor does he perceive that it is wishless; he does not perceive that feeling is wishless, nor does he perceive that it is wishless; he does not perceive that perception is wishless, nor does he perceive that it is wishless; he does not perceive that formations are wishless, nor does he perceive that they are wishless; he does not perceive that consciousness is wishless, nor does he perceive that it is wishless.”

A single object that serves as the focal point for many minds is common to all; indeed, it is neither imagined by a single mind nor imagined by multiple minds, but rather exists independently. How so? Because there is a difference in the minds despite the identity of the object: depending on *dharma*, there arises a cognition of pleasure even when the object is identical; depending on *adharma*, there arises a cognition of pain from that very same object; depending on ignorance (*avidyā*), there arises a cognition of delusion from that very same object; and depending on right vision (*samyagdarśana*), there arises a cognition of equanimity from that very same object. By whom, then, has that object been imagined by the mind? Furthermore, it is not logical that the coloring of one person's mind should occur through an object imagined by the mind of another. Therefore, the paths of the object and the cognition—which are distinguished by the respective roles of the grasped (*grāhya*) and the grasper (*grahaṇa*)—are distinct. There is not even a scent of confusion between these two.

Furthermore, according to the Sāṃkhya position, the entity (*vastu*) consists of the three *guṇas* and is mobile; since it is the functioning of the *guṇas*, it becomes connected with the mental states (*citta*) in dependence upon causes such as merit (*dharma*). And for the cognition (*pratyaya*) that arises in conformity with those causes, it serves as the cause by means of this or that specific nature. Some say: "The object (*artha*) exists simultaneously with the cognition, because it is an object of experience (*bhogyatva*), like pleasure and so forth. By this line of reasoning, they deny the commonality [of the object], and thereby they negate the very nature of the entity in preceding and succeeding moments.
"And since an object does not depend on a single mind, what would become of that object at that time if it were without a means of valid cognition?

If an object were dependent solely upon the mind, then when the mind is distracted or ceased, that object would exist merely as its own form, untouched by the mind, not becoming an object for anything else, lacking any means of valid cognition (*apramāṇaka*), and its nature ungrasped by anyone; what then would it be at that time? Furthermore, from where would it arise again when it is once more connected with the mind? Moreover, those parts of it that have not yet presented themselves would simply not belong to it; thus, if there were no back, the belly could not be perceived either. Therefore, the object is independent and common to all persons, and minds are independent, operating according to each person. From the connection between these two comes perception, which constitutes the experience (*bhoga*) of the Person (*puruṣa*).
"Because the mind depends upon the coloring by that [object], the object is either known or unknown.

Objects, which are like magnets, attract and color the mind, which possesses properties similar to iron. That object by which the mind is colored is known, whereas any other object remains unknown; thus, because the nature of an entity consists of both the known and the unknown, the mind undergoes transformation.
However, for one for whom that very mind is the object—
"The fluctuations of the mind are always known by its master, the Puruṣa, because of his unchangeability.

If the Puruṣa, like the mind, were subject to transformation, then the mental modifications directed toward him would be either known or unknown—just as objects such as sound and so forth are—yet the fact that they are always known leads one to infer that his master, the Puruṣa, is unchanging. One might raise the objection: "The mind itself may manifest both its own form and the form of the object, just like fire."
"That [consciousness] does not have itself as its appearance, because it is an object of perception" (4.19).
Just as the other sense faculties and the objects such as sound are not self-manifesting because they are visible, so too should the mind be understood.

Nor is fire an appropriate illustration here; for fire does not illuminate its own nature when that nature is non-luminous, and illumination is observed only upon the conjunction of the illuminated and the illuminator. Furthermore, there can be no conjunction with respect to a mere intrinsic nature. Moreover, the meaning of the statement "the mind is self-illuminating" is that it cannot be grasped by anything else. This is just as space is established in itself and not established in another. The activity of sentient beings is seen to proceed from the awareness of the movements of their own intellects—such as "I am angry," "I am afraid," "I have passion for that," or "I have anger toward that"—and this would not be possible if one's own intellect were not apprehended.
"And at one time, there is no determination of both" (4.20).

Furthermore, it is not logical for the determination of both its own nature and the nature of another to occur in a single moment; for the proponent of momentariness maintains that what constitutes existence is itself the action, and that very same thing is the agent.
One might think: "The mind, having ceased by its own inherent nature, is grasped by a subsequent mind."
"If one thing were perceivable by another mind, there would be an infinite regress of cognitions perceiving cognitions, as well as a confusion of memories. (4.21)

Now, if consciousness were to be apprehended by another consciousness, by what would the cognition of that cognition be apprehended? That too by another, and that too by another—this leads to an infinite regress (*atiprasaṅga*). Furthermore, there would be a confusion of memories (*smṛtisaṃkara*); for as many as are the experiences of cognitions of cognitions, so many memories would result. And from that confusion, there would be an inability to determine a single memory. Thus, by those nihilists (*vaināśika*) who deny the existence of the Person (*puruṣa*) who is the witness of cognition, everything has been thrown into disorder. Yet, postulating the nature of the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*) in some way or another, they do not accord with reason. Some, having even postulated a mere "being" (*sattva*), saying, "There exists a being who, casting off these five aggregates (*skandha*), takes up others," are nevertheless terrified by that very [postulate]. Likewise, having said, "I shall practice the holy life (*brahmacarya*) in the presence of a teacher for the sake of great disenchantment with the aggregates, for dispassion, for non-arising, and for peace," they again deny the very existence of that being. But philosophical systems such as Sāṃkhya and Yoga accept, by their own terminology, the Person alone as the master and the experiencer of the mind.
How so?
"By citing [the example of] non-transference, when there is an assumption of that form, there is the self-awareness of one's own intellect (4.22).

For the power of the enjoyer (*bhoktṛśakti*) is indeed unchanging and non-transferring, yet it follows the modification of the object—which is subject to change—as if it had been transferred to it. And because it merely imitates that mental modification (*buddhivṛtti*), which has acquired the support of consciousness as its nature, the cognitive function is described as being indistinguishable from the mental modification. Thus it has been said:"
“Neither in the underworld, nor in the clefts of mountains, nor in darkness, nor in the wombs of the oceans—
there is no cave wherein the eternal Brahman is deposited, which the seers perceive as the undifferentiated activity of the intellect.”
Thus it is said.
And for this reason, the following is accepted:
"The mind, colored by the seer and the seen, has all things as its object. (4.23)

For the mind (*manas*) is colored by the object to be thought; and because it itself is an object, it is connected with the subject, the *puruṣa*, through its own function (*vṛtti*). Thus, this very consciousness (*citta*), colored by both the seer and the seen, appearing as both object and subject, having assumed the nature of both the conscious and the unconscious, though consisting of objects, appears as if it were not an object; though unconscious, it appears as if conscious—resembling a crystal gem—and is called "all-encompassing" (*sarvārtha*).

Therefore, due to this similarity between the mind and its objects, some are deluded and claim that consciousness itself is that [object]; others say, "All this is merely mind; indeed, this world consisting of cows, jars, and so forth, along with its causes, does not exist. These people are to be pitied. Why? Because they possess the seed of delusion: the notion that the mind manifests in the form of all objective appearances. In the wisdom (*prajñā*) of meditative absorption (*samādhi*), the object to be known appears as a reflection; it is distinct [from the mind] because it serves as the objective support (*ālambana*). If that object were merely mind, how could the very nature of wisdom be determined by wisdom itself? Therefore, the object that appears as a reflection within wisdom and that by which it is determined is the *puruṣa*. Thus, those who see correctly distinguish these three—the grasper, the grasping, and the grasped—as being of different kinds according to their essential nature; by them is the *puruṣa* realized.
And for what reason?—
"Though variegated by those innumerable latent predispositions, it acts for the sake of others because it functions through cooperation.

Thus, although this mind is variegated by innumerable latent impressions (*vāsanā*), it exists for the sake of another—that is, for the sake of the experience and liberation of another—and not for its own sake, because it acts through association, like a house. A mind that acts through association cannot exist for its own sake; neither the mind of pleasure nor knowledge exists for the sake of itself, but both of these exist for the sake of another. And that person who is enriched by the object consisting of experience and liberation is indeed the "other," not merely a generic "other. Whatever generic "other" a proponent of annihilationism (*vaināśika*) might cite as an essential nature, all of that would necessarily exist for the sake of another because it acts through association. But that specific "other" which is the Person (*puruṣa*) does not act through association.
"For one who perceives the distinction, there is the cessation of the cultivation of self-existence" (4.25).

Just as the existence of a seed is inferred by the sprouting of a blade of grass during the rainy season, so too, when the horripilation and shedding of tears are observed upon hearing the path to liberation, it is inferred that there exists within that person the seed of special insight (*viśeṣadarśana*), produced by karma conducive to final release (*apavargabhāgīya-karma*). For such a person, a natural contemplation of their own being (*ātmabhāvabhāvanā*) proceeds; it is because of the absence of this [contemplation] that it was said: "Apart from their innate nature, those who take pleasure in the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*) due to defects and feel aversion toward the definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*)—for them, the contemplation of their own being takes the form: 'Who was I? How was I? What is this? How is this? Who shall we become? Or how shall we become? However, for one who possesses special insight, that contemplation ceases. Why? Because this is merely the manifold transformation of the mind (*citta*); but the Person (*puruṣa*), when ignorance (*avidyā*) is absent, is pure and untouched by the qualities of the mind. Therefore, the contemplation of one's own being ceases for the virtuous person.
"At that time, the mind is inclined toward solitude and tends toward isolation. (4.26)

At that time, his mind—which had previously been inclined toward sense objects and submerged in ignorance—becomes otherwise; it becomes inclined toward isolation (*kaivalya*) and submerged in knowledge born of discrimination (*vivekaja-jñāna*).
[Yoga Sūtra 4.27:
"In the intervals between these, other thoughts arise from latent impressions (*saṃskāra*)."

[201,iv] For the mind—which is inclined toward the discernment of the conditions and flows solely as the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*—there arise other cognitions during its intervals, such as "I am," or "it is mine," or "I know," or "I do not know. Why? Because of the seeds of former latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) which are being exhausted.
"Furthermore, it has been stated regarding these that they are like the afflictions (4.28):

just as afflictions, having their seed-nature burnt, are no longer capable of sprouting, so too a prior latent impression (*pūrvasaṃskāra*), its seed-nature burnt by the fire of knowledge, does not give rise to conditions. However, the latent impressions of knowledge persist until the completion of the mind's activity; thus, they are not further considered."

"For one who is not indolent even regarding discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*), there arises through the complete manifestation of discriminative discernment the *dharmamegha* samādhi. (4.29)

When this Brahmin is not indolent even regarding discriminative discernment (*prasaṃkhyāna*) and thus does not desire anything even from that, then for one who is detached even from that, there arises only discriminative discernment in every respect. Because of the destruction of the seeds of the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), no other cognitions arise for him; at that time, his samādhi is called the Cloud of Virtue (*dharmamegha*).
"From that, there is the cessation of afflictions and karma" (Yogasūtra 4.30).

Through that attainment, the afflictions such as ignorance are scraped away together with their roots, and the latencies of wholesome and unwholesome karma are destroyed along with their very foundations. When afflictions and karma cease, the wise person becomes liberated even while living. Why? Because error is the cause of existence. Indeed, no one whose error has been exhausted is ever seen to be born anywhere by anyone.
"Then, because the knowledge that is free from all stains of obscuration is infinite, the knowable is small. (4.31) [203,ii]

For one who is liberated from all afflictions (*kleśa*) and karmic obscurations (*karmāvaraṇa*), there is infinity of knowledge (*jñāna*). The infinite essence of knowledge (*jñānasattva*), though infinite, is overcome and obscured by the darkness of obscuration; it becomes capable of apprehension only when, in certain instances, it is set in motion and opened up by passion (*rajas*). In that regard, when it has become free from all stains of obscuration, then its infinity occurs. Due to the infinity of knowledge, the knowable (*jñeya*) becomes small, like a firefly in the sky. As it is said: “The blind man pierced the jewel; the fingerless man strung it.”
He who was without a neck put it on; he who was without a tongue offered him praise.
Thus [it is said].
"Then, for those whose purpose has been accomplished, there is the completion of the sequence of transformation of the *guṇas* (4.32).

Upon the arising of that Cloud of Dharma (*dharmamegha*), the sequence of transformation of the *guṇas*—whose purpose has been fulfilled—is brought to an end; for once enjoyment and liberation have been achieved and their sequence completed, they are not able to persist even for a moment.
Now, what is this so-called "sequence"?—
"Succession (*krama*) is the counter-correlative of the moment (*kṣaṇa*), and it is to be grasped by the final limit of transformation (*pariṇāma-aparānta-nirgrāhya*).

(4.33)" [204, vi] Succession, whose nature is the immediate succession of moments, is apprehended by the end—that is, the conclusion—of transformation; for antiquity does not occur at the end of a cloth unless the succession of its moments has been experienced. Furthermore, succession is observed even in the case of eternal things.

[205,i] The Blessed One said: “Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever as real, nor does he apprehend any dharma as existing. He does not perceive form, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive forms, nor does he apprehend them; he does not perceive sounds, odors, tastes, tangibles, or mental phenomena, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the eye-consciousness, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the ear-consciousness, nose-consciousness, tongue-consciousness, body-consciousness, or mind-consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive eye-contact, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the feeling born of eye-contact, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the feeling born of ear-contact, nose-contact, tongue-contact, body-contact, or mind-contact, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the realm of form or the formless realm, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive volitional formations, consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or aging-and-death, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the perfection of giving, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the perfections of morality, patience, vigor, meditation, or wisdom, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the emptiness of the internal, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the emptiness of the external, the emptiness of the internal and external, the emptiness of emptiness, the great emptiness, the emptiness of ultimate reality, the emptiness of conditioned phenomena, the emptiness of unconditioned phenomena, the absolute emptiness, the emptiness of the beginningless and endless, the emptiness of non-dispersal, the emptiness of nature, the emptiness of all dharmas, the emptiness of own-marks, the emptiness of non-existence, the emptiness of existence, the emptiness of both existence and non-existence, the emptiness of the unobservable, or the emptiness of essential nature, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the ten powers of a Tathāgata, nor does he apprehend them; he does not perceive the four grounds of self-confidence, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, or the great compassion of a Buddha, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the state of a Stream-enterer, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the state of a Once-returner, a Non-returner, or an Arhat, nor does he apprehend them. He does not perceive the state of a Pratyekabuddha, nor does he apprehend it; he does not perceive the state of a Bodhisattva or the state of a Tathāgata, nor does he apprehend them. Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, nor does he apprehend any dharma. This is called the practice of the perfection of wisdom by a bodhisattva mahāsattva.”

This permanence is twofold: immutable permanence (*kūṭasthanityatā*) and transformative permanence (*pariṇāminityatā*). Among these, immutable permanence belongs to the *puruṣa*; transformative permanence belongs to the *guṇas*. That which remains unchanged in its essential nature (*tattva*) while undergoing transformation is permanent; both possess permanence because their essential nature is not destroyed. In this regard, the sequence of transformations among the attributes of the *guṇas*—such as the intellect (*buddhi*) and so forth—is perceivable through its final limit and thus reaches a conclusion; however, regarding the *guṇas* as the permanent substrata, such a sequence has no final limit. In the case of the eternally immutable *puruṣas*, who are established solely in their own nature and are liberated, the existence of their own nature is experienced only sequentially; therefore, even there, the sequence has no final limit. This [sequence] is merely a conceptual construction based on the verbal expression "existence" (*astikriyā*).

[205,ii] Now, regarding this saṃsāra, as it proceeds through its qualities by way of both staying and going, is there an end to its sequence or not? This is not something to be stated categorically. How so? The question "Will everyone who is born die? is one to be answered with a definitive statement: "Yes, sir. [206,i]

Now, as for the question, "Will everyone who dies be reborn?", this is to be answered by way of analysis (*vibhajya-vacanīya*). One who has realized true knowledge (*pratyudita-khyāti*), whose craving is exhausted, and who is skillful will not be reborn; others, however, will be reborn. Likewise, when asked, "Is the human birth superior or not superior?", such a question is to be answered by way of analysis: it is superior with respect to animals, but it is not so with respect to gods and sages. However, this question—"Is this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) finite or infinite?"—is one that is not to be answered categorically. For there is the exhaustion of the sequence of the cycle of existence for the skillful, but not for the other; thus, there is a fault in determining either alternative exclusively. Therefore, this question is indeed to be explained by way of analysis.
[207,i] When the sequence of the exercise of the *guṇas* has reached its conclusion, isolation (*kaivalya*) is said to occur; its essential nature is now determined—
"Isolation (*kaivalya*) is the reversion of the *guṇas* which are devoid of the purpose of the *puruṣa*, or it is the power of consciousness (*citiśakti*) established in its own nature" (4.34).

Isolation is that reversion of the *guṇas*—which consist of cause and effect and are now devoid of the purpose of the *puruṣa* since experience and liberation have been accomplished. Furthermore, being established in its own nature means that, due to the *puruṣa*'s lack of connection with the *buddhi-sattva*, there remains only the power of consciousness; its perpetual abiding in that very state is isolation.
[207,iv] Thus ends the fourth chapter, the Kaivalya-pāda, in the Yoga-śāstra, the Exposition of Sāṃkhya, the commentary by Vyāsa on the venerable Patañjali’s work. 4.
